stories.title: The Kocak and Garms family connection
stories.hook: Diane discovered her birth mother’s identity after Evelyn had died and formed a relationship with twin half-sisters.
body: Evelyn Kocak Garms was Diane’s birth mother, as the family knows and as Rachel’s own DNA bears out. Diane grew up in her adoptive family and learned who Evelyn was only after Evelyn had died. She came to know twin half-sisters, and a relationship grew between them. The family remembers that the adoption followed a difficult time in Evelyn’s life; just what happened is not known.

Evelyn Anna Kocak was born on 15 February 1921 in Jackson County, Minnesota, to a mother whose maiden name was Stinar. As Evelyn Garms she died in Nobles County on 1 August 1978. How the adoption came about, and who Diane’s birth father was, are not known for certain.

In 1930 Andrew Kocak, thirty-five and a widower, was raising his daughters Evelyn, nine, and Elizabeth, six, and his son John, two, all three born in Minnesota. Andrew’s homeland was by then called Czechoslovakia. Mary Pavalko, twenty-one, lived in the house as a servant, not as Andrew’s wife. She may well have been the Mary Adeline Pavelko of later years, though that is not certain.

Evelyn’s sister Elizabeth, later Elizabeth Lev, was the daughter of Andrew Kocak and Mary Stinar. She counted Evelyn Garms as her sister and Mary Pavelko as her stepmother. When Evelyn died, she was remembered as the daughter of Andrew and Mary Stinar Kocak. The little Evelyn of 1930 was certainly Andrew’s daughter, and everything points to her being the Evelyn Garms of later years.

Andrew Kocak and Mary Stinar had married in Jackson County on 27 November 1919. When Mary Kocak died, her husband was Andrew and her parents were Jan Stinar and Anna Breznay, and that carries Evelyn’s probable birth family back one more generation, beyond her mother.

Evelyn and Henry Garms married on 20 February 1939 at St. Joseph’s Catholic parsonage. The Lakefield Standard wrote up the wedding, and The Lake Park News reprinted the report on 2 March: Evelyn was Andrew Kocak’s eldest daughter, and Henry the second son of John Garms and his wife. Evelyn’s sister Elizabeth attended her, and Henry’s brother Leonard was best man. Evelyn wore blue crepe and carried carnations. About thirty relatives and friends shared dinner at her parents’ home, followed by an evening dance at the Hintze Log Cabin.

Evelyn’s half-brother Stephen Joseph Kocak, the son of Mary Adeline Pavelko, died in 2008 and counted Evelyn Garms among the sisters who had gone before him. Her son John Henry Garms, who died in 2023, was the son of Henry and Evelyn (Kocak). Between them they keep the two Marys apart and tie Evelyn to her Garms family.

She and Henry farmed near Round Lake until 1969 and then moved into Worthington, where both worked at the Campbell Soup plant. She died at the Worthington hospital on 1 August 1978 and was buried at Round Lake.

stories.title: The two Marys in Evelyn’s Kocak family
stories.hook: Mary Stinar was Evelyn’s probable birth mother; Mary Adeline Pavelko was the mother of her younger half-brother.
body: Elizabeth “Betty” Kocak Lev was born on the family farm in Minneota Township in 1923, the daughter of Andrew Kocak and Mary Stinar. Her mother died in 1930, and Mary Pavelko became her stepmother.

Stephen Joseph Kocak was born in the same township in 1936, the son of Andrew John Kocak Sr. and Mary Adeline Pavelko, and Evelyn Garms was his sister, who died before him. So the Kocak household was a blended one: Evelyn and Stephen shared a father but not a birth mother.

Evelyn’s own mother was a Stinar. Mary Pavelko belonged to Evelyn’s family as her stepmother, but it was Mary Stinar who bore her, and Mary Stinar was the daughter of Jan Stinar and Anna Breznay. Andrew’s parents were probably András Kocák and Anna Janasko, though the dates given for his birth do not agree. That Evelyn was the birth mother of Diane Rivers comes down through the family, not through her brothers and sisters.

Evelyn Anna was born in 1921, Elizabeth Mary in 1923 and John Andrew on 5 May 1927, all in Jackson County and all to a Stinar mother. John was very probably the brother John whom the family remembered.

Mary Stinar Kocak died in Jackson County on 2 February 1930. She was Andrew Kocak’s wife and the daughter of Jan Stinar and Anna Breznay, a name also spelled Brezney, and she had been born in 1892, or perhaps 1893.

That spring of 1930 the widowed Andrew was raising Evelyn, Elizabeth and John, and Mary Pavalko was living in the house as a servant. They were not married then. She may well have been the Mary of his later family, though that is not certain.

stories.title: The Stinar family: Illinois children and a Minnesota farm
stories.hook: Mary Stinar grew up on a Minneota farm with her probable parents, John and Annie, years before her marriage to Andrew Kocak.
body: In June 1900 John and Annie Stinar, written Stinor that year, lived on a farm in Minneota Township, Jackson County, Minnesota. John was forty-eight and Annie forty-six. They had been married twenty years, and Annie had borne ten children, eight of them still living. Seven were at home, among them John’s daughter Mary, seven, born in Minnesota in September 1892.

The children’s birthplaces trace a move between states. George, John and Andrew had been born in Illinois; Thomas, Mary, Joseph and the youngest boy, Frank, were born in Minnesota. John farmed, and the older children went to school. John and Annie came from what was then called Hungary, though from which town or village is not known.
John had come to America about 1874 and Annie about 1879. Their children’s birthplaces show where the family went afterward, though why they moved from Illinois to Minnesota is not known.

Five years later John, Anna, George, John Jr., Andrew, Thomas, Mary and Joe were still together in Minneota. John was farming and Mary was thirteen. This time the parents gave their homeland as Austria, another name of the time for the lands they had left.

By April 1910 John Stinar Sr. and his wife Annie had five children still at home in Minneota: George H., twenty-six, and Andrew R., twenty-two, born in Illinois, and Thomas G., nineteen, Mary E., seventeen, and Joseph R., fifteen, born in Minnesota. It was the same family, ten years on.
Andrew, the Illinois-born son, was very probably the Andrew Stinar born on 15 April 1888 who died in Martin County on 7 July 1964, the son of a mother born a Brezney. If so, he was Mary’s brother.

On 27 November 1919 Mary Stinar married Andrew Kocak. She died on 2 February 1930, Andrew’s wife and the daughter of Jan Stinar and Anna Breznay, who were, it seems, the John and Annie of the Minneota farm.

By 1930 George Stinar, forty-six and Illinois-born, was farming in nearby Hunter Township with his wife Marie and their children, among them Grace M., fifteen. Two households along lived John J. Stinar, forty-three, also born in Illinois. George was the right age to be the son George of 1910, and John the younger John of 1900 and 1905, and living side by side they were very probably those two brothers, though that is not certain.

In 1940 an eighty-three-year-old widow, Anna Stinar, was living on Fifth Street in Lakefield with her granddaughter Grace, twenty-five; the two had shared the house since at least 1935. Grace’s parents were George Stinar and Marie, or Mary, Sable, so this Anna was very probably the Annie of the Minneota farm, living with her son George’s daughter.

Ages in the family were never quite fixed. Mary was born in September 1892, or perhaps in 1893. Annie was forty-six in 1900, forty-five in 1905, fifty-three in 1910 and, it seems, eighty-three in 1940, and John’s age in 1910, fifty-six, does not square with his age in 1900 either. Much of this stays probable while Mary’s original death certificate is unexamined. Who Jan and Anna’s own parents were, and the villages they came from, are still unknown.

Three more of Mary’s brothers very probably died in Jackson County. A Thomas Stinar died there on 13 December 1918, most likely the Thomas G. who was nineteen in 1910, though his age at death is not known. Joseph Robert Stinar, born on 2 April 1895, died in Jackson County in 1957, and John Stinar, born on 6 April 1886, died there in 1961. Both were sons of a mother born a Breznay, or Bresznay, like Mary herself, and they fit the Joseph R. and John of the Minneota household.

stories.title: John Garms and the Sioux Valley connection
stories.hook: Evelyn Kocak Garms’s son John grew up in Sioux Valley, worked for years in construction and, once retired, kept helping the township with its roads.
body: John Henry Garms was born on 23 May 1943 and grew up in Sioux Valley, Minnesota, the son of Henry and Evelyn (Kocak) Garms, both of whom died before him.

John spent years working for KLK Construction. After retiring in 2010, he continued helping Sioux Valley Township and neighbors with roads and backhoe work. He also rebuilt tractors and remodeled homes.

John died on 30 July 2023, at eighty. Through his mother he was a younger half-brother of Diane Rivers, the daughter born to Evelyn in 1939 and raised by the Riverses of Rollingstone; who Diane’s father was is still not certain.

stories.title: Twenty years and countless jumps
stories.hook: Bob Johnson left the Oklahoma farm country, became a paratrooper, served in Vietnam and twice in Korea, and retired a Warrant Officer 3.
body: Bob Johnson spent his childhood in southeastern Oklahoma. In 1950 he was twelve and living near Hunter in Choctaw County, on the road east of Sunkist. His father Joe farmed, and the household included Joe’s wife Opal, her son Don and two young daughters. Bob’s mother, Nettie, had remarried and lived elsewhere. Opal was Nettie’s younger sister, making her both Bob’s aunt and his stepmother.

Bobby Joe Johnson was born at Buckhorn, Oklahoma, on 17 July 1937. As a young man he went to Texas, graduating from Decatur High School in 1957 and attending Decatur Baptist College before entering the Army. In later years his schooling was sometimes remembered as having been at Savoy. During his youth he met Marjorie Bell at a skating rink. They married on 21 December 1961.

Bob entered the Army in February 1958 and completed basic training at Fort Ord, California. By August he had earned his parachutist wings at the 82nd Airborne Division Jump School at Fort Bragg, North Carolina. The course included five training jumps. Within months, the Buckhorn boy had gone from basic training on the Pacific coast to an airborne unit in North Carolina. Jump school at Fort Bragg was the gate to the Army’s airborne divisions, and the 82nd Airborne, headquartered there, was a Strategic Army Corps unit, which the Army described as ready to deploy anywhere on short notice. The Hugo Daily News carried the news on 31 August 1958, in one of the Army’s own hometown releases mailed from Fort Bragg to the papers in a soldier’s home county. His father, Joel G. Johnson, was then on the Boehler Route near Boswell, and his mother was Mrs. Nettie B. McCarter of Route 2, Sherman.

By January 1961 he was a Specialist Four serving as a supply clerk in the Mortar Battery of the 504th Infantry, 82nd Airborne Division. He had already been stationed in Germany and was again based at Fort Bragg. That month he marched with the 504th in President John F. Kennedy’s inaugural parade in Washington, as the Durant Daily Democrat reported on 29 January 1961. By then his mother was Mrs. Nettie B. Tillery of Sadler, Texas. She had been Nettie Tyson, and the household she grew up in is told in the story of the two Tyson sisters; she died on 6 February 1980 and is buried at Sunnyside Cemetery in Savoy, Fannin County, Texas, her last residence. His later service included one tour in Vietnam and two in Korea, though just when is not known. Army life also shaped the early years of his marriage and the childhoods of his three children.

After "twenty years and countless jumps," he retired as a Warrant Officer 3 and returned to Oklahoma. A warrant officer is a technical specialist, usually promoted from the enlisted ranks after years of experience, a long way from the Buckhorn farm boy who left for the Army. In retirement he read military biographies, watched westerns, and kept his yard and vehicles immaculate. His family remembered the uniform of civilian life: button-up shirts rolled to the elbows, starched jeans, cowboy boots and one of his many Airborne hats. A daily request to Margie was whether they could go and get the grandkids.

Bob and Margie raised Joey, David and Leatha. They lost David in a highway crash in October 1988, when he was twenty-four. Bob died on 28 September 2024, aged eighty-seven, and was buried at Restland Cemetery in Boswell. His father Joe, a World War II veteran, and his son David are also buried there. After an Army career that had taken him far from home, Bob’s life ended in the southeastern Oklahoma community he loved.

stories.title: Forty years of helping people breathe
stories.hook: Margie Bell met Bob Johnson at a Texas skating rink, followed his Army career for twenty years, then spent four decades at the bedside of patients who could not catch their breath.
body: Marjorie Ann Bell grew up in a Grayson County, Texas, farm family with two sisters, Sylvia “Sue” and June, and a brother, Glenn “Sonny.” Born on 16 March 1943 to Wayne and Melba Bell, she was seven in 1950, when the family was together on the farm. Basketball and skating were among her favorite pastimes. At a skating rink in her teens, she met Bobby Johnson, the young Oklahoman she would marry.
At school Margie was more than a student. She was named “Best All-Round,” alongside Johnny Godsey, and “Most Athletic”: two glimpses of the girl who would later return to train in health care.

Margie graduated from S&S Consolidated High School in 1961 and began studying nursing in college. On 21 December that year she married Bob and paused her studies to join him during his Army career. They raised three children, Joey, David and Leatha, while military assignments took the family across the United States and overseas. David was born in Christian County, Kentucky, in 1964. With each move, Margie made another home for the family.

She later returned to her education and qualified as a respiratory therapist. Her career lasted forty years, and she also worked as an emergency medical technician. The nursing student who had interrupted college became a health professional with decades of practical experience caring for patients. Her family remembered the smile she brought to that work.

After Bob retired from the Army, they settled in southeastern Oklahoma. Cooking was one of the ways Margie cared for her family. She worked without a cookbook, making homemade ice cream, German chocolate cake, fried chicken and pot roast that became regular family requests. Visitors went home with leftovers. Her children and, later, grandchildren knew her table as a place where they would be fed.

Her attention extended to the flower beds. As she watered, she would say the flowers needed “a good drink.” Church and hymn singing were part of her life, and a piece of Extra gum was a familiar small offering to the people around her. These everyday details belong alongside the moves, the children and the long healthcare career in the family’s memory of Margie.

The family lost David in an October 1988 highway crash, when he was twenty-four. Margie and Bob remained married for sixty-two years, until his death in September 2024. She died at Calera, Oklahoma, on 12 February 2025, aged eighty-one. Her memorial service was held at First Baptist Church in Boswell on 17 February.

stories.title: David Glenn Johnson, 1964–1988
stories.hook: An Army childhood, school sports in Boswell and a life remembered by the Johnson family.
body: David Glenn Johnson was born on 8 July 1964 in Christian County, Kentucky, the county that holds Fort Campbell, while his father Bob was a career paratrooper. He was the middle child between Joey and Leatha. He grew up in the Army's moves and then in Boswell.

In the family’s photographs David is a schoolboy in his portraits, a basketball player wearing number 21 and a batter at the plate. They show the boy and young man he was, and not only the way he died.

At about 7:35 on the evening of Wednesday, 19 October 1988, an Oklahoma Highway Patrol lieutenant was driving east on Highway 3, seven miles east of Atoka, when he clocked an oncoming 1980 Chevrolet pickup at 96 miles an hour. By the time he turned around the driver had lost control on a curve. The pickup rolled at least five times and came to rest on its side beside a fence line. The rear bumper seemed to have caught a tree, spinning the truck and tearing the tires off the rims. Both men inside had been thrown out: the driver, twenty-one, of Bennington, and his passenger, David Johnson of Boswell.

The Lane First Responders and two ambulances took them to Atoka Memorial Hospital. David was moved on to Texoma Medical Center in Denison, Texas, where he died at about 3 a.m. on Thursday, 20 October, of head and internal injuries. He was twenty-four. The trooper said alcohol was involved and that neither man wore a seat belt. The driver was charged with manslaughter on Friday.

David was buried at Restland Cemetery in Boswell, where his grandfather Joe Johnson had been buried in 1972. His parents, Bob and Margie, and his brother and sister survived him. When Bob died in 2024, thirty-six years later, David remained among the family members remembered before him.

stories.title: Joe Johnson of the Boehler route
stories.hook: A Soper-born stockman who built airfields in World War II and married two Tyson sisters, one after the other.
body: On 16 October 1940, a few weeks before the first peacetime draft numbers were drawn, Joel Gilbert Johnson filled out his registration card at Boehler, Oklahoma. He was thirty-two and self-employed, five feet eight and 180 pounds, with a ruddy complexion, black hair and brown eyes. As the person who would always know where to find him, he named his father, Joel.

Everyone called him Joe. He had been born at Soper in Choctaw County on 24 July 1908, the year after Oklahoma became a state, to Joel A. Johnson and Winnie Bozarth. Soper itself was barely six. It had sprung up in 1902 when the Arkansas and Choctaw Railway ran a line through southern Choctaw County, and it was named for the railroad’s attorney. Joe grew up in the cotton, corn and cattle economy of that railroad country, and by 1930, at twenty-one, he was living at home in Boswell, where his father bought stock for a living.

Joe married Nettie Beatrice Tyson, and their son Bobby was born in 1937. In April 1940 Nettie, twenty-six, and the little boy, written down as “Bobbin J.,” two, were at her father Albert Tyson’s rented farm at Oakes, while Joe was at Boehler with his own father. The marriage did not last, and Nettie later married Bob Tillery. By 1950 Joe was farming on the road east of Sunkist, near Hunter, and his wife was Opal, Nettie’s younger sister, whose first husband had been a Wilson. Bob lived with them. The two sisters have a story of their own.

The war interrupted. Joe enlisted on 25 May 1942, at thirty-three, and served until 21 October 1945 as a Technician Fifth Grade in the 872nd Engineer Aviation Battalion. Engineer aviation battalions were built to build airfields: each was organized to put in an advanced airdrome on its own, with runways, taxiways and the roads and buildings around them. The Army fielded 157 of them, and by war’s end aviation engineers had built or improved more than a thousand airfields around the world.

The 872nd was one of a handful of airborne engineer aviation battalions, equipped with small machines that could be flown in by transport plane. In 1943 it and the 871st were flown up the Markham Valley of New Guinea to build the airfield at Gusap, with its fighter runway and steel-plank surfacing finished by the end of that year, and the 872nd served later in the Philippines. By the Army Air Forces’ own account, the airborne battalions were mostly kept on routine rear-area work and felt neglected. Where Joe himself served with the battalion is not known.

Joe came home to the Boehler route and to work with cattle. He belonged to the American Legion at Boswell and was remembered as a former stockman. He died early on 25 November 1972, aged sixty-four, after an apparent heart attack. His funeral was held at the Church of Christ in Boswell, with burial at Restland Cemetery, and his military headstone remembers his service in the 872nd Engineer Aviation Battalion. His son Bob was then in the middle of his own Army career.

stories.title: Two sisters under one roof in 1940
stories.hook: In April 1940 Nettie and Opal Tyson, both young mothers, were back at their father’s farm at Oakes. Ten years later Opal was married to Nettie’s former husband.
body: That April Albert Tyson’s rented farm at Oakes, in Choctaw County, held a full house. Albert was sixty-five, born in Texas, schooled through the third grade, and farming on his own account. With him were his wife Elizabeth, fifty-nine, and their son Marion, seventeen. Also in the house were two grown daughters and their babies: Nettie Johnson, twenty-six, with her two-year-old son, written down that spring as “Bobbin J. Johnson”; and Opal Wilson, twenty-one, with an infant son, Don.

The county was cotton, corn and hay country in the Depression years. Two married daughters and two grandchildren back under the parents' roof was not unusual. Nettie's husband Joe Johnson was not in the house; that October he was at Boehler with his own father. Opal had taken out a marriage license in July 1938, at eighteen: "Seidel Wilson to Opal Tyson, Boswell," a line that ran that month among the Boswell licenses in both the Paris News and the Southeast Oklahoman. When the wedding itself took place is not known.

A decade later the household had rearranged itself. In 1950 Joe Johnson was farming on the road east of Sunkist, near Hunter, with Opal as his wife. In the house were Bob, twelve, Opal’s son Don, ten, Joe’s stepson, and two little daughters. On 3 December 1968, in Sevier County, Arkansas, Joel Gilbert Johnson, sixty, married Opal Wilson, “the former Opal Tyson.” Nettie, meanwhile, married Bob Tillery, and their son Y. Q. Tillery, born at Boswell in 1942, became Bob’s half-brother.

Nettie was Bob’s mother; Opal was his aunt and later his stepmother, though just when she and Joe first made a home together is not known, and the two sisters are easy to confuse. Nettie was Mrs. Nettie B. McCarter of Sherman in 1958 and Mrs. Nettie B. Tillery of Sadler in 1961. She died on 6 February 1980 and is buried at Sunnyside Cemetery in Savoy, Texas. Bob’s wider family included his half-brother Y. Q. Tillery, his stepbrother Don Wilson and his sisters Kay and Sue, but Opal was never his birth mother.

stories.title: Wayne and Melba Bell’s Grayson County family
stories.hook: Wayne Bell and Melba Williams married in 1937 and raised the Texas farm family in which Margie grew up.
body: Wayne Douglas Bell and Melba Nena Williams were married at Van Alstyne, Texas, on 18 September 1937. He was twenty-three, born at Anna in Collin County on 18 April 1914, the son of Charles H. Bell and Mary Alice Baker. She was nineteen, born at Van Alstyne on 13 March 1918, the daughter of Cleave and Willie (Parker) Williams. Both had grown up within a few miles of Mantua, the seminary town that had died when the railroad missed it in 1872, and of the two railroad towns that replaced it.

They married in the Depression, when farming in the Blackland country was shrinking. Collin County lost more than 1,200 farms between 1930 and 1940, and Grayson County nearly 900. In 1940 the Bells were renters in Grayson County, with their first baby, a daughter. Wayne was twenty-six, five feet ten, 175 pounds, with brown hair and gray eyes; when he registered for the draft that October he was working for Kimble Farms Inc.

By 1950 the family had grown to four children: Sue, eleven; Margie, seven, Rachel’s grandmother; Glenn, four; and Norma June, two, the youngest two known in the family as Glenn “Sonny” and June. In 1954 the Bells were on Route 1 near Collinsville. On 9 April Melba gave birth prematurely at St. Vincent’s Hospital in Sherman to a son. He lived seven hours. Dr. H. L. Brown gave the cause of death as pulmonary edema due to premature birth, and Wayne himself gave the particulars for the certificate. The baby was buried the next day in West Hill Cemetery, Sherman. Margie was eleven.

Wayne came from a large family. When one of his sisters died in 1968, four sisters and four brothers were still living: Ora Bell Russell, Mrs. J. R. Chapman, Mrs. Cecil Field and Mrs. S. W. Turner, and Charlie of Van Alstyne, Wayne of Denison, Jack of Galesburg, Illinois, and Hardy of Anna.

Melba belonged to Cherry Mound Baptist Church. She died at home in Denison on 22 September 1981, aged sixty-three, and was buried at Cedarlawn Memorial Park in Sherman. Wayne lived until 22 July 1991. Their daughter Margie carried the Bell family into another chapter: she married Bob Johnson in 1961, raised three children through Army moves and eventually settled in southeastern Oklahoma.

stories.title: Sixty years of buying cattle in Choctaw County
stories.hook: Born in Milam County, Texas, in 1875, Joel Anderson Johnson came to Choctaw County around 1900 and was still called a rancher when he died in 1961.
body: In 1930 Joel Johnson of Boswell, Oklahoma, was a stock buyer, working for a cattle compress. He was fifty-five. In a county where the land ran to cattle, hay and cotton, a stock buyer was the man who bought animals from farmers and sold them on, and the work depended on knowing every farm, fence and creditor for miles around. He owned his house. His son Joel Gilbert, twenty-one, and a granddaughter, Lila Smith, lived with him and his wife Winnie.

Joel was very probably the son of George W. Johnson and his wife, M. Rebecca. In 1880, in Lee County, Texas, a five-year-old Joel A. was living in their house, and by 1900 George and Rebecca were in the Choctaw Nation with children named Carl, Sallie and Arthur, the names of three of the brothers and sisters who survived Joel. George was twenty-nine in 1880 and born in Mississippi, or fifty-three in 1900 and born in Arkansas. Which is right, what Rebecca’s maiden name was, and who George’s parents were are not yet known for certain.

Two of Joel’s sisters were very probably Sallie Mae Johnson, born on 9 May 1890, and Nannie Lou Johnson, born on 9 May 1883, both in Lee County and both daughters of George Washington Johnson and Marjorie, or Margerie, Rebecca Fails. Sallie was still at home in 1900. If they were his sisters, Joel’s mother was born a Fails, though that is not quite certain.

He had been born on 2 April 1875 in Milam County, Texas, cotton and ranch country east of Austin, where most of the settlers had come from the South. By 1910 his father was said to have been born in Arkansas and his mother in Mississippi. In 1896 he married Winnie Bozarth in Texas. A few years later the couple crossed the Red River into the Choctaw Nation, and he lived in the community sixty years, which puts the move at about 1900, though his children born through about 1904 were born in Texas, so it may have come a few years later. Soper and Boswell had both started in 1902, the year the Arkansas and Choctaw Railway came through, so the family arrived just as the towns did.

By 1910, three years after statehood, the Johnsons were in Oakes township with five children: Aletha, twelve; Porter, nine; George, six; Willie, four; and Joel, one, the future Joe who would father Bob. The county then raised mainly cotton. By 1930 it had diversified into corn, oats, prairie hay and peanuts, which suited a man who dealt in stock. In 1940 Joel and Winnie were farming on the road to Sunkist in Hunter township, and in October of that year their son Joe named him on a draft card as the person who would always know where to find him.

Joel died on a Wednesday night in March 1961 at Memorial Hospital in Hugo. He was eighty-five. He was a retired farmer and rancher, a resident of the community for sixty years and a member of the Church of Christ. He was buried at Restland Cemetery. Winnie survived him, along with sons George F. Johnson of Soper and Joe G. Johnson of Boswell, and their daughter Audrey, Mrs. Riley King, of Sterling City, Texas. His sisters were Penny Cole, Nannie Harrison and Sallie Smith; his brothers were Carl and Arthur Johnson. There were also six grandchildren.

stories.title: A reception for 350 on the Rivers lawn
stories.hook: On a July morning in 1958 an eighteen-year-old from a Luxembourger village married a Winona carpenter's son, and half of Rollingstone ended up on her father's lawn.
body: The Saturday began early. At 9:30 on the morning of 26 July 1958, Diane Rivers, eighteen, walked up the aisle of Holy Trinity Catholic Church in Rollingstone, Minnesota, to marry David Nelton, who had turned twenty a week earlier. The Rev. George Moudry performed the double-ring ceremony and celebrated the nuptial Mass, and the altars were banked with pink and white gladioli and lighted candles. Her father, Edward, gave her away.

Her dress was Chantilly lace and tulle over bridal satin, with a lace bodice, long sleeves, a sabrina neckline, a full floor-length skirt, and a veil of silk illusion falling from a lace cap. She carried a cascade of white roses and a double orchid. The pearl necklace and bracelet were David's gift.

Diane’s sister Mary Lynn was maid of honor. Angela Rivers played the organ, Uncle Paul Rivers ushered and cousins served the Mass. Douglas Trainor of Winona was David’s best man, and his sister Sandra was a bridesmaid. The ceremony brought the family into Holy Trinity’s limestone church, built in 1869 with parishioners supplying labor and money and enlarged in 1893. It was a familiar center of life for the Rivers and Frisch families.

After a wedding dinner in the Flamingo Room of the Hotel Winona, a reception for 350 guests was held on the lawn of Edward and Viola Rivers’s home. Edward sold insurance in Rollingstone, where Viola had lived throughout their marriage. The couple’s families had deep local roots: earlier Rivers generations had run the post office and carried rural mail, while Viola’s Frisch relatives farmed at Oak Ridge.

The two families came from different sides of the same county. The Riverses and Frisches were Luxembourg Catholics who had settled the hills west of Winona in the 1850s and 1860s. The Neltons were Germans in town: George Nelton, David's grandfather, was a Winona house carpenter who became a contractor, and David himself was a Winona Senior High graduate who had spent time at Winona State College and now worked for his father, Arthur, a carpenter. Diane had finished Holy Trinity High School and Winona Secretarial School. Winona was a lumber, river and railroad city whose population had long been a mix of German, Polish and Yankee families, and weddings like this one stitched the town to the villages above it.

After a trip to the Wisconsin Dells, Diane and David made their home in Minnesota City, where his parents lived. They later moved to Houston, Minnesota, and then rural Holmen, Wisconsin. Five children were born during their marriage. Their wedding photograph preserves the beginning of that family, gathered at the church and home that had anchored Diane’s childhood.

stories.title: David Nelton, carpenter’s son and father of five
stories.hook: From Winona and Minnesota City to the La Crosse YMCA, David’s life followed the Mississippi valley.
body: David John Nelton had been born in Winona on 19 July 1938, the son of Arthur and Helen (Canfield) Nelton. In 1940 the family was renting on Lake Park Boulevard in Winona; by 1950 they were in Minnesota City, where his father worked as a carpenter in building construction. He graduated from Winona Senior High, worked for his father the carpenter, and in 1958 married Diane Rivers at Rollingstone.

The couple lived in Minnesota City and then Houston, Minnesota, before crossing the Mississippi to rural Holmen, Wisconsin, about 1971. They had five children. David had become assistant superintendent of maintenance at the La Crosse YMCA.

Before the YMCA, David very probably taught school. A David Nelton was on the faculty of Holmen High School between 1969 and 1973, the years Rachel’s grandfather was moving his family to Holmen, and the family remembers him as an English teacher. In 1969 he was “David Nelton, B.S., Physics; B.A., English, Winona State College: English,” a young teacher in a dark suit and narrow tie. By 1971 he was teaching general science and English, coaching debate and advising the sophomore class. In 1972 he again taught English and general science, and in 1973 he taught English and advised the chess league and the junior class. Over those four years the clean-shaven teacher of 1969 grew the full beard he wears in every later picture.

David’s working life began in the family building trade. His father Arthur and grandfather George were both carpenters, and before his 1958 marriage he worked for Arthur. His later maintenance role at the YMCA placed him in another practical occupation, caring for a building used by the wider community.

At 2:44 a.m. on Saturday 12 February 1977, David Nelton was driving north on Highway 53 near the George Street intersection in La Crosse, Wisconsin, when his car and a southbound pickup truck collided head-on in the south lane. He was taken to Lutheran Hospital and died there at 3:13. His death and five others that weekend brought Wisconsin's 1977 traffic toll to eighty.

His funeral was at St. Paul's Catholic Church in Minnesota City, with a Rosary at Fawcett Funeral Home in Winona the night before. The Rev. Joseph C. Frisch officiated; the priest shared the surname of Diane’s mother’s family, though whether he was kin is not known. The ground was frozen, so burial at Oakwood Cemetery, Minnesota City, waited until spring. His pallbearers were Richard Hohensee, Wayne Valentine, Charles Neuman, John Brown, Hollis Donehower and Robert Rolbiecki.

David was thirty-eight. His parents Arthur and Helen survived him, as did Diane and their five children. Arthur lived until 1984 and Helen until 1982. David’s grave at Oakwood Cemetery in Minnesota City places him back in the community where he had grown up and begun married life.

stories.title: Diane Rivers Nelton: family and working life
stories.hook: Raised in Rollingstone, Diane made homes in Minnesota and Wisconsin, raised five children and worked in La Crosse.
body: Diane Mary Rivers was born in St. Paul on 10 August 1939 and grew up at Rollingstone with her adoptive parents, Edward and Viola (Frisch) Rivers. Edward sold insurance. She graduated from Holy Trinity High School and Winona Secretarial School. On 26 July 1958, aged eighteen, she married David Nelton at Holy Trinity Catholic Church. They began married life in Minnesota City and later lived in Houston, Minnesota, and rural Holmen, Wisconsin.

Diane and David had five children. Alongside family life, she worked in La Crosse. After E.T.C. Inc. dismissed her in January 1975, she filed a sex-discrimination complaint with Wisconsin’s labor department. By December 1976, as the La Crosse paper reported, the complaint had been dismissed after the hearing examiner found no evidence that the dismissal was based on sex.
Her mother Viola died in August 1975. In February 1977 David died after a head-on collision in La Crosse, leaving Diane widowed at thirty-seven.

Her father, Edward, died in January 1980. On 13 August 1983 Diane married Charles Antony in La Crosse and they lived at Bangor. She worked at Hillview Nursing Home until December 1986. Diane M. Antony died of cancer at St. Francis Medical Center on Friday 27 March 1987, at forty-seven, and after a funeral at St. Peter's Catholic Church in Middle Ridge she was buried in St. Mary's Catholic Cemetery at Bangor.

Diane’s family remained connected to the Rollingstone generations before her. Her mother Viola had been only sixteen months old when her own mother, Maggie Frisch, died in 1906. Diane’s five children belonged to that continuing Rivers and Frisch family as well as to the Nelton and Canfield branches along the Mississippi.

Diane’s birth mother was Evelyn Kocak Garms, as the family knows, and in later life Diane came to know twin half-sisters. Her birth father is unknown, in the sense that no one can say for certain who he was. The Rivers and Frisch generations were the family who raised her; the Kocaks were the family she was born into.

Even so, Diane's birth father was probably Anton "Tom" Klemenčić, known in Minnesota as Tom Klensky, a Croatian-born farmhand who in 1938 worked on a farm a few households from the Kocaks in Minneota Township. His story follows his life from the hamlet of Jarnevići in Croatia to Lakefield and Omaha.

stories.title: Arthur Nelton, carpenter and fireman
stories.hook: Arthur Nelton framed houses around Winona through the Depression and after, sat on the Minnesota City council, fought fires as a volunteer, and outlived his only son.
body: Arthur Nelton was a carpenter in a family of carpenters. In 1940 he and Helen rented a home on Lake Park Boulevard in Winona, with their small son David. Arthur was thirty, had a year of college behind him and earned $1,800 a year. His father George was a local contractor, and Arthur and his brother Irwin worked in the family firm.

Arthur R. Nelton had been born in Winona on 27 October 1909, one of four children of George Nelton and Anna Brose, both of German background, and his father was already a house carpenter working his way toward a contracting firm. His mother died in April 1928, when he was eighteen. When George later organized his own firm, his sons Arthur and Irwin joined him in it.

On 15 August 1934, with the building trades still near their lowest point, he married Helen Canfield in Winona. She had been born on 9 November 1910 at Kellogg, in Wabasha County, to James and Nel (Heffernan) Canfield. Her father died at Wabasha on 19 June 1912, when she was nineteen months old. After the wedding she kept house in Minnesota City for most of her life and belonged to St. Paul's Catholic Church there.

By 1950 Arthur and Helen lived in Minnesota City with David and their daughter Sandra. Arthur continued as a self-employed building carpenter in the Winona area until retiring in 1979. He belonged to Carpenters Union Local 307, served on the Minnesota City council and volunteered with the local fire department. His work and public service both kept him closely involved in the community. David worked for him before marrying Diane Rivers in 1958.

Helen died at home on 30 November 1982, aged seventy-two, and her grandsons carried her coffin. Two years later, on 7 October 1984, Arthur died at Lutheran Hospital in La Crosse, the same hospital where his son David had died in 1977. He was seventy-four. Grandsons were his pallbearers too. He had spent his working life putting up other families' houses; in the last seven years of his life he buried his only son and then his wife.

stories.title: George Nelton built Winona
stories.hook: George Nelton framed Winona houses for four decades, went south to the Florida boom for two winters, and was working until three months before he died.
body: George Nelton "built many of the homes in the city and some of the early stores, and also remodeled some of the Winona store fronts." He had gone on working until 1 August 1952; one of the last houses he finished was the Arthur Tarras home in Glen Mary. Three months later, on 12 November, he died at Winona General Hospital at seventy after a long illness.

George John Nelton was born on 17 January 1882 to German-born George Nelton and Eda Zenk, in Winona, or perhaps at Minneiska, Minnesota, which is where he himself said he was born when he registered for the draft in 1942. Winona remained his home through much of his life, although contracting work sometimes took him elsewhere. The river city’s houses, businesses and changing storefronts became the setting for his long building career.

In 1910 he was at 617 West King Street, twenty-eight years old, a house carpenter renting with his wife Anna (Brose) and four small children: Myrtle, Irwin, Edward and the baby, Arthur, who was Rachel's great-grandfather. His father is said to have died the year after, on 19 October 1911. George worked as a carpenter, then for the contracting firm of Hanson & Nelton, and finally organized a firm of his own, in which his sons Arthur and Irwin worked.

In the winters of 1924 and 1925 he went to Florida and took contracting work there. Those were the peak years of the Florida land boom, when Northern money and Northern builders poured into Miami and the new planned towns around it, and when the shortage of building supplies grew so bad that the railroads put an embargo on freight in October 1925. Within a year the boom was over, and the 1926 Miami hurricane finished it. A Winona contractor went south twice and came home.

Anna died in April 1928, when Arthur was eighteen. In 1930 George married Christine Walstad, a Norwegian immigrant who had come to America in 1904, and the second marriage brought three stepsons, three stepdaughters and nine step-grandchildren into the family. He was a member of the Eagles Club and of the Winona Contractors Association, and "an enthusiastic fisherman."

George was buried at Woodlawn Cemetery. Ernest Brose was among his pallbearers, linking the funeral to Anna’s family. His sons Arthur and Irwin continued the family’s connection with carpentry. Through Arthur and his son David, George’s building trade became part of the story of three Nelton generations.

stories.title: The Rivers family of Rollingstone
stories.hook: Edward Rivers sold insurance from the village where he was born and buried; Viola, who lost her mother at sixteen months, lived there all her married life.
body: Edward Nicholas Rivers was born at Rollingstone on 20 October 1910, the eldest of nine children of Edward Rivers and Johanna Johns, and he did not leave. On 14 June 1933, at Rollingstone, he married Viola Frisch, who had been born on 9 June 1905 at Oak Ridge, a few miles away, to John and Maggie Frisch. The wedding came in the third year of the Depression and he was twenty-two. The next March Viola's father died, and that same year Edward began as an insurance agent in the village.

Insurance ran in the village. His own father had carried the rural mail out of Rollingstone for thirty years, and Viola's father had been secretary of the Rollingstone Mutual Fire Insurance company for twenty-four. Edward would sit on that company's board and serve as president of the Rollingstone Business Association and of the St. Nicholas Society, the parish society his father had belonged to before him. He was also a Knight of Columbus and an Elk.

Their daughters were Diane, born in St. Paul on 10 August 1939, and Mary Lynn. In the Rivers house the family was never small: when Diane married in 1958 the cousins served the Mass and an uncle ushered, and 350 people ate on the lawn. Viola belonged to Holy Trinity Church, the ladies aid and the St. Theresa Society, where she was a charter member.

Viola died on 13 August 1975, aged seventy, while on the way to St. Elizabeth’s Hospital in Wabasha. Her funeral Mass was held at Holy Trinity, and she was buried in the parish cemetery. Edward, their daughters Diane and Mary Lynn, her sister Gertrude Koetter and eight grandchildren survived her. From her 1933 marriage until her death, Rollingstone had been her home.

Edward married again in 1976, to Elizabeth "Betty" Lehnertz Greden, who died in 1977. He died at home in Rollingstone on 14 January 1980, after an illness of several months, and his brothers Bernard, Norbert, Arthur and Paul carried him to the cemetery. His brother Francis died on 22 November 1944 at the age of seventeen.

Edward's life also ran through Holy Trinity's men's society. In 1952 the St. Nicholas Catholic Aid Society of Rollingstone, then celebrating its 59th year, chose Edward N. Rivers as marshal and put him on the sick committee, with Wilfred Rivers as vice president. By 1968 Edward was its president. On the evening of 23 October 1968 about 300 people filled Holy Trinity for a concelebrated Mass marking the society's 75th birthday, its diamond jubilee. The Winona Daily News photographed Bishop Edward A. Fitzgerald of Winona talking with the Mass servers before the service; standing at the left of the picture is "Edward N. Rivers, Rollingstone, society president."
Viola died on 13 August 1975, on the way to St. Elizabeth's Hospital in Wabasha. Edward died at home in Rollingstone on 14 January 1980.

stories.title: A horse, a prison, and Cleave Williams's brother
stories.hook: Melba Bell's father farmed at Van Alstyne. His youngest brother went to the state prison at seventeen for stealing a horse and was dead at twenty.
body: George Williams was born near Mantua, Texas, on 1 February 1891, the youngest child of Thomas and Rebecca Williams. The family tells of his arrest at seventeen, with John Leo Skipworth, for stealing a horse, and of a prison term at Huntsville. As the story comes down, George had found another caller visiting a girl, taken the other man’s horse and ridden it to death. It is the family’s story; how the courts saw it is not known.

In the same story, George developed diabetes in prison, was released and died a few weeks later with his parents beside him. He died on 31 May 1911, aged twenty, and was buried at Van Alstyne. Yet at his death he was described as a married man, something the family story does not explain.

His brother Grover Cleveland "Cleave" Williams was four years older, born in 1887 in Tennessee, the farm country around the old Shiloh battlefield, before Thomas and Rebecca brought the family to Texas about 1891. Thomas, born 9 February 1847, died on 25 December 1933, and Rebecca, born 14 February 1850, on 20 September 1927; they lie in Van Alstyne Cemetery.

Willie Parker was born in Texas on 13 January 1891 to James and Amanda (Pipkin) Parker. She and Cleave married and farmed near Van Alstyne. Their daughter Melba was born there in 1918 and married Wayne Bell in 1937. Through Melba and her daughter Margie, the Williams and Parker families connect to Rachel’s Johnson branch.

Cleave died on 5 December 1949. Willie lived another twenty-five years, a member of the Van Alstyne First Methodist Church, and died in a Sherman hospital on the morning of 18 November 1974, aged eighty-three. Their daughter Melba's family would grow into the Bell farm story told elsewhere on this site. Cleave and Willie are buried at Van Alstyne.

The family’s roots were in Tennessee. In 1850 Thomas Henry Williams was a three-year-old in the McNairy County home of Thomas and Dorcas Williams, and Rebecca was a three-month-old in the Hardin County home of William and Mary Britton. Willie Parker's father, James M. Parker, came from Jefferson County, Illinois, and reached Texas with Amanda Pipkin by 1886.

On 10 August 1909 George and John Skipworth stood before the Grayson County court, pleaded guilty to horse theft and were each given two years. They reached the penitentiary at Huntsville together on 17 September. George was seventeen, five feet nine and 142 pounds, grey-eyed, with a scar at the corner of his left eye and a slight stoop.
Neither served the full term. Both were pardoned in April 1910, George on the fifteenth and John the next day. George lived just over a year after he came home.

stories.title: The Canfields of Canfield Springs
stories.hook: In the summer of 1855 a Pennsylvania farmer built a small house in Cook's Valley, Minnesota, and four generations later his great-granddaughter married a Winona carpenter.
body: John and Margaret (Grier, also written Greer) Canfield brought their family from Pennsylvania to Wabasha County, Minnesota, in 1855. John and Patrick McDonough were among the earliest Euro-American settlers in Highland Township. The Canfields settled in the upper part of Cook’s Valley, at the place that became known as Canfield Springs. Their move was part of the settlement of Dakota homelands following the contested land cessions of the 1850s.

John Canfield was a community man. On 8 November 1857 the neighbors met in G. A. Cook's house to organize a school district, and named him director. The first road in the township, laid out in 1858, ran between Appel's Mill and Canfield Springs. The couple farmed there for the rest of their lives and raised ten children. Margaret is said to have died in 1865 at Kellogg.

Their son John A. Canfield was born in Pennsylvania in June 1848 and came to Highland as a boy. On 24 December 1874 he married Annie E. Hall. Anna Hall was the daughter of George and Sarah Hall of Wabasha. She bore a son, James Garfield Canfield, in September 1881, and died at Kellogg on 24 February 1882, five months later.
Anna Hall’s parents, George and Sarah Hall, kept a furniture store and later a meat market at Wabasha, and their household has a story of its own.

James grew up to marry Helen “Nel” Heffernan in Wabasha County on 5 September 1906. By 1910 they had a daughter, Marion, two, and Nel’s sister Maude was living with them; their daughter Helen was born that November. James died at Wabasha on 19 June 1912, aged thirty, and was buried at St. Agnes Cemetery in Kellogg.

John A. Canfield remarried after Anna Hall’s death. On 3 April 1884 he married Anna Thompson, and by 1900 he and Annie, who had been born in Norway, had been married sixteen years. Walter, Homer, Edith and Ruth were among their children, James’s younger half-brothers and half-sisters.

By 1920 Nel had married again and was living in Winona as Nellie Miller, the wife of Tom Miller, with her daughters Marian and Helen Canfield, Tom’s stepdaughters. When and where she married Tom is not known. Helen Berle Canfield married Arthur Nelton in Winona in 1934, carrying the line to Rachel’s Nelton family.

As a boy of seven John A. Canfield came to Reads Landing, “making the trip from Illinois up the river in a boat,” and the family took up the homestead at Canfield Springs in May 1855. In 1882, the year Anna Hall died, he went to work for the J. G. Lawrence & Krick Elevator Company, and he stayed “for over thirty years.” He was a Mason for more than fifty years and twice worshipful master of the Kellogg lodge. In 1914 he moved to Spooner, Wisconsin. He died in the Methodist hospital at Rice Lake on 29 November 1925 and was brought back to Kellogg for a Masonic funeral and burial in Greenfield cemetery. “All business places were closed during the funeral hour.”

James was not an only child. John and Anna Hall had three sons: George, later of Spooner; Wilson, of Carrington, North Dakota; and James, “who died at Kellogg, June 19, 1912.” In 1885 George, 9, Wilson, 6, and James, 3, were living at Kellogg with their father, their stepmother Anna and a baby half-sister. John’s second marriage, to Anne Thompson on 3 April 1884, brought eight more children: Mrs. Howard Flint, Walter, Homer, Elmer, Mrs. Edith Jones, Mrs. C. J. Byer, Ruth and Beryl.

James’s working life was short. “When the rural route from the postoffice at that place was established ten years ago, he was appointed the carrier,” the paper recalled at his death in June 1912. Rural Free Delivery had only become general across the country around 1902. James carried the Kellogg route for eight years and resigned when an illness that “began with a throat trouble” grew worse. His half-brother Walter later held the same kind of job; he was one of Kellogg’s two rural carriers when the county’s carriers organized in 1914. At James’s death his birth was given as 2 September 1883 and his elder daughter as “Mary, aged five,” slips, it seems, for 1881 and Marion.

The Canfield Springs road also had a darker reputation. In 1866 a book agent riding along it was shot from the bushes and robbed. The killer “was never discovered,” though years later “a rusty rifle was found in the bushes on the top of a neighboring bluff.” John’s sister Frances, “one of the ten children,” was “one of the early school teachers in Wabasha County” before marrying George Calvin and then Martin H. Tobias of Kellogg.

Two Canfields from Wabasha County served in Company G of the Third Minnesota Infantry. Thomas Canfield enlisted in October 1861, re-enlisted on 1 January 1864 and served to the end. At Wood Lake on 23 September 1862, the last battle of the Dakota War, a “J. G. Canfield” of Company G was among the regiment’s wounded, and a James A. Canfield also served in the regiment. John and Margaret had a son James at home in 1865. The soldiers may have been John A.’s brothers, but no one knows for sure.

quotes.t: Patrick McDonough and John Canfield were the first settlers of this town. They came in the summer of 1855 and built small homes for themselves, installed their families therein, and went to work.

stories.title: The year the railroad came to Choctaw County
stories.hook: In 1902 the Arkansas and Choctaw Railway laid track through southern Choctaw County, and two towns the Johnsons and Tysons would live in either began or moved to meet it.
body: By 1901 Mayhew, in the Choctaw Nation, was down to an estimated twenty-nine people, one cotton gin and one general store. It had once been the capital of the Pushmataha District, with a Presbyterian mission school from 1839 and a court ground. Federal measures including the Curtis Act of 1898 curtailed tribal authority and abolished tribal courts, diminishing Mayhew’s role. In 1902 the Arkansas and Choctaw Railway ran its line about two miles south. The businesses and families moved to the tracks. In September the post office became Boswell, named for Amity V. Boswell, who had surveyed the right-of-way.

The same railway helped establish Soper in 1902. Named for the line’s attorney, Pliny L. Soper, the town opened its post office in April 1903. A Methodist congregation organized in 1904 and the Soper Herald began publishing by January 1907. At Oklahoma statehood in 1907 Soper had 296 residents; by 1920 it had 538, with two doctors, two banks, four churches, a newspaper and three cotton gins. Boswell grew from 836 at statehood to 1,212 in 1920, shipping cotton, corn and fruit from its depot.

Rachel's Johnson and Tyson families belonged to this new country. Joel A. Johnson crossed from Texas between about 1900 and 1905 and bought and sold cattle for the next sixty years. His son Joe was born at Soper in 1908, the year after statehood. Nettie and Opal Tyson were in Albert Tyson's rented farmhouse at Oakes in 1940, and Opal had been born in 1919 at Sand Bluff. Joe died at home on the Boehler route near Boswell in 1972. His son Bob, after twenty years in the Army, retired to Oklahoma and was buried at Restland Cemetery in Boswell in 2024, near his own son David, killed in 1988 at twenty-four.

The railroad towns did not last at their peaks. Boswell stayed a farm town, but Soper shrank from 481 people in 1940 to 322 in 1970. In 1960 a tornado destroyed most of its brick downtown. By 1990 the cotton fields had become pasture, and the town was down to about 300.

Compare the Texas side of the family. The Williams and Bell ancestors farmed Grayson and Collin counties, where another railroad, the Houston and Texas Central, had killed one town (Mantua) and made two more (Van Alstyne and Anna) about thirty years earlier. Bob and Margie's families each grew up beside a railroad's route, one on each side of the Red River.

stories.title: The Vice President question
stories.hook: A Kentucky family gave the United States a vice president; whether Rachel’s Johnson line belongs to it is still an open question.
body: Great Crossing, in Scott County, Kentucky, was home to Col. Robert Johnson and Jemima Suggett. Their son Richard Mentor Johnson served as Vice President of the United States from 1837 to 1841. Another son, Joel Johnson, married Verlinda Offutt in 1817. In 1831 he traveled to Chicot County, Arkansas, and established Lakeport, a plantation sustained by enslaved labor.

Richard Mentor Johnson enslaved Julia Ann Chinn, a Black woman who managed his Kentucky estate during his absences and provided medical care to people at the plantation and the Choctaw Academy. Johnson acknowledged their two daughters, Imogene and Adaline. Chinn died during a cholera epidemic in 1833, still enslaved. The National Park Service describes the relationship as sexual exploitation: slavery meant that Chinn could not freely consent, regardless of how Johnson publicly presented their family.

Imogene married Daniel B. Pence, and their Kentucky home and farm were later put forward for the National Register. Adaline married in 1832; a contemporary newspaper attacked the marriage in explicitly racist terms. After Chinn’s death, Johnson exploited other enslaved women, and, the National Park Service reports, those women and their children were sold. Who the children were, and who their fathers were, is not known. Nothing yet ties Rachel’s Johnson line to Chinn or her daughters.

It has been suggested that Joel Anderson Johnson descended from the Kentucky family through his father, George Washington Johnson, and a Jonathan T. Johnson. Joel’s parents were very probably George W. and M. Rebecca Johnson, in whose house he was living at five and whose later children shared names with his brothers and sisters. Rebecca was probably born a Fails: a Sallie Mae and a Nannie Lou Johnson, very probably Joel’s sisters, were daughters of Marjorie, or Margerie, Rebecca Fails, though that is not certain. But who George’s own parents were is still unknown, and no one has shown a line through Jonathan T. to Lakeport.

Joel and Verlinda had nine children, by one account, with Lycurgus the eldest. Five of them, Julia, Lycurgus, Cyrus R., Victor M. and John T., shared with their mother in the settlement of the Lakeport estate in 1858; the names of any others are not known.

There may be another road. In 1850 a Georgia-born Jonathan Johnson was living in Pontotoc County, Mississippi, with Penelope and a six-month-old George. In 1860 a Sarah A. Johnson headed a household in Sevier County, Arkansas, and by 1870 a George W. Johnson was living with a Sarahann in Milam County, Texas, next door to a George W. Failes. They may be one family moving west, though nothing shows that the Georges were the same man, or that he was Joel’s father, or how any of them were related.
If that Georgia-born Jonathan was of this family, he was not the Kentucky-born Jonathan of the Lakeport line, though even that would not quite rule out a tie to the vice president’s family.

What is known is closer to home. Joel Anderson Johnson was born in Texas in 1875 and later lived in the Choctaw County communities of Soper and Boswell. His parents were very probably George W. and M. Rebecca Johnson, and three of their children at home in 1900 bore the names of his brothers and sisters. George was said to have been born in Mississippi, and later in Arkansas, and where his own family came from is still a mystery. Rebecca was probably born a Fails, though that, too, is not quite certain.

George's own family can probably be followed west. In the autumn of 1850 Jonathan and Penelope Johnson, both Georgia-born, were farming in Pontotoc County, Mississippi, with children Joel and John, born in Alabama, three more besides, and a baby, George. By June 1860 Jonathan was gone, and Sarah A. Johnson, very likely the same Georgia-born mother, was farming on her own in Sevier County, Arkansas, with Joel, John, William, George and a little Arkansas-born son. Ten years later Sarah Ann was keeping house for George and his brothers and sister in Milam County, Texas, next door to George W. Fails. George's eldest brother was Joel, and Joel was the name George gave his own first son.

stories.title: Rollingstone: a Luxembourg village on the Rolling Stone creek
stories.hook: A utopian colony failed at the mouth of a creek, and a few miles up the valley farmers from Luxembourg built a limestone church that still anchors the village where Diane Rivers was married.
body: Rollingstone developed inland from the Mississippi, near the meeting of the north and west branches of Rolling Stone Creek. Minnesota City had been laid out nearer the river in 1852 by the Western Farm and Village Association, a colony organized in New York. Luxembourg immigrants began settling the surrounding hills in the 1850s. Their farms, parish and businesses gave Rollingstone a distinct community life within the same township.

Among the immigrants were Michael and Margaret Rivers, who reached America in 1854 and settled on a Winona County farm in 1855. The Frisch family followed in 1864 or 1865, making their home at Oak Ridge. The two families belonged to a larger Luxembourg community whose ties continued through marriage, farming, local businesses and the Catholic parish.

By 1883 Rollingstone had three stores, two hotels, two blacksmith shops, a stone Catholic church and parsonage, a schoolhouse and several saloons. The church served much of the surrounding population. This was the village in which the Rivers family carried mail, kept stores and later sold insurance, while the Frisches farmed nearby.

Holy Trinity Church was built in 1869 under Charles Wender from rough-cut limestone, originally measuring 35 by 60 feet. Parishioners supplied labor and financial support. A transept and chancel added in 1893 under local carpenter Nicholas Arnoldy doubled the seating. A grade school opened in 1886, followed by a new school and the community’s first high school in 1921. Edward N. Rivers was among its graduates. The church was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1984.

For the families in this history the church marks every turning point. John Frisch's funeral in 1934, Viola Frisch Rivers's in 1975 and Edward N. Rivers's in 1980 were held at Holy Trinity, and Diane Rivers and David Nelton were married there in 1958. Parish societies carried the social life: Edward Rivers Sr. and his son Edward both belonged to the St. Nicholas Society, and Edward Jr. served sixteen years as its president, while Viola was a charter member of the St. Theresa Society. The village also sustained its own Rollingstone Mutual Fire Insurance company. The local historian Mary E. Nilles told the village’s story in Rollingstone: A Luxembourgish Village in Minnesota (1983).

The family also belonged to Winona and Minnesota City down the valley. The Neltons worked in carpentry and building, while the Brose siblings belonged to several different churches. Diane Rivers and David Nelton’s 1958 wedding brought these town and village branches together at Holy Trinity. Their reception on the Rivers lawn was both a family celebration and part of Rollingstone’s continuing social life.

quotes.t: In 1855, the first German settlers from Luxembourg arrived in the rolling hills of Winona County. Bringing with them their strong Catholic religious heritage, the immigrants had, by 1861, established a cemetery and built a church.

stories.title: The Rivers family: from Heffingen to the Rollingstone post office
stories.hook: Michel Rivers brought his children from Luxembourg in 1854; two sons and a grandson kept Rollingstone's mail moving for most of the next eighty years.
body: In February 1903 the Post Office opened a new rural route out of Rollingstone, and Edward Rivers, aged twenty-one, was named its carrier. Rural Free Delivery was new; Congress had mandated it in 1893, but it did not spread across the country until about 1902, and until then a farm family had to fetch its mail from the nearest post office or pay a private carrier. Edward kept the route for thirty years and retired on 1 March 1934. His father, Henry, had held the Rollingstone post office until his death in 1886.

Michel Rivers and Margaretha Adehm left Luxembourg in 1854 and settled on a Winona County farm in 1855. Their son Henry had been born at Heffingen, in the canton of Mersch, on 11 April 1838. The move placed the family among the Luxembourg immigrants who formed a lasting community around Rollingstone. The family was already called Rivers in Heffingen, as it would be in America.

John Baptiste Rivers, born in Luxembourg on 16 June 1840, made the family's public name. In March 1865 he enlisted in Co. K of the 48th Wisconsin Volunteer Infantry, a regiment organized that spring and sent to the Kansas frontier, and he served at Fort Lyon, Colorado, 'protecting the frontier against the Indians.' After the war he farmed in Norton township, and in 1872 opened a store in Rollingstone village. He was postmaster for 27 years, first president of the village council and a founder of the First State Bank of Rollingstone. In the words of the village post office’s history, “In 1886, J. B. Rivers succeeded Hy. Rivers.” Henry, his brother, had held the office and died on 10 June 1886.

Henry's widow Elizabeth Lehnertz, born in Luxembourg in 1847 by her memorial, though her age at death pointed to about 1845, had come over in 1860. After Henry's death the family ran a hotel in the village. Their son Edward, born at Rollingstone on 4 November 1881, went to the parochial school, carried the rural mail, helped found the Rollingstone Co-operative Oil Association, sold insurance for Farmers Home Mutual and served as mayor from 1938 to 1948. On 22 June 1909 he married Johanna Johns, and nine children followed. The first, Edward Nicholas, was born on 20 October 1910.

Edward was sixty-nine when he died at his home in Rollingstone at six on a Thursday evening, 28 June 1951, four days after a stroke. Besides the oil association and the insurance agency he had belonged to the St. Nicholas Society and the Winona County Rural Letter Carriers' Association, and he was buried from Holy Trinity.

Edward N. Rivers went into insurance at Rollingstone in 1934, the year after he married Viola Frisch, and died at home on 14 January 1980. His brother Francis, born 1927, died on 22 November 1944, aged seventeen. The families were already tied before Edward and Viola married: Viola's aunt Katherine Frisch had married Matthew Rivers, a son of John B., on 19 November 1907, and the couple ran a grocery in Rollingstone. 'Mrs. Mathew Rivers, Rollingstone' was among John Frisch's sisters at his death in 1934.

When Michel married Margaritha Adehm at Heffingen on 12 January 1832, he was written down as Michael Rivers, son of Johann Nicolas Rivers, tavern keeper, and Anna Molitor, and he signed himself “Michell Rivers.” The family was already Rivers before it emigrated.

Elizabeth Lehnertz probably also came from Heffingen. Her sister was Mrs. Margaret Michels of Ellensburg, Washington, who, as the Ellensburg Daily Record told it on 30 November 1931, “was born in Heffingen, Luxemburg,” came to America in 1856, married Martin Michels at Aurora, Illinois, and reached Ellensburg in 1880 “by covered wagon from the Dalles, Ore.” The sisters’ parents are said to have been Michael Lehnertz and Elisabeth Neuhegen, who both died in Luxembourg, but no one has yet confirmed it.

stories.title: Oak Ridge, autumn 1906: two funerals in three weeks
stories.hook: Viola Frisch was sixteen months old when her mother died fourteen days after giving birth, and nineteen days later her grandfather, the Luxembourg pioneer, was dead as well.
body: Maggie (Haines) Frisch died at home on Oak Ridge on the evening of 1 October 1906, the day remembered as her fifth wedding anniversary. She was thirty-one. She and John Frisch had three young children: Gertrude, about three; Viola, sixteen months; and a baby only fourteen days old. Maggie’s funeral was held that Thursday at the Oak Ridge Catholic church. John, a former schoolteacher, was left to raise the children on the family farm.

Nineteen days later, on Saturday 20 October, John’s father died of diabetes. He had been born at Beaufort, Luxembourg, on 28 October 1837 and baptized there the same day, so he was eight days short of sixty-nine, though he was remembered as sixty-nine; at Oak Ridge his birth is sometimes given as 18 October 1836. Jacques, or Jacob, Frisch was remembered as a respected early resident of Winona County.

Jacques and Anna (Speltz) Frisch had emigrated from Luxembourg and settled at Oak Ridge. Anna was born at Fischbach on 24 October 1836. They landed at Winona on 4 July 1864, or perhaps 1865; when they died, it was remembered both ways. Jacob helped establish the Oak Ridge Catholic congregation, organized at John Speltz’s house on 5 December 1875. Anna died on 7 May 1902 after nearly a year of illness.

So within four years the Oak Ridge farm lost Anna, who had come from Luxembourg, then Maggie, who had married into the family, and then Jacques. John Frisch, born 25 July 1873 and remembered as John P., though the initial probably belonged to his elder brother, had taught school for eight years before he married Maggie Haines of Arcadia, Wisconsin, in October 1901. He was left with three children and the homestead. The baby was very probably Raymond, John and Margaret’s son, born on 16 September 1906, who was still living when his father died in 1934.

John kept the family together. He farmed the old Frisch place on Oak Ridge until about 1929, then moved to Rollingstone, where he served as secretary of the Rollingstone Mutual Farmers Fire Insurance Company for twenty-four years and in 1932 as president of the state association of mutual insurance companies. He remarried in 1931, to Mrs. Anna Breitbach of Winona. Viola married Edward Rivers in June 1933, and John died on 16 March 1934 of an acute heart attack, 'while members of his family were at his bedside.' Edward N. Rivers began as an insurance agent at Rollingstone that same year.

A parent left alone with young children recurs in this family. John did it on Oak Ridge in 1906, and across the river in Wisconsin in 1977 the same shape came around again when Viola's daughter Diane was left with five. The Frisch farm had two funerals in three weeks, and the girl who was sixteen months old grew up to marry the insurance agent in the next village.

stories.title: The town the railroad missed
stories.hook: In 1872 the Houston and Texas Central laid its tracks two miles east of Mantua, Texas. By the middle of 1873 the town was deserted, and the Williams, Parker and Bell families ended up in the places that replaced it.
body: Mantua was founded in 1854 to pay for a school. Three men bought 200 acres from a son of Collin McKinney, cut it into lots and sold them to fund Mantua Seminary. The town banned gambling, horse racing and the sale of liquor, "to insure the proper environment" for the students. By 1860 it had three stores, a church and about fifty people, and by 1870 about 300.

Then the Houston and Texas Central Railway laid its tracks two miles east. Some Mantua citizens bought land by the line and started a new town, Van Alstyne, in Grayson County. The post office closed on 11 July 1873, and by mid-1873 Mantua was deserted except for the churches, which moved in 1888. Van Alstyne incorporated in 1890 with about 400 people, two gristmills, a flour mill, a newspaper and a college, and had about 1,940 residents around 1900.

Anna, five miles southeast of old Mantua, came a decade later: platted in 1883 with twenty people, two stores, a steam gristmill and a Baptist church, with 100 to 200 people by 1890, a first bank in 1902 and incorporation in 1913. The population was 538 in 1929, 467 in 1931. A traction line, the Greenville and Northwestern, ran from Anna to Blue Ridge from about 1915 to 1920.

The living came from the land. Collin County had 903 farms in 1870 and 6,001 in 1920, when it grew 49,311 bales of cotton and nearly 2.6 million bushels of corn. Grayson County's farms peaked at 5,762 in 1900. In the Depression Collin County lost more than 1,200 farms between 1930 and 1940, and Grayson County nearly 900.

Rachel's families sit within a few miles of the dead town. Thomas and Rebecca Williams brought their sons from Tennessee about 1891, to the Mantua country, and a youngest son, George, was born there that year. The Parkers died at Monta and Van Alstyne. Wayne Bell was born at Anna in 1914. He married Melba Williams at Van Alstyne in 1937, and the two of them farmed Grayson County for the rest of their working lives. The Williams and Parker graves are at Van Alstyne, in the town the railroad built.

stories.title: Raford Failes, sixty, in Milam County
stories.hook: In 1870 Raford Failes, a North Carolina native of sixty, was living in Milam County, Texas, with a little Mississippi-born daughter. The Fails had come west during or just after the Civil War.
body: In 1870 Raford Failes, sixty, born in North Carolina, was the head of a household in Milam County, Texas, and in the same house was a seven-year-old, Elizabeth, born in Mississippi. It was five years after the Civil War. Milam County, east of Austin, had seen its farm values fall by more than half between 1860 and 1870, from about $1.14 million to $505,000, and recovery was slow, because transportation was poor and everyone lived off the land. Complete recovery waited for the railroads of the 1870s.

Rayford Fail was born on 16 March 1806, probably in Johnston County, North Carolina, and married Polly Anne Wallace by 1838. Their children were born in Jasper County, Mississippi: George Washington in August 1847, Young Rayford in December 1853, Jeremiah Marsh in March 1854, Thomas in February 1857 and Temperence Elizabeth in February 1863. The dates given for Young Rayford and Jeremiah, three months apart, cannot both be right. Because Temperence was born in Mississippi in 1863 and the family was in Texas by mid-1870, the move west came in those seven years, during or just after the war. Rayford died in Milam County on 26 January 1885.

His children made Milam County theirs. George Washington Fail married Margaret Ann Johnson there in 1870 and died in the county in 1923. Young Rayford married Viney Allison in 1873, had three sons, and died on 6 September 1880. Temperence, called Lizzie, married Joseph Franklin Keen in Lee County on 7 March 1878.

The Keens went on to Lamar County, Texas, and soon after 1900 into the Choctaw Nation. By 1910 Lizzie Keen was a widow at the head of her own household at Oakes, Choctaw County, Oklahoma, the same township where Joel Anderson Johnson and Winnie were living; she was said to be fifty-nine, far older than her 1863 birth would make her. She was buried at Forest Chapel Cemetery in Lamar County, and the Southeast Oklahoman of Hugo noted her death on 14 December 1939. Other Fail descendants, Thomas Fail (died 1936) and Jim “Tobe” Fail (died 1957), ended up in Choctaw County or Greer County, Oklahoma. It was the same road Joel Anderson’s family took, a generation later: out of Mississippi to Texas, then over the Red River.

Whether Joel Anderson Johnson’s mother belonged to this family is still an open question. His sisters Sallie Mae and Nannie Lou Johnson were very probably the girls born in Lee County to George Washington Johnson and Marjorie, or Margerie, Rebecca Fails, which would make Rebecca a Fails by birth, but who her own parents were, and whether she was Rayford’s daughter, is not yet known. The names cross confusingly: Rayford’s son George Washington Fail married Margaret Ann Johnson in Milam County in 1870.

stories.title: Anna Brose Nelton and twenty-one years of illness
stories.hook: Anna Nelton died on a Sunday evening in April 1928 at forty-four, and her husband told the newspaper where he thought it had started: a rattlesnake bite in June 1907.
body: Anna Louise (Brose) Nelton lived with a long illness while raising four children in Winona. Her husband George traced its beginning to a rattlesnake bite “across the lake” in June 1907, as the family told it after her death. What the illness really was, and whether the bite had anything to do with it, no one can now say.

Anna died at the family home on West Broadway on the evening of 8 April 1928, aged forty-four. She had been ill, the family said, for twenty-one years, since 1907. Her youngest child, Arthur, had been born in October 1909 and was eighteen when she died. The long illness was part of her life, though just what it was remains unknown.

She had been born Anna Louise Brose in Winona on 26 December 1883, to Ernest and Augusta Brose, German immigrants, and "spent all her life here." She married George, then a house carpenter, and by 1910 had four children: Myrtle, Irwin, Edward and Arthur. The family rented at 617 West King Street that spring, and later lived on West Broadway.

She left her husband and the four children, with Myrtle still at home and unmarried, two brothers, Ernest and John Brose, and three sisters, Minnie Brose, Mrs. Max Schulze and Mrs. Niels Skow. The funeral was held at the house and then at McKinley Methodist Church, with burial at Woodlawn Cemetery. Arthur was eighteen. A little more than two years later George married again.
