stories.title: Ernest and Augusta Brose and their six Winona children
stories.hook: Two Germans from Posen reached Winona by 1883, raised six children there, and left behind a railroad yardmaster, a World War I veteran and a family lot at Woodlawn.
body: Ernest Brose, born in May 1847, and Augusta, born in December 1856, came from Germany to Winona before the birth of their daughter Anna in December 1883. They are said to have come from Wolwark, near Schubin, in the Bromberg district of the former Prussian province of Posen, though that is not certain. Their American life was lived in Winona.

The town they reached had been drawing Germans since 1856 on the strength of its lumber, wheat, steamboats and railroads; the first railroad out of Winona had opened in 1862. Six of their children grew to adulthood, all born in Winona: Anna (1883), Ida (1885), Louise (8 December 1886), Ernest Gustav (23 December 1890), Minnie (27 June 1893) and John H. (1 July 1895).

Augusta died on 28 April 1924, aged sixty-seven. Ernest lived ten more years and died in Winona on 4 September 1934, aged eighty-seven. Both are buried at Woodlawn Cemetery, Section AA, Lot 66, where their son John also lies.

The children made their lives in Winona. Ida married Niels Petersen Skow in 1922 and died in 1946. Louise married Max E. Schulze on 2 January 1911 and "lived in Winona most of her life." Anna married the carpenter George Nelton. Ernest Gustav became a yardmaster for the Northwestern Railway, retired in September 1948 and later married Lydia Zambrocki. He was a veteran of the First World War. Minnie married William Julius Schellhas and died in 1971 in Winona, the last of the six.

The siblings’ lives crossed several Winona institutions. Anna’s funeral was held at McKinley Methodist Church, Louise’s at Grace Presbyterian, and Ernest Gustav married at St. Casimir’s Catholic Church. Building work, the railway and these congregations placed the family within different parts of the same river city.

Louise married Max E. Schulze on 2 January 1911 and had a son, Arthur, and a daughter, Ruth Louise. By the end of her life she was living at the Odd Fellows Nursing Home in Northfield. She died at Northfield City Hospital on 18 April 1962; her funeral returned her to Winona and Grace Presbyterian Church.

Ernest Gustav’s working life was tied to the railway. He retired as a Northwestern Railway yardmaster in September 1948 and died at the Minneapolis Veterans Hospital on 1 June 1965. His wife, Lydia, and his sister Minnie survived him. He was buried at St. Mary’s Cemetery in Winona.

Wolwark, the village named as Ernest’s and Augusta’s birthplace, is a real place. It was a small farming village of a few hundred people about five kilometers southwest of Schubin (now Szubin), in the Prussian province of Posen, and it is now in Gmina Szubin. Kreis Schubin belonged to the Bromberg government district. Augusta’s family name, Kienitz, was common there: a Wilhelmine Kienitz, born in 1855, daughter of Friedrich Kienitz and Rosina Warmbier, married at Gromadno in Kreis Schubin in 1880, and her brother Carl Julius married there in 1883, though neither is known to have been Augusta’s kin. Where Ernest and Augusta themselves married is not known; it may have been in Winona.

Their departure was part of a much larger exodus. Through 1907 about 2.3 million people left Prussia's eastern provinces, Posen among them, and in the 1880s, when the Broses came, America was still the main destination. Winona was a natural place for them to land. Germans had been arriving since 1856, and between 1859 and 1900 some 5,000 Poles and Kashubians from the same Prussian borderlands made up a quarter of the city. In 1895 the Broses' neighbors on both sides came from 'Pamera', which is Pomerania.

In 1885 Ernest, or Ernst, and Augusta, 25, were in Winona with Anna, 2, and a baby, Augusta, under a year old, of whom nothing more is known. In 1895 the family was in the Third Ward: Ernest 46, Augusta 40, Anna, Ida, Louise (that year written Elisabeth), Ernest, Minnie and John, one month old. In 1905 Ernest was 58, Augusta 48 and five children still lived at home.

Augusta was born a Kienitz. At the deaths of three of her children the name was written three ways: Kienitz for John in 1957, Keinertz for Louise in 1962 and Kinetz for Ernest G. in 1965. Ernest and Augusta lie under matching granite markers at Woodlawn, “Ernest Brose 1847–1934” and “Augusta Brose 1856–1924,” though Augusta may have been born on 30 December 1855.

stories.title: Eda Zenk Nelton and her Winona children
stories.hook: Ida Zenk Nelton came from Pomerania, raised a large family in Winona, and at eighty-nine still did her own housework and grew her own vegetables.
body: Ida Zenk, also known as Eda, was born in Germany on 15 March 1852, in Pommern: most likely Pomerania, the Prussian province, rather than the village of Pommern on the Mosel in the Rhineland. Her father was Ernest Zenk, and her mother’s surname was Stack. An Ernst Zenk, born in Prussia about 1823, was farming in Mount Vernon Township, Winona County, in 1885, aged 62, with a Caroline Zenk of the same age. He was the right age to be her father and lived in the right county, but nothing yet ties that household to Ida, and Caroline’s maiden name is unknown, so whether he was her father is uncertain.

Ida had come to Winona by about 1872, and on 9 December 1879 she married George Nelton there; her name was written as Ida Sink, or Zink. The family was in Winona by the early 1880s. George, born in January 1855, is the family’s other unsolved German. The surname itself is unexplained; the original form may have been Nölte, Nelte or something similar.

They raised a large family in Winona. Anna was born in 1879 and later married Joseph Knopp. George John, the contractor, was born on 17 January 1882, at Minneiska or perhaps Winona. Winnie was born in March 1882 or 1883: the fourth of March 1882 by her family’s reckoning at her death, though the ages given for her as a girl point to March 1883, and the 1882 dates for George John and Winnie cannot both be right. Edith Thelma (1888–1962), Harry (1892–1966) and Elsie (1896–1968) followed, and there were also Charles, William and Lizzie.

The family was larger and more tangled than the six children usually named. When Winnie died in 1966 she was remembered as the daughter of George and Ida Zenk Nelton, survived by Harry Nelton, Anna Knopp and Elsie Bitu, and predeceased by brothers Charles and George Nelton and William Lutz and by sisters Edith Eaton and Lizzie Plank. William Lutz and Lizzie Plank are otherwise strangers to the family story, and whether every one of these brothers and sisters had the same two parents is not known. Nor is it clear which Charles Nelton of Winona was Winnie’s brother. A Mrs. Charles Nelton was badly hurt in a train accident in 1913, but whether she was his wife is only a possibility.

On 14 March 1941 the Winona Republican-Herald marked the coming eighty-ninth birthday of “Mrs. Ida Nelton of Gilmore Avenue,” who, “formerly Miss Ida Zenk, was born in Pommern, Germany, March 15.” She had lived in Winona for 69 years, still did her own housework, and in summer raised her own garden vegetables. She had three sons, Harry, George and Charles, and four daughters, Mrs. Victor Bitu, Mrs. Harry Eaton, Mrs. Winnie Beeman and Mrs. Annie Knopp, with 32 grandchildren and 49 great-grandchildren. A daughter, Lizzie, had died in Colorado twenty-three years before; a son, William, had died on 16 March 1939; and her husband, George Nelton Sr., had died in 1912, or on 19 October 1911, as other family accounts have it.

Two years later, for her ninety-first birthday, the paper counted 52 great-grandchildren and noted that a grandson, Victor Bitu Jr., was the first Winona man to join the paratroops. Ida died in Winona on 30 December 1943, at ninety-one, in the third winter of the United States’ war with the country she was born in. She was buried at Woodlawn Cemetery.

Her son George John built houses around Winona. His second wife was Christine Walstad, a Norwegian born on 3 December 1888, who came to America in 1904 and married him in 1930. She worked at the Williams Hotel Cafeteria, Winona Cleaning Works and Miller Waste Mills, and became a United States citizen in September 1941. George’s surviving children were sons Irwin, Arthur and Edward and a daughter, Mrs. Andrew (Myrtle) Wally. Elsie’s eldest son, Jenus Arvid Bitu, died in 1927 at thirteen.

When Ida died in December 1943, at her daughter Anna Knopp's home, her only surviving brother was Richard Zenk of Minnesota City. He was sixteen years younger, had come to Winona County as a boy about 1877, and spent his working life as a mail handler on the Chicago and North Western. Her daughter Edith had first married George Pickart, a railroad brakeman, in November 1904, and it was from the Pickarts' house at 516 Wilson Street that George Nelton was buried in October 1911.

stories.title: Jacob Johns of Hart Township: from Baltimore to Fort Blakely
stories.hook: At twenty Jacob Johns left a Winona County farm for the Sixth Minnesota Infantry, and ended up in the swamps of Arkansas and the last siege of the Civil War; he later fathered twelve children, one of whom married into the Rivers family.
body: Jacob Johns was born in Germany on 5 August 1842, or perhaps in 1840. He came to America as a small child, after a two-month voyage to Baltimore. The family spent seven years in Missouri, moved to Hazel Green, Wisconsin, and in 1856 settled in Hart Township, Winona County.

On 15 August 1862, just turned twenty, he enlisted in Company E of the Sixth Minnesota Infantry. His first battles came within weeks, in the U.S.–Dakota War: Birch Coulee on 2 September 1862 and Wood Lake on 23 September. The conflict brought severe losses and displacement to Dakota communities as well as deaths among soldiers and settlers, and that December thirty-eight Dakota men were executed at Mankato. The Sixth Minnesota stayed on the frontier and took part in military expeditions into Dakota Territory in 1863.

In June 1864 the regiment was sent to Helena, Arkansas, where disease devastated it: by late September, 654 of its 950 men were sick, mostly with malaria. In 1865 Jacob served in the Mobile campaign at Spanish Fort and Fort Blakely. He was discharged on 19 August 1865, and in the words of his county biography, “He was never wounded nor taken prisoner, and served from first to last as a private soldier.”

Back in Hart Township he bought eighty acres in section 28, a farm that grew to 440. On 18 May 1868 he married Theresa, whose maiden name was probably Kreuzer; his biography printed it as “Kryzer,” and Kreuzer is how that name would be spelled in German. They had twelve children, seven daughters and five sons: Mary, Sophia, Lizzie, Emma, Annie, Jacob, Henry, Rose, Willie, Hannah, Eddie and George. The family was Catholic; Jacob was a Democrat, served as township supervisor and constable, and belonged to the Grand Army of the Republic.

Theresa was a German-speaker from Bohemia, then part of the Austrian Empire, born about 1848 to 1850. In 1885 the Hart Township household was Jacob, 44, born in Germany, and Theresa, 37, born in Austria, with eight children from Mary, 14, down to Rosina, six months, and Jacob’s father, also named Jacob and aged 84, lived close by with his wife, Rosina. The elder Jacob’s wife is also remembered as Maggie, so either he had married again by 1885 or Maggie and Rosina were one woman. In 1895 Theresa was 46 and born in “Bohemia,” and Johanna, 6, was among the children at home. In 1905 “Tressa,” 55, born in Austria, and Jacob, 65, still had Henry, Rosella, William, Johanna, 16, Edward and George with them.

Annie, the fifth of the twelve, married John Franklin Ebner, a Fillmore County farmer’s son born on 31 July 1883, on 30 April 1907. They farmed for some years in Hart Township, and in 1912 bought 224 acres in sections 26 and 27 of Wilson Township, where he kept Shorthorn and Durham cattle. Their three daughters, Lorine, Evelyn and Leona, were born between August 1908 and March 1912.

Johanna Johns was very probably the Hannah of the twelve. She was born on 11 November 1888 at Rushford in Fillmore County, “to Jacob and Theresa Johns,” her mother’s maiden name was given at her death as Kreuzer, and she was in Jacob and Theresa’s household in 1895 and 1905. When she died, her surviving siblings were a brother, George, in Canada and a sister, Mrs. Rose Tiernan, in Albertville, and five sisters and four brothers had gone before her: counts that fit the seven daughters and five sons exactly. It is not quite proved, but it is very probable.

On 22 June 1909 Johanna married Edward Rivers Sr. of Rollingstone. The marriage joined a German Catholic farm family to the Luxembourg Catholic Riverses, and both her father and her husband’s uncle, John B. Rivers of the 48th Wisconsin, had worn Union blue. She died at home in Rollingstone on 4 March 1967 and was buried at Holy Trinity Catholic Cemetery.

Jacob died in Winona County on 16 April 1924, and Theresa outlived him by nine years. She died in Fremont Township on 21 September 1933, aged 84, born in Bohemia in 1848, the wife of Jacob Johns. At her death her father’s name was set down as “Mr. Kruger,” probably a garbled Kreuzer, and her mother’s was left blank. She is remembered at Holy Trinity, Rollingstone, with a birth date of 28 September 1848.

stories.title: The Rivers store and the families around it
stories.hook: John B. Rivers opened a store in Rollingstone in 1872, and his sons carried its trade into groceries, dry goods and, very probably, a Winona candy factory with forty hands.
body: John B. Rivers, Henry Rivers’s brother, married Anna Heber, a daughter of Nicholas Heber, on 29 October 1866, the same year he bought a farm in Norton Township. In 1872 he opened a store in Rollingstone. Their children were John H., Matthew, John P., Elizabeth and Josephine.

John B. Rivers was a public man as well as a storekeeper. He spent ten years as assistant postmaster before his twenty-seven as postmaster, sat on the Rollingstone village council and was its first president, and belonged to the John Ball Post of the Grand Army of the Republic. In 1889 the Winona County Old Settlers’ Association made him its vice-president for Rollingstone, and in June 1892, when the village decided not to incorporate, he was one of three men named to its board of inspectors with John Kohner and Nic. Schnell Jr. He counted himself among the founders and directors of the First State Bank of Rollingstone, which was incorporated on 2 January 1905 with $10,000 in capital and opened a few months later, though he was not among the men who signed it into being. Those who did read like a roll of the village: M. N. Reiland, Mathew Speltz, John Speltz, Frank Jung and Jacques Frisch, who would die in October 1906, among some thirty others, with J. H. Hans as the first president and Edmund E. Hans as cashier. Andrew Rinn Jr. replaced Hans as cashier in 1907 and A. A. Walch took the desk in 1910.

Anna Heber came from Luxembourg stock too. A Mazeppa blacksmith, Nicholas J. Almeter, married a Maggie Heber in June 1887, a daughter of Nicholas and Anna (Majerus) Heber, both natives of Luxembourg. Anna’s father was Nicholas Heber, and the name, the country and the decade all fit, so Maggie was very probably her sister and Anna Majerus their mother.

John H. Rivers, born in Norton Township on 13 December 1867, studied at Winona State Normal School and a Winona business college before working with his father. He later ran a grocery in Winona with his brother John P., and in 1896 he came back to Rollingstone and opened a general dry goods business. His brother Matthew, born at Rollingstone on 8 December 1874, stayed in the family general store and served as assistant postmaster. The brothers carried their father’s work into a new generation.

One brother went into manufacturing. By 1913 the Winona Candy Company, with a capital of $50,000, was one of the city’s manufacturers, with J. P. Rivers as president, treasurer and general manager and forty employees making chocolates, peanut candies and hard candies. Since John H. had gone into the grocery trade at Winona with his brother J. P. Rivers, the candy maker was very probably John B.’s son John P.

John H. married Bertha Jung on 10 October 1894. Her parents, the merchant John Jung and Margaretha Kohner, were among Rollingstone’s 1855 settlers. Their children Andrew and Angeline were born on 10 December 1895 (or a year earlier) and 13 October 1899. The marriage joined two village business families, while their Rivers cousins kept up the mail route.

stories.title: Sarah and George Hall: a Wabasha household
stories.hook: Pennsylvania, Iowa and Minnesota connect Sarah Butturff’s family to the Canfields of Kellogg.
body: Sarah Butturff was born in Cumberland County, Pennsylvania, in February 1825, a daughter of Frederick and Elizabeth. She married George W. Hall on 6 February 1849. George, born in Perry County in 1824, was the son of Moses and Catharine Hall. Their daughter Anna later married John A. Canfield of Kellogg.

George entered the grocery trade in Muscatine, Iowa, in 1854. Three years later, the family reached Wabasha, Minnesota, where he opened a furniture store with Sarah’s brother Samuel Butturff. A move to a Glasgow Township homestead in 1860 lasted three years; poor health brought George back to town. He worked as a store clerk and later kept a meat market.

By George’s death on 7 May 1870, the household owned two adjoining residences on Allegheny Street. Sarah still held them in 1884. Anna had died by then. Her brothers Henry, William Parker and George connected the family to Greenfield, Minnesota, and Prairie View, Kansas.

George’s father very probably put his name to a protest at home in Pennsylvania. In the April term of 1833, residents of Saville Township petitioned the Perry County court against licensing a tavern selling spirits in Ickesburg, saying it “would only tend to injure the morality, peace and comfort of the community,” and Moses Hall was one of the signers. Moses Hall, sometimes written Haal, lived in Saville Township and died at Eshcol in 1849, so the signer was probably George’s father.
Sarah Butturff had been baptized at the First Evangelical Lutheran Church in Carlisle, Pennsylvania, in 1833, when she was eight, as Sarah Battorf, daughter of Frederick and Elizabeth.

stories.title: Five Williams brothers in one photograph
stories.hook: A family photograph shows Cleave Williams with four of his brothers, the Tennessee-to-Texas family in five faces.
body: In this formal photograph, by the family’s own label, John Arthur Williams and William stand at the back, with Arch, Cleave and George seated in front. White shirts, dark jackets and carefully arranged hands give the picture its studio formality. The surviving print is creased and torn, but all five faces can still be seen. Its date and photographer are unknown.

Their lives spread beyond the same household. Arch, born in Tennessee on 27 November 1871, came to Texas around 1891 and later made his home west of Tom Bean. He married Fannie Racer of Collinsville. At his death in 1938, his surviving brothers were Bud and Cleve at Van Alstyne and John at Dallas; his sisters lived in Van Alstyne, Hamlin, Brownfield and Sherman. The family had stayed connected while making homes across the state.

George, the youngest man in the front row, was born on 1 February 1891 and died on 31 May 1911, at twenty; he lies at Van Alstyne. Cleave lived until 1949; through his daughter Melba and granddaughter Margie, his branch leads to Rachel. The photograph keeps the brothers together, before the losses carved on the cemetery stones.

stories.title: Audrey Johnson King: from Soper to Sterling City
stories.hook: Joel and Winnie Johnson’s daughter made her home on a West Texas ranch and supported the next generation of farmers.
body: Audrey Johnson was born in Soper, Oklahoma, on 8 January 1911, the daughter of Joel Anderson Johnson and Winnie Bozarth. She grew up in the southeastern Oklahoma community where her father bought livestock and worked the land. Her brother Joe remained near Boswell and later became Bob Johnson’s father.

On 29 December 1928, Audrey married Riley James King in Paris, Texas. The couple settled in Sterling City, west of San Angelo, where they ranched. Their daughter Bonnie Ruth was born in San Angelo on New Year’s Day 1930.

Audrey and Riley supported 4-H and the Future Farmers of America, organizations that gave local young people a place to learn about agriculture and livestock. Audrey was active in the Church of Christ and taught Bible classes. In 1967 the Kings attended an American Cancer Society meeting in Houston, taking part in sessions on service and public education.

Audrey lived in Sterling City until 1988, then moved to San Angelo. She died there on 7 December 1989 and was buried in the Sterling City cemetery, remembered as the daughter of Joel and Winnie Johnson of Oklahoma and the wife of Riley King.

The Kings ran sheep, and the San Angelo ranchmen's magazine caught Riley at it. In July 1953, in the depth of the long drought, Riley King of Sterling City bought sixteen Rambouillet rams for $1,077.50 at the San Angelo ram sale, and in June 1960 he was again among the buyers at the twenty-fourth annual San Angelo Rambouillet sale, a year of dry weather and weak wool and lamb prices when the sale chairman called it "really a bargain day."

The ranch itself turns up too. In late April 1958 the Riley King ranch was one of four Sterling County places sprayed from the air with 2,4-D against bitterweed, a range weed that poisons sheep, and the early results looked good. And on 30 October 1961, when Sterling County ranchmen met in Sterling City to raise money for the screwworm eradication program, at ten cents a head for sheep, goats and swine, Riley King was one of the men chosen to ask his neighbors to give.

stories.title: Bonnie King Alley: from Sterling City to Saudi Arabia
stories.hook: After a West Texas wedding, Bonnie and Gene Alley made a home thousands of miles away on the Arabian Peninsula.
body: Bonnie Ruth King was born on 1 January 1930 in San Angelo, the daughter of Audrey Johnson and Riley King. Raised in Sterling City, she studied at Abilene Christian College and San Angelo Business School and worked for agricultural offices in West Texas. There she met Marvin Eugene “Gene” Alley, a Texas A&M graduate who worked in soil conservation.

At the Sterling City Church of Christ on 6 December 1952, Bonnie and Gene married. Her bridal clothes included a lace and nylon gown and a fingertip veil; she carried a Bible inlaid with mother of pearl, a gift from Gene. The local paper printed her bridal portrait on its front page.

Gene had a job supervising a farm in Saudi Arabia, at “Al Khari,” very likely al-Kharj. The couple planned to leave on 12 January 1953, though the family later remembered them setting off right after the wedding. For Bonnie it was her first airplane journey and her first trip beyond the Oklahoma visits of her childhood.

The Alleys spent a little over two years in Saudi Arabia. They returned to Texas and ranched in Sterling County for about sixteen years. Their son Robert Eugene was born in 1963. The family later moved to Midland, where Gene worked as a land appraiser and Bonnie as a teacher’s aide.

Robert died in 1981, and Gene died in 2000. Bonnie died in San Angelo on 4 January 2012 and was buried at Sterling City. Her life connected an Oklahoma farming family, a West Texas ranching town and an unexpected chapter in Saudi Arabia.

stories.title: Winnie Nelton Beeman and the Wacouta Street family
stories.hook: Winnie Nelton Beeman made her life in Winona and Plainview, and she may have begun it as Alvina, a year later than her family remembered.
body: Winnie Nelton Beeman was the daughter of George Nelton and Ida Zenk. She and Arthur Oscar Beeman raised a family in the Winona area, with periods in nearby Plainview. The family included sons Arthur Chester and Harold Oscar and daughter Berniece May.

In 1910 Winnie, twenty-seven, and Arthur were living in Plainview with their two young sons. By 1930 the couple were in Winona with Harold, Berniece and a grandchild. Arthur died in 1932; by 1950 Winnie was widowed and shared a household with her daughter Berniece, who was working as an assistant cook at a hotel.

Winnie was very probably the Winona-born bride Alvina Nelten, daughter of George and Edith, who married the blacksmith Arthur O. Beeman at Bluff Siding, Wisconsin, in 1899. In 1900 Alvina and Arthur were living at 576 Wacouta Street, the address later connected with Winnie. The husband, the father and the address all fit, though the first names, hers and her mother’s, do not, and it is not quite certain.
Alvina was born in March 1883, and Winnie’s ages in 1910, 1930 and 1950 fit that year, but at her death she was remembered as born on 4 March 1882. Which is right is not known.

Winnie died in Winona on 3 January 1966 and was buried at Woodlawn Cemetery. She was remembered with brothers and sisters scattered across the Winona area, some of whom are still hard to place in the family.

stories.title: Nel Canfield and her daughters
stories.hook: After James Canfield died, his widow Nel raised their two small daughters into a new family in Winona.
body: In September 1906, James Garfield Canfield and Helen Heffernan married in Wabasha County, Minnesota. James was a son of John A. Canfield and Anna Hall. His own mother had died when he was an infant, leaving his father to raise him in the Kellogg area.

In 1910 the household was James, twenty-eight; Helen, twenty-five; their daughter Marion, two; and Helen’s sister Maude Heffernan, nineteen. The sisters’ father had been born in Ireland and their mother in Minnesota. A second daughter, Helen Berle, was born on 9 November 1910.
James died on 19 June 1912, aged thirty, leaving Nel with two small daughters. He was buried at St. Agnes Cemetery in Kellogg. The girls’ next home was in Winona.

By 1920 Nel had married Tom Miller, and the two, he twenty-eight and she thirty-three, were living in Winona with Marian and Helen Canfield, Tom’s stepdaughters. Nel was Mrs. Thomas S. Miller, once Helen Heffernan, for the rest of her life, and the mother of both girls.

Nel had grown up in a houseful of Heffernans. In 1900 John and Mary’s children at home were Nelly, Kathy, Loy, Maudie and Villy, and in later life Nel’s sisters were Maude Kling and Catherine Ley and her brothers Lloyd and William. Her parents were John H. Heffernan and Mary Shea, as she herself gave them in 1939; at her death in 1948 they were set down instead as Patrick Heffernan and Ellen Shea, but it was John who died in 1910 with Mrs. James Canfield among the children at his bedside.

Mary Shea Heffernan died in Winona in March 1903, leaving her husband John; five children, Helen, Katie, Loy, Maud and Willie; her parents, Mr. and Mrs. J. Shea of Kellogg; and a brother, P. W. Shea. Her parents were Jeremiah Shea, or Shay, and Ellen, whose maiden name was Holland or perhaps Holliham, both born in Ireland. Mary herself was born at Watopa, Minnesota, probably in March 1859, though her later ages point to 1863 or 1864 and one account made her a native of St. Louis.

Helen Berle later married Arthur Nelton, a Winona-area carpenter and firefighter. Her sister Marion Canfield married in Winona in 1926 and settled in Wisconsin. Nel died at home in Winona Township in January 1948. Her daughters carried the Canfield and Heffernan family into another generation.

In 1895 the Heffernans were in Winona. John was 35 and born in Ireland, and Mary was 33 and born in Minnesota. Their children were Frank, 12, Nellie, 10, Kate, 9, Loy, 7, and a three-year-old who was almost certainly Maude, born in October 1891. When Maude died in 1958, her mother’s maiden name was given as Shay, the Shea family of Kellogg. John died in Wabasha County, the Sheas’ home county, on 26 January 1910, with Mrs. James Canfield, his daughter Nel, among the children at his bedside.

Her 1939 application names John and Mary as parents; the 1948 death index gives a different father. John’s 1910 obituaries name Mrs. James Canfield among his children, which supports John and Mary over the death index; the tree still marks them probable. stories.title: Winnie Bozarth and a family across the Red River
stories.hook: Winnie Bozarth crossed the Red River with Joel Johnson and kept a house full of children, grandchildren and, it seems, her own mother in Choctaw County.
body: On 17 May 1896, Joel A. Johnson and Minnie or Winnie W. Bozarth were married in Lee County, Texas. The young couple later crossed the Red River into what became Choctaw County, Oklahoma.

In 1910 Winnie and Joel were living in Oakes Township with five children: Aletha, Porter, George, Willie and Joel, then one year old. The older children had been born in Texas, Willie and little Joel in Oklahoma. Joel Gilbert, the youngest boy, became Rachel’s great-grandfather.

By 1920 another daughter, Audrey, had joined the family, and there was a two-year-old granddaughter, Lila Smith. Living with them was Florence Minton, fifty-eight, Joel’s mother-in-law: very probably Winnie’s own mother, whose earlier life is told below.

In 1930 Winnie and Joel lived in Boswell with their son Joel Gilbert and their granddaughter Lila, then twelve. Joel worked buying livestock, and the family remained in the Choctaw County communities where the younger children had grown up.

Joel died in 1961. Winnie, born on 1 July 1881, lived until 5 April 1969, and the two share a headstone in Boswell’s Restland Cemetery. Who Winnie’s father was, and much of her mother’s earlier life, are still uncertain, but in 1920 the Johnson house held four generations.

Florence Minton was Sarah Florence (Wilkinson) Bozarth Menton, born in Texas on 8 August 1861, the daughter of Warren G. Wilkinson, a Kentuckian by her son’s account. She had married Frank P. Bozarth in Lee County in 1876 or 1877, and in 1880 they were living there with Stella and Miles, a year before Winnie was born. Florence died in Taylor, Texas, on 28 February 1929, and her son Miles T. Bozarth answered for her at her death. Winnie’s middle name is remembered as Warren, the name of her probable grandfather. Frank and Florence were very probably Winnie’s parents, though no one has yet found them named as such.

stories.title: Building a church on Oak Ridge
stories.hook: A gathering in a neighbor’s home became a brick church for the Luxembourg families of Oak Ridge.
body: On 5 December 1875, Catholics living near Oak Ridge in Winona County met at John Speltz’s house to organize a congregation. Their meeting grew into a brick church on the ridge, where many immigrant families had settled.

Peter and John Speltz, Jacob Frisch and other neighbors saw the building through to completion. Jacob and his wife, Annette Speltz, had come from Luxembourg and made their home in the area; the Speltz men were, it seems, her kin.

Several of the Frisches were buried in the churchyard. Jacob and Annette lie together in lot 49, with an Anna said to have been Jacob’s daughter. A young son, Alois, is remembered there too, though when he lived and where his grave lies are uncertain.

Jacob died in 1906, four years after Annette. Their son John Frisch continued to farm on Oak Ridge, and his daughter Viola later married Edward Rivers. From an immigrant household on the ridge, the family had reached another generation in the Rollingstone area.

The Speltz men were probably Annette’s brothers. She was the daughter of Nicolas Spelz and Catharina Michels, and when her brother Nicholas died in 1914 he left brothers Peter and John “of Winona.” Their mother, Katherina Speltz, died in 1884 and lies in lot 49 with Jacob and Annette.

Peter Speltz was a man of standing in the township. He was chairman of the Mount Vernon Township board of supervisors in 1876 and 1877, and in 1889 the Old Settlers’ Association named him its vice-president for the township. His wife, Anna Rivers Speltz, a daughter of Michel and Margaretha Rivers, died on 16 October 1876, the year the brick church was finished, and hers was the first burial in the new churchyard.

The Speltz name stayed strong around Rollingstone. When the First State Bank of Rollingstone was incorporated in January 1905, Mathew Speltz and John Speltz stood among the incorporators beside Jacques Frisch; they may have been the Speltz brothers who had married Rivers sisters. By 1913 Roman Walch of Rollingstone had married Katherine Speltz, his sister Laura had married Arthur Speltz, and Jerome Speltz of Rollingstone had married Aline Guidinger in 1907. How those younger Speltzes were related to Anna Speltz Frisch’s brothers is not known.

stories.title: John Frisch and the farmers’ mutual
stories.hook: John Frisch served his neighbors’ fire insurance company for twenty-four years, and in 1933 his name reached the United States Senate.
body: John Frisch farmed the family place at Oak Ridge and worked for a farmers’ mutual insurance company. In January 1911 the Rollingstone Farmers Mutual Fire Insurance Company held its annual meeting in Winona, with its debts paid and a $7,000 surplus in hand, and chose John Frisch of Mount Vernon as its secretary.

His work for the mutual went on for years. He rose to be president of the Minnesota association of farmers’ mutual insurance companies. The following January his name reached Washington: John Frisch of Rollingstone, secretary of the local mutual, was among those who sent messages in support of the banking bill then before the Senate.

The bill, S. 4412, dealt with banking and the use of bank assets in the depths of the Depression. What John wrote is not known, but a farmer’s name from Rollingstone went into the Congressional Record beside those of the many businesses and organizations that joined the debate.

John moved from Oak Ridge to Rollingstone around 1929. He died on 16 March 1934. His daughter Viola had married Edward Rivers the previous year, and Edward began work as an insurance agent in Rollingstone in 1934.

His standing among the farm mutuals reached well past Winona County. At the annual meeting of the State Association of Farmers Mutual Insurance Companies in St. Paul in January 1931, John Frisch of Rollingstone was elected its president, with officers from Harris, Cottonwood and Carlton beside him, and the meeting went on record in support of the state insurance commissioner, Garfield Brown.

In October 1933, five months before he died, the national movement came to Minnesota. The National Association of Mutual Insurance Companies held its thirty-eighth annual convention at the Nicollet Hotel in Minneapolis from 9 to 12 October, and on the opening Monday, in the question-box session of the windstorm and hail group, John Frisch sat among the helpers who took questions from the floor. The program named him twice over: a director of the Farmers Home Mutual Tornado and Cyclone Insurance Company, and secretary of the Rollingstone Farmers Mutual Fire Insurance Company.

stories.title: From Rollingstone to the Mayo Clinic
stories.hook: A Rollingstone boy who served in the Navy Medical Corps in the First World War spent the rest of his career at the Mayo Clinic, studying digestive disease.
body: Andrew Baptiste Rivers was born in Rollingstone, Minnesota, on 10 December 1894, or a year later by his father’s reckoning. He followed a path into medicine that led him to Rochester. After graduating from St. Francis College in Wisconsin in 1913, he earned his medical degree at Creighton University in Omaha in 1917. He interned at the City and County Hospital in St. Paul and served in the Navy Medical Corps during the First World War.

He joined the Mayo Foundation as a fellow in medicine in 1920. He became an instructor in 1925, an assistant professor in 1932 and an associate professor of medicine in 1947, and he was also a consultant in medicine at the Mayo Clinic. His research included digestive disease.

His work went into the medical literature. In May 1933 the Journal of Clinical Investigation published “Studies of Gastric Pepsin. II. Secretion of Pepsin in Cases of Duodenal Ulcer and Pseudo-Ulcer” by Frances R. Vanzant, Arnold E. Osterberg, Walter C. Alvarez and Andrew B. Rivers, all of the Section on Chemistry and the Division of Medicine at the Mayo Clinic. Alvarez was one of the best-known American gastroenterologists of his day, and the paper measured the secretion of pepsin in people with duodenal ulcers and related symptoms.

He died suddenly on the morning of Sunday, 3 October 1948, at fifty-three, struck by a heart attack while he was at Mass in the chapel of St. Mary's Hospital. The Rochester paper filled in the rest of his life. After the first war, in which he served as a Navy lieutenant at the Marine barracks in Norfolk, Virginia, he was an assistant in medicine at the University of Minnesota before he came to Rochester in 1920. He took a master's degree in medicine from the university in 1929 and an M.A. from St. Francis College in 1930. In the Second World War he commanded the medical battalion of the Minnesota Defense Force as a lieutenant colonel, with a nurse corps battalion that drew units from Minneapolis, St. Paul, Duluth and Rochester. Among his close friends were the Notre Dame football coaches Knute Rockne, Hunk Anderson and Frank Leahy. He was buried at Rollingstone, where he was born.

Andrew died on 3 October 1948. His sister Angela, the daughter of John and Bertha Jung Rivers, outlived him by many years and died in 1976. Andrew was very probably the son Andrew whom John H. Rivers counted among his children in 1913, born on 10 December 1895 by that family account.
Just how Andrew was related to Rachel is still uncertain. The generations that would join his Rivers family to hers are not yet clear, so his exact place in her family is not known.

stories.title: Andrew Kocak on the Minneota farms
stories.hook: In 1917 Andrew Kocak was a farmhand working for John Stinar of Minneota, two years before he married Mary Stinar.
body: On 5 June 1917 Andrew Kocak registered for the draft in Minneota Township, Jackson County. He was twenty-one and single, a farm laborer working for John Stinar, with Lakefield as his home and Austria as his country. So he was already living among the Stinars before he married Mary Stinar on 27 November 1919, though whether that John Stinar was her father is not known.

By 1930 Andrew was a widower, raising Evelyn, Elizabeth and John. In April 1940 he was farming in Minneota Township with a wife named Mary, thirty-one and born in Minnesota, and children who included Elizabeth, sixteen, John, twelve, and Stephen, three, all Minnesota-born. This Mary was very probably Stephen’s mother, Mary Adeline Pavelko, the wife of Andrew John Kocak Sr.

Andrew registered again on 27 April 1942, farming on his own account in Minneota Township, with a rural Lakefield address. The person who would always know where to find him was Mrs. Andrew Kocak of Lakefield. He gave his age as forty-six and his birthplace simply as Austria–Hungary.

Andrew’s birthday moved about. In 1917 it was 24 October 1895 and in 1942 it was 24 September 1895, and his ages were thirty-five in 1930 and forty-four in 1940. At home in his village he had been born on yet another date.

He was very probably the boy András born on 25 September 1894, and baptized the next day, in the Greek Catholic parish of Magyar-Izsép, now Nižný Žipov in Slovakia, the son of Kocák András and Anna, whose surname was probably Janasko or Jánosko. The name, the place and the parents all fit, though the September 1894 date does not match the ones he gave in America.

In America his mother was remembered as Annie Janasko. Andrew Kocak of Jackson County was born, by one account, on 24 October 1895 at Magyar-Izsép, Austria–Hungary, the son of Annie Janasko; and by another, as Andrew John Kocak, on 24 October 1896, the son of Anna Janasko and Andrew Kocak. Both fit the baptism, though neither date does.

So Andrew’s family very probably goes back to András Kocák and Anna Janasko. On 23 July 1894 András Kocák, nineteen and Greek Catholic, married Anna Jánoskó, twenty and Roman Catholic, in the Roman Catholic parish of Lastovce; both lived at Magyar-Izsép. András was the son of János and the late Mária Hancsin. Anna was the daughter of Mihály and Mária, whose surname, in the priest’s hand, is read cautiously as Korpás. Two months later, it seems, their son András was born.

What became of András and Anna afterward, and how and when their son came to America, is not known. They were Evelyn’s probable grandparents and Diane’s probable great-grandparents on her mother’s side; who Diane’s birth father was is another story.

Andrew had come to America at seventeen, first to Wilkes-Barre, Pennsylvania, and a year later to Minneota Township. In the First World War he served in France. He died at the veterans' hospital in Sioux Falls on 26 June 1967, aged seventy-two, and was buried with military rites at St. Joseph's in Lakefield. His birthday was remembered as 12 September 1894, in Austria-Hungary, and his parents as Andrew and Anna Janasko Kocak, which brings him back within a fortnight of the Magyar-Izsép baptism.

Its connection to the baptism is probable, and that uncertainty carries through the added ancestry. stories.title: Beaufort, January 1862: Jacob Frisch marries Anna Spelz
stories.hook: Two years before they landed at Winona, Jacob Frisch and Anna Spelz married in the castle village of Beaufort, and both signed the register.
body: On a January day in 1862, probably the 24th, in the parish church of Beaufort in eastern Luxembourg, the pastor wrote up the marriage of Jacobus Frisch and Anna Spelz. The banns had been read three times without objection, in Beaufort and in Rosport, and the bride’s parish had sent its release. The groom was “the legitimate son of Nicolas Frisch and Maria Simon, married people in Beaufort.” The bride was the daughter “of the late Nicolas Spelz and of Catharina Michels, married people in Dickweiler, parish of Rosport.” Paulus Frisch of Beaufort and Catharina Michels of Osweiler were the witnesses. Bride and groom both signed. Anna wrote “Anna Speltz,” the spelling the family later used in Minnesota.

Jacob had been born in Beaufort on 28 October 1837 and baptized the same day, the son of Nicolas Frisch and Maria Simon; his godparents were Jacob Simon and Magdalena Frisch, both of Beaufort. That was the birthday remembered at his death in 1906, though at Oak Ridge it is sometimes given as 18 October 1836. Beaufort lies in the canton of Echternach, in the wooded sandstone country Luxembourgers call Little Switzerland, beneath the ruins of its medieval castle.

Anna came from the parish of Fischbach. She was born there on 24 October 1836, the day remembered at her death in 1902, and baptized the next day, the “legitimate daughter of Nicolas Spelz, farmer, and Catharina Michels,” in a village the priest wrote as something like “Wickelesch.” Her godparents were Nicolas Oswald of Junglinster and Anna Michels of Contern. By 1862 her father was dead and the family was living in Dickweiler, near Rosport on the Sauer River border with Prussia.

By the time of the wedding, several of Anna’s brothers were already in America. Nicholas Speltz, born at Fischbach in 1825, had married Catherine Blasen in 1852, and the couple came to America that same year and farmed at Holy Cross in Dubuque County, Iowa. When he died in 1914 he left brothers Peter and John “of Winona” and a sister, Mrs. Catherine Herber of Rollingstone. Mathew Speltz, born in 1828, is said by his family to have sailed from Antwerp on the Leopold I, reached New York on 3 July 1854, and settled near Rollingstone in 1855. Peter and John Speltz were the men who, with Jacob Frisch, saw the Oak Ridge church built. They were probably Anna’s brothers.

Jacob and Anna went later. They “came to this country in 1864, and landed at Winona on July 4 in that year,” as Anna’s family told it at her death, or in 1865 by the reckoning at Jacob’s. They were part of one of the heaviest emigrations in Europe. About 75,000 Luxembourgers left for North America in the second half of the nineteenth century, and in peak years about a tenth of the population left. Most went to farm country around the Great Lakes, traveling with people from home and settling beside earlier emigrants, as the Frisches did beside the Speltz brothers. Nicolas Gonner, whose Luxembourgish poems in Prairieblummen became the voice of these settlements, emigrated in 1865 as well.

Anna’s mother also came. In St. Mary’s cemetery on Oak Ridge a German-language stone reads “Hier ruhet Katherina Speltz, geboren zu Contern, Luxembourg, den 2 Feb. 1799, gestorben den 9 Jan. 1884.” She lies in lot 49, grave 4, the Frisch lot where Jacob and Anna, or Annette, were later buried. She is sometimes remembered as born on 2 December 1799, and as a Wagoner, but she was born Catharina Michels, the name the priest wrote at her daughter’s baptism.

The Speltz family also linked Viola Frisch's ancestors to her husband's. By the family’s account, Mathew, Peter and John Speltz married three daughters of Michel and Margaretha Rivers. Seventy years later, Anna's granddaughter Viola Frisch married Edward N. Rivers, Margaretha's great-grandson.

Nicolas Speltz came from farther up the Moselle than the family later remembered. He was born on 5 July 1796 at Greiveldange, a village in the wine country below Remich, the son of another Nicolas Speltz and the grandson of an Oswald. The elder Nicolas had been born in 1752 and died at Greiveldange on 30 April 1820. In 1822 the younger Nicolas married Katherina Michels of Contern, and over the next twenty years they had at least eight children: Nicholas in 1825, Mathew in 1828 at Contern, Maria in 1830, Catherine, called Anne, in 1833, Anna in 1836 at Fischbach, Peter in 1838, Theodore in 1840 and John in 1842. The family moved with the work, from Contern to Fischbach and at the end to Dickweiler on the Sauer, where Nicolas died on 12 October 1859 and was buried in the village churchyard, probably in an unmarked grave. He never saw Minnesota. His widow did, and so did most of her grown children: Anna and Jacob Frisch at Oak Ridge, Mathew, Peter and John near Rollingstone, and Catherine, who married a Herber.

stories.title: Margaretha Adehm, the blacksmith's daughter of Junglinster
stories.hook: In 1832 Margaretha Adehm could not write her name at her own wedding. Fifty-two years later she was buried in Rollingstone under a German stone.
body: On 12 January 1832, in the church at Heffingen, the pastor Theodor Neu married 'the honest young people' Michael Rivers and Margaritha Adehm. Michael was the son of Johann Nicolas Rivers, whom the pastor called a popinator, a tavern keeper, and of Anna Molitor, of Heffingen. Margaritha was the daughter of Johann Adehm and Margaritha Michels of Junglinster. The civil marriage had already taken place, two of the three banns had been read, and the third was dispensed. Both fathers stood by as witnesses. Michael signed 'Michell Rivers'. The bride, 'not knowing how to write', made her mark. The family was already writing its name as Rivers in Luxembourg, years before it came to America.

Margaretha had been born a few miles away in Junglinster. Maria Margaretha was born and baptized there on 16 October 1807, the daughter of Johann Adam, a ferrifaber, or blacksmith, and Margaretha Michaels, or Michels, with Henricus Adam and Maria Margaretha Hansen of Junglinster as godparents. Luxembourg was then part of Napoleon's France, as the département des Forêts. The priest spelled the family name Adam; in 1832 the pastor at Heffingen wrote Adehm, and that is the form on her gravestone.

The couple raised their children at Heffingen. Their son Henry was born there on 11 April 1838 and John Baptiste on 16 June 1840. There may have been twelve children in all, two of whom died young. In 1854 Michel and Margaretha left with their family; in the words of the county history, they “came to America in 1854, and settled on a farm in Winona county in 1855,” and by the family’s account they crossed on the Vulture, arriving at New York on 22 May 1854.

In Winona County three of Margaretha's daughters married into another Luxembourg family, the Speltzes. Margaretha married Mathew Speltz at Winona on 20 February 1857, and Mathew's brothers John and Peter married the younger Rivers girls, Elizabeth and Anna. Anna Rivers Speltz, born on 15 September 1846, died at thirty on 16 October 1876 and lies at Oak Ridge, and so does Elizabeth Rivers Speltz, John’s wife, born on 10 June 1850, who died on 10 January 1905 after a lamp explosion. The Speltz brothers were probably the brothers of Anna Speltz Frisch, the grandmother of Viola Frisch.

Michel died suddenly in January 1880. 'He attended a special mass at the church on Saturday and was, apparently, in his usual health when he went to bed, but during the night he was taken ill, and died about five o'clock,' the Winona Daily Republican reported. His stone in Holy Trinity cemetery quotes the Book of Wisdom in German: 'Die gerechten Seelen sind in Gottes Hand.' Margaretha outlived him by four years. Her stone, in row 9, reads 'Margarehta Rivers, geboren Adehm, geboren Junglinster, Luxembourg 1808. Gest. den 9 Oct. 1884.' The carver gave her a birth year one later than the true one.

Her family and the Speltz family met again in 1933, when her great-grandson Edward N. Rivers married Viola Frisch, a great-granddaughter of Katharina Michels Speltz. Both women had come from Catholic villages a few hours' walk apart in the Grand Duchy. One was buried in Rollingstone's Holy Trinity cemetery, and the other on Oak Ridge.

stories.title: Eleven Neltons under one roof
stories.hook: In 1895 eleven Neltons shared one house in Winona’s First Ward, with a Zenk widow and her seven children close by, and no grandmother named Elsie anywhere.
body: In 1895 the Nelton house in Winona’s First Ward was full. George Nelton, 39, born in Germany, was the head of it. Next came Eda, 40, also German-born, and then Willie, 21, born in Germany, followed by Anna, 16, Charles, 15, George, 14, Winnie, 13, Lizzie, 11, Eda, 6, Harry, 5, and the baby Elsa, 1. Everyone after Willie had been born in Minnesota. Ten years later George, 52, and Eda, 53, were still in the First Ward, with Henry, 15, and Elsie, 11, at home.

George’s mother is sometimes said to have been an Elsie Nelton, born in Germany about 1837, but no one has yet found any trace of her. No older Nelton woman lived anywhere in Winona County in the years from 1865 to 1905, and no one of her generation lived with George and Eda in 1895 or 1905. The only Elsie in the family was their youngest daughter, Elsa in 1895 and Elsie in 1905, later Elsie Bitu, who died in 1968. The grandmother Elsie is doubtful at best, and quite possibly a mistake in which the daughter’s name was given to a grandmother.

Eda had family close by. Two doors from the Neltons lived a widow, Theresa Zenk, 38, born in Wisconsin, with Mary, Charles, Eda, Rosa, George, Frank and a little Theresa. She had been in Winona at least twenty years. In 1875 George Zink, 26, and his wife Theresa, 19, were living in the city, and in 1885 George Zink, 35, born in Germany, and his Wisconsin-born wife, 27, had children named Mary, Chas, Ida and Rosa. By 1905 Theresa Zenk was still in the First Ward with her grown children. The name was spelled the same way when George Nelton married “Ida Sink (Zink)” on 9 December 1879. A German-born George Zink, close to Eda in age, whose daughter was named Ida and whose widow lived two doors away, was very likely Eda’s brother, though no one has yet found it said outright.

There may have been an older generation too. In 1885 Ernst Zenk, 62, and Caroline Zenk, 62, both born in Prussia, were living in Mount Vernon Township in Winona County, and in 1895 Caroline, or Carlina, Zink, 75, born in Germany, was still in Mount Vernon. They were old enough to be Eda’s parents, but nothing yet connects them to her, and whether they were is uncertain.

Where Eda was born is not quite settled. She is sometimes placed in Pommern in the Rhineland, a wine village on the Mosel in Cochem-Zell, but in America she was only ever German-born, and the Zenks of Mount Vernon called themselves Prussian. “Pommern” is also the German name of Pomerania, the Prussian province on the Baltic, which sent a large share of Germany’s emigrants overseas, about 95,000 of them between 1881 and 1885 alone. The Mosel village was in Prussia’s Rhine Province too, so “Prussia” does not settle the question. Germany is the safest answer, with Pomerania the likelier reading of “Pommern” and nothing to point to Cochem-Zell.

Eda was certainly the mother of the children who carried the family on. Charles Nelton (1 January 1880 – 1963), Anna Bertha Knopp (7 June 1879 – 1974) and Elsie E. Bitu (29 January 1896 – 1968) were each born to a Zenk mother. Anna’s and Charles’s birth dates, seven months apart, cannot both be right, and the ages of 1895 do not all fit: Elsa was one in 1895, though Elsie was born in January 1896, and Willie, born in Germany around 1874, was older than the 1879 marriage. When Winnie died in 1966 she was remembered with a deceased brother, William Lutz, and a deceased sister, Lizzie Plank. Whether they were the Willie and Lizzie of 1895 is not known. Eda died in Winona on 30 December 1943, aged ninety-one. Her small flat stone at Woodlawn reads simply “Mother.”

stories.title: Margaretha Bill of Wilsenroth
stories.hook: Margaret Bill Haines remembered a German village called “Wilsenrode.” Its register, kept by the priest at Frickhofen, names the farmer’s daughter born there at one in the morning at the end of August 1839, and her parents and grandparents with her.
body: Margaret Bill Haines told her family she had been born at “Wilsenrode” in Germany, and the place is real. Wilsenroth is a farming village on the eastern edge of the Westerwald, and in her childhood it belonged to the Amt of Hadamar in the Duchy of Nassau. It had no parish of its own. Its births, marriages and deaths were entered by the priest of the neighbouring parish of Frickhofen, in printed books with a column for everything: the hour of birth, the father’s trade, the mother’s birthplace.

In the book for 1839 the eleventh child of the year is Margaretha Bill, a daughter, born in Wilsenroth on the thirty-first of August at one o’clock in the night. Her father was Johann Bill, a farmer, born and living in Wilsenroth; her mother was Katharina Göbel, his second wife, born at Weltersburg, farther up in the Westerwald. The priest added that she was the second child of the second marriage, and that the first marriage had left no children.

In America she would give her birthday as 22 August 1840. The register puts it a year and nine days earlier. It holds no other Margaretha Bill in 1839 or 1840, and no Bill birth at all in 1840. Why the dates part is not known; the register is the older witness.

Her parents had married in the parish on 17 January 1837. Johann was twenty-seven and already a widower, born in Wilsenroth on 17 November 1809, the son of Johann Georg Bill, a farmer, and Maria Paul. Katharina was nearly thirty-two, born on 13 January 1805, the daughter of Matthias Göbel, a farmer, and Anna Maria Weiß of Weltersburg. Their first child, a girl, was stillborn in April 1838. Margaretha came next, and a sister, Catharina Mauritia, was born on 20 September 1841.

The rest of the story was told in America. Margaret came over as a child with her parents, who settled at Utica, New York, and in 1856 she married Christian Haines at Herkimer; the years after that are told in “Maggie Haines of Arcadia.” When she died in 1916 she left two sisters: Mrs. Kundt, still in Utica, and Elizabeth, the wife of Engelhart Doelle of Cross Township, Buffalo County. The valley in Arcadia Township where she and Christian farmed had been settled in 1860 by a John Bill, Sr., and was named for him. He was very probably her father, Johann, come west from Utica.

The family cannot have left Nassau before the autumn of 1844. On the last day of September that year Katharina gave birth to a son at Wilsenroth, at four in the afternoon, and the priest entered him as Johann Gerhard Bill in the same book as his sisters. In America he would be John Bill Jr. The Bills settled at Utica, in upstate New York, where they would remember living about twenty years, and there a last daughter, Elizabeth, was born in July 1847.

By 1870 John and Catharine were farming in Arcadia Township, in Trempealeau County, with their son John, then twenty-four, still at home. The census taker wrote all three down as natives of Prussia, which by then had swallowed Nassau, and noted that Catharine could not read or write. She died on 2 February 1873 and was buried at St. Joseph's, Glencoe, just over the line in Buffalo County, under a stone that calls her the wife of Johan Bill and carries a German verse. John outlived her by twenty-four years. He died on 30 April 1897, aged eighty-seven, and lies near her.

Catharina, the sister born in 1841, married Nicholas Kaut and stayed in Utica when the rest went west. She died there in September 1921 and was buried in St. Peter's Cemetery, and she was very probably the 'Mrs. Kundt of Utica' who outlived Margaret in 1916. John Jr. farmed near Glencoe and died in January 1914; Elizabeth, Mrs. Engelhart Doelle, died in April 1920.

So both halves of the Haines farm in Bill’s Valley came out of small German states that Prussia later swallowed. Christian was born a subject of Hohenzollern, which passed to Prussia in 1850; Margaret was born in Nassau, which Prussia annexed in 1866, ten years after she married.

stories.title: Maggie Haines of Arcadia
stories.hook: Viola Frisch’s mother grew up across the Mississippi in Arcadia, Wisconsin, the daughter of a beekeeper who once took 7,500 pounds of honey from his hives in a single year.
body: Maggie C. Haines was born on 17 July 1875 at Arcadia, in Trempealeau County, Wisconsin, about twenty-five miles up the Trempealeau valley from the Mississippi crossing at Winona. She was a daughter of Christian C. Haines (1835–1914) and Margaret A. (or Margareta) Bill (1840–1916), of Bill’s Valley in Arcadia Township, and she carried her mother’s name.

Her father had come a long way. Christian Haines was born in Hohenzollern, Germany, on 11 October 1835 and came to America with his parents in 1856. They settled at Herkimer, New York, where he married Margaret Bill that same year. She had been born at “Wilsenrode, Germany,” on 22 August 1840 as the family remembered it (the village register says 31 August 1839), and had grown up at Utica. Two years after they landed, Christian’s father died at Herkimer and was buried there, and the family moved on to Canastota; his brother John B. Haines would follow him west to Arcadia. Christian kept a store at Canastota, New York, until the end of the Civil War. “He was unfortunate in business, however, and lost all he had,” as the county’s historian put it in 1917, and he came west to Fountain City and then to a farm in Bill’s Valley, the valley John Bill Sr., very probably Margaret’s own father, had settled in 1860.

There he did well with bees. He was “a skilled apiarist, keeping numerous colonies of bees, and producing as much as 7,500 pounds of honey in one year, also taking first premiums at county and state fairs.” He served on the Arcadia town board. He and Margaret belonged to the Church of Our Lady of Perpetual Help at Arcadia, and by 1917, “of their family of 14 children nine are now living.” Maggie would have been one of the five who had died. Two of the sons, John and Adam, bought 372 acres from their father and built a two-story brick house on what was called “one of the best farms in Trempealeau County.”

Maggie’s brothers did well on the Arcadia ridges. Edward, born in Herkimer County, New York, on 12 March 1858 and brought west as a boy in 1865, married Julia Woutchik on 23 October 1882 and took her to a rented farm in Bill’s Valley. In 1883 he lost nearly everything he had, but in August 1884 he bought 180 acres of partly improved land in Meyers Valley, moved his family into a log house covered with boards, and built the place up until it was 488 acres, with an eleven-room brick house and a stone milk house. Two of his fifteen children, Anna and Agnes, entered the Convent of Notre Dame at Milwaukee, and he served two years as supervisor of Arcadia Township. Joseph W., born on 7 July 1863, bought the 200-acre Pleasant View Farm in 1889, married Anna K. George of Glencoe on 7 January 1890, and kept bees like his father; he and Anna had eighteen children, and he sat for many years on the Cortland school board.

Maggie married John Frisch, a schoolteacher from the Luxembourg settlement on Oak Ridge, Winona County, Minnesota, the son of Jasques Frisch and Anna Speltz. The wedding is remembered as 1 October 1901, and she died on what was called their fifth anniversary, but at Arcadia it was set down under 6 October, five days later, and which is right is not known. Like the Frisches, the Haineses were Catholic farmers, and Maggie’s sister Anna Haines Frisch (1869–1956) seems to have married a Frisch too.

Maggie had little time. She died on Oak Ridge in October 1906, on what was remembered as their fifth wedding anniversary, fourteen days after the birth of her third child. The Winona Republican-Herald gave her origins in a single line: “She was formerly Miss Maggie Haines of Arcadia and thirty years of age.”

Her life joined two immigrant valleys that faced each other across the river. On the Minnesota side were the Luxembourg Catholics of Oak Ridge and Rollingstone; on the Wisconsin side, German Catholic farm families like the Haineses, who had reached Arcadia by way of New York State. The daughter she left at sixteen months, Viola, grew up to marry Edward Rivers of Rollingstone. Maggie lies in St. Mary’s Cemetery on Oak Ridge beside John, who outlived her by twenty-seven years.

In Germany the family name had been Hoeneß. Christian was baptized at Stetten unter Holstein, in the hills of Hohenzollern, the son of Anton Hoeneß and Genofeva Würz, who had married at nearby Hörschwag in 1833; their eldest son, John Baptist, was the John B. Haines who followed Christian to Arcadia. Genofeva, Genevieve in America, outlived her husband by nearly thirty years and died at Arcadia in 1885.

Behind them stood a small walled town on the Swabian Alb. Anton Hoeneß had been born at Trochtelfingen in the spring of 1798, the son of Anton Henes and Anna Maria Görle, who had married there in 1791. Genofeva Würz grew up in the same town, the daughter of Christian Würz and Christina Locher; by the time she married Anton in 1833, her family had moved over the hills to Hörschwag, and her mother lay buried in the churchyard at Stetten unter Holstein.

When Anton was born in 1798, Trochtelfingen was not yet a Hohenzollern town at all. Since 1534 it had belonged to the counts, later princes, of Fürstenberg, who had it from the last of the Werdenbergs, and the Werdenberg castle of about 1450 still stood inside the walls near the old church of St. Martin. A boundary map drawn in 1717 shows the town as a huddle of red roofs and a round tower on the edge of the Alb, with the arms of Württemberg, Fürstenberg and Hohenzollern painted on the fields around it. Napoleon's reordering of the German states handed it to Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen in 1806, when Anton was eight, and in 1850 all of Hohenzollern passed to Prussia. The boy born a Fürstenberg subject left for America, six years later, a Prussian.

Christian Haines died of cancer at Arcadia on 26 November 1914 and was buried from the Catholic church there two days later. Margaret, an invalid after many strokes, followed on 3 May 1916. Of their children, nine survived her, among them Annie, Mrs. Matt Frisch of Oak Ridge. Margaret left two sisters: Mrs. Kundt, still in Utica, and Elizabeth, the wife of Engelhart Doelle of the town of Cross, in Buffalo County. Where Margaret herself began, in a Westerwald village of the Duchy of Nassau, is told in “Margaretha Bill of Wilsenroth.”

stories.title: From Monticello to Elm Grove
stories.hook: Charles H. Bell came to Collin County as a Kentucky boy, buried his first wife at twenty-nine, and fathered at least thirteen children around Anna.
body: On 4 February 1870 A. F. Snow wrote a short note to the clerk of the Wayne County Court in Kentucky: “give Benjamin Bell licens to marry Marry Ann Snow.” Benjamin Bell and C. T. Bell signed the bond that day, and on 10 February the couple were married at A. Snow’s house in Monticello, the county seat. The clerk set down the groom as a twenty-six-year-old farmer and the bride as eighteen, both born in Wayne County. Wayne County lies on Kentucky’s southern border with Tennessee, on the edge of the Cumberland Plateau; eight years earlier the Battle of Mill Springs had been fought on the Cumberland River at its northern edge.

Ben had been born in Wayne County on 15 January 1848, a son of Jerry Mitchel Bell and Nancy Ellen Davis. A “Jerimiah” Bell and Nancy Davis had married in the county on 1 June 1837, and in 1850 Jeremiah and Nancy Bell, 32 and 31, were living there with children who included a Benjamin, 2. His bride, Mary Ann, called Polly, was a daughter of A. J. Snow and his wife, Mary Ann.

The man who stood surety for Jerimiah Bell’s bond in 1837 was a Linsey Bell, who may have been an older brother, an uncle or a cousin. The county had more than one Jeremiah Bell by 1840, and which of them was Ben’s father is still not known.

Ben and Polly had nine children. Alice Vida came first, in 1871, and Charles H. Bell second, on 2 June 1873. Dora Ellen followed in 1875, Tom in 1878, Martha Clementine in 1881, Frank Marion in 1883 and John Anderson on 19 September 1885, all in Wayne County. In June 1880 the family was living at Mullentown, in the Susie district of Wayne County: Benjamin, 33, and Polly A., 28, both born in Kentucky, with Alice V., 9; Charles H., 6, born in Kentucky; Dora A., 4; and Thomas A., 1. The next child, Joseph Wade, was born on 12 January 1889 at Plano, in Collin County, Texas, so the family made the move west sometime in those three years.

Charles was very probably Ben and Polly’s son, though no one has yet found his parents named. The signs all point the same way: the six-year-old Charles H. in Ben and Polly’s house in 1880, his Wayne County birth in the gap between Alice and Dora, the family’s move to Collin County, his burial in the same cemetery, and the name of his son Willie Ben. And on a family photograph of Ben and Mary Ann in their later years, someone wrote by hand that they were the “parents of Charles H. Bell.”

In Collin County Charles married Clara Jane Snow, born in Kentucky in April 1875. Their son Lewis Browder Bell was born on 13 October 1892, when Charles was nineteen. Two more sons followed, Troy Leonard and Lee Hercules, both said to have been born at Anna in 1897, three weeks apart, on 12 August and 4 September; one of those dates must be wrong. When Lee died in 1949, his mother was named as Clara Shelton. There was also a daughter, Marietta. Clara died in 1902, aged twenty-six or twenty-seven, and was buried at Elm Grove Cemetery near Anna.

Charles married again that year. Mary Alice Baker was born on 19 June 1875 in Wayne County, Kentucky, the daughter of Charles W. Baker and Amanda Joe Pate, though some records give 1874; she was still at home there, single, in 1900. Charles and Mary Alice did not start out at Anna. Their first child, Willie Ben Bell, was born on 1 June 1903 in Red River County, Texas, on the Oklahoma line, and by 2 May 1908, when Edna Lola was born, the family was back at Anna. Between 1903 and 1920 Mary Alice had ten children: Willie Ben, Ora, Iva, Edna Lola, Bonnie Alice, Effie Jane, Charlie, Wayne Douglas, Jack Watson and Glen Hardy. Wayne, Rachel’s great-grandfather, was born at Anna on 18 April 1914.

Anna had been platted beside the Houston and Texas Central tracks in 1883 and incorporated in 1913. Collin County was then at its peak as farm country, with 6,001 farms in 1920 and a crop that year of 49,311 bales of cotton and more than two and a half million bushels of corn.

Ben Bell, a farmer, died at Anna on 22 May 1926, aged seventy-eight by the 1848 on his gravestone, although the age of twenty-six the clerk wrote down at his wedding points to about 1844. Charles died in Collin County on 2 October 1930, aged fifty-seven, and Polly on 22 August 1936. All three lie at Elm Grove, with Clara, Charles’s brother Frank, and Lee Hercules nearby. Willie Ben died at Sherman on 15 August 1950, aged forty-seven, and was buried at Elm Grove too. Mary Alice lived until 1945 and shares a marker with Charles.

Not every Bell child stayed at Anna. Dora, John and Martha Clementine are buried in Van Alstyne Cemetery, which also holds Cleave and Willie Williams, whose daughter Melba married Wayne Bell in 1937. When one of Charles’s daughters died in 1968, her surviving brothers and sisters were spread from Van Alstyne to Galesburg, Illinois, but Hardy was still at Anna, a few miles from the Elm Grove graves.
Charles, a farmer, died at Rosamond Chapel on 2 October 1930 and was buried at Elm Grove the same day; Mary Alice died at McKinney on 16 May 1945 after a third stroke and was buried beside him.

stories.title: Florence Wilkinson and the wagon to Mexico
stories.hook: Winnie Bozarth's mother married at fourteen or fifteen in Lee County; in 1882 a sheriff's posse caught a Frank Bozarth and his family's wagon on the Matagorda prairie.
body: In June 1882 the Brenham Weekly Banner carried the news that Sheriff Brown of Lee County and three men had captured Frank Bozarth, “charged with crockedness in cattle transactions in Lee county, he being specifically charged with the theft of oxen.” Bozarth had taken his family to Matagorda County. The posse found him on the open prairie fifteen miles from the town of Matagorda: “he was on horseback and his family was in a wagon; they were on the move to Mexico.” When he ran, one of the posse shot his horse in the shoulder; it went two hundred yards on three legs and fell. He drew his revolver, thought better of it, and surrendered. The sheriff took him by train to Giddings, and “the prisoner’s family will follow him to Lee county to-day—Saturday.” Two weeks later the Banner noted that the Giddings Plaindealer could not find out how “Bozarth, the escaped prisoner,” had got hold of whatever he used to bulldoze the jailer.

His wife was not named, but she was very probably Florence. Frank P. Bozarth married S. F. Wilkinson in Lee County on 25 January 1877, or perhaps on 21 January 1876. Born on 8 August 1861, she was fourteen at the earlier date and fifteen at the later. In June 1880 the household of Frank Bozart, or Bozarth, twenty-one, born in Mississippi, farming in Precinct 1 of Lee County, included Florence, eighteen, born in Texas, Stella, two, and Miles, one, both children born in Texas. Winnie was born on 1 July 1881. If the Frank Bozarth of 1882 was the same man, as the name, county and family suggest, then the wagon on the Matagorda prairie probably carried Florence and three small children, the youngest under a year old.

When Florence died, her son gave her father’s name as “Waren G. Wilkingson,” born in Kentucky, and her mother’s only as “Miss Daugherty,” born in Tennessee. In 1880, when the answer very probably came from Florence or Frank, both her parents had been Tennesseans; forty-nine years later her son, who may never have known his grandfather, said Kentucky. Either could be wrong. A Warren Gall Wilkinson was a brother of James Gore Wilkinson, a San Jacinto veteran born in Hardin County, Kentucky, in 1805, whose family settled in what became Washington County in the days of the Republic of Texas. James fought at San Jacinto in April 1836 in Captain William W. Hill’s company; he received a bounty certificate for 320 acres in 1837 and a donation certificate for 640 acres in 1838, and his father, Captain James G. Wilkinson, held a league of land in Austin’s Fifth Colony. James died in 1848 and was first buried near Dime Box, in country that became part of Lee County when the county was formed in 1874 from parts of Burleson, Washington, Bastrop and Fayette counties. In 1938 the State of Texas moved James and his wife Amanda from their graves near Yegua Creek to the Texas State Cemetery in Austin. That Warren may have been Florence’s father, but nothing yet links the two, and the idea rests on the Kentucky birthplace, which the Tennessee of 1880 makes less likely. Somewhere in or near the old Washington and Burleson county country that became Lee County in 1874 there was, very probably, a Wilkinson household with a daughter, Sarah Florence, born in Texas about 1861, and a mother born a Daugherty. No one has yet found it, and until someone does, Warren G. Wilkinson’s birthplace, Kentucky or Tennessee, is uncertain.

Little is known of the years after 1882. A Florence Bozarth married N. C. Olsen in Lee County on 4 May 1890; she may be the same woman, but nothing more is known of an Olsen household. By 1920 Florence was living across the Red River at Oakes, Choctaw County, Oklahoma, in the house of Joel and Winnie Johnson, as Florence Minton, fifty-eight, born in Texas, Joel’s mother-in-law. Winnie, who had married Joel in Lee County in 1896, had the middle initial W, and she is remembered as Winnie Warren Johnson.

About August 1923 Florence moved to Taylor, in Williamson County, where her son Miles T. Bozarth also lived. Taylor was a railroad and cotton-shipping town founded in 1876 and settled heavily by Czech and German immigrants; two years before she arrived, floods on the San Gabriel River and Brushy Creek had killed eighty-seven people around it. She lived at 1129 Victoria Street. She died there on 28 February 1929, aged sixty-seven, of pneumonia, with influenza as a contributing cause, as “Mrs. Sarah F. Menton,” a widowed housewife. M. T. Bozarth gave the particulars, and she was buried in the Taylor City Cemetery on 1 March.

Miles was her son, and when he died in 1946 he was remembered as the son of Frank Bozarth and Florence Wilkinson. So Mrs. Sarah F. Menton of Taylor, the Florence Minton of Oakes and Florence Wilkinson Bozarth were very probably one woman, Sarah Florence (Wilkinson) Bozarth Menton. Her age, birthplace and married names, and the 1920 household, all agree. She was very probably Winnie’s mother, though no one has yet found Winnie’s parents named.
