stories.title: Anton Klemenčić, the hired man from Jarnevići
stories.hook: Diane's birth father was probably a Croatian farmhand known in Minnesota as Tom Klensky, who worked a few farms from Evelyn Kocak's family in 1938.
body: In April 1940 Lawrence Roslansky’s rented farm in Minneota Township, Jackson County, was home to Lawrence, his wife Mamie, two small children and a hired hand, Thomas Klensky, 49, divorced, born in Yugoslavia, with three years of schooling. He had worked there all year and had lived in the same house in 1935. Six households further along the same road was the farm of Andrew Kocak, Evelyn’s father, and Evelyn’s uncle Joe Stinar lived close by as well.

His name was written a dozen ways. He was born Anton Klemenčić (Croatian Antun) in Jarnevići, a hamlet of a few houses in the parish of Lipnik, municipality of Ribnik, in the hills of Karlovac County northwest of Karlovac, near the Kupa river and the Slovenian border. American clerks wrote him down as Anton Klemencic, Tom Klensky, Tom Klenskiy, Thomas Klensky, Thomas Klinsky, Anton Klenskiy and Anton Klensky; his brother in Kansas used Klements. His birthday wandered too: 12 June 1887 in 1942, 2 July 1887 in 1917, 9 June 1886 to the immigration authorities, and 6 June 1886 on his gravestone.

He came to America at seventeen, sailing from Bremen on the steamer Dresden and landing at Baltimore in May 1903 as “Anton Klemencic,” a single Croatian laborer whose last home had been Ribnik. He could not read or write, and he was bound for a friend in Plum Alley, Pittsburgh. Within three weeks another seventeen-year-old from his hamlet, Lovro Klemenčić, a kinsman but probably not a brother, followed him on the Köln to an uncle in Braddock, Pennsylvania; as Lawrence Klements he later settled in Kansas City, Kansas, married Helen Dragush in 1910, raised eight children and died there on 26 March 1933. When he died, at the home of his brother Peter, the survivors named were brothers Peter, Steve and John and a sister Anna; neither Anton nor Rudolph was among them. Like many young men from Lipnik parish, Anton went on to the packing-house districts: in 1908 and again in 1916 a Tom Klensky was living near Thirtieth and Q streets in South Omaha, the stockyards neighborhood. By June 1917 he was in Minnesota. Registering for the draft that month, he signed himself “Tom Klenskiy,” gave his age as 30 and his birthplace as “Jarnevic, Austria,” and was single and working as a farm laborer for John Denker in Sioux Valley Township, Jackson County. He did not stay long. In 1918 and 1920 he was back in South Omaha, rooming at 2701 Q Street with other Croatian packing-house hands.

On 3 August 1929 he married Hazel Stevens in Jackson County. The couple moved to Omaha, where in 1932 Thos and Hazel Klensky were living on South 12th Street and Hazel worked as an inspector at the Brandeis department store. The marriage did not last. In October 1933 Hazel filed for divorce in Omaha, citing non-support, and by 1935 Tom was back in Jackson County as Lawrence Roslansky’s hired man. There seem to have been no children of the marriage.

Evelyn Kocak was seventeen in the autumn of 1938, living at home on the Kocak farm. In February 1939 she married Henry Garms in a small ceremony at the St. Joseph’s parsonage in Lakefield, and on 10 August 1939 Diane was born; she was adopted by Edward and Viola Rivers of Rollingstone. No one knows for certain who Diane’s father was. Her descendants’ DNA shows that he was of Croatian ancestry, from the same small corner of Karlovac County as Jarnevići, a heritage Henry Garms did not share. Anton was the only Croatian-born man living in Minneota Township in 1940, his home was a few farms from the Kocaks’, and the surnames of his close family, Klemenčić and Fabac, run through the families of Diane’s distant Croatian cousins. Together these make him her probable father, though not a proven one.

Rachel carries the same heritage. Some 13 percent of her DNA traces to Central Croatia, the region that takes in Karlovac and the hills around Lipnik, and another 2 percent to Northwestern Croatia and Istria. All of it comes from one parent, the same parent who carries her Pomeranian German Nelton ancestry and the Eastern Slovak share that comes from Evelyn Kocak’s family, so the Croatian ancestry came down through David Nelton and his mother, Diane. About 15 percent is close to what one fully Croatian great-grandfather would leave, and it fits a man born in Jarnevići to Croatian parents, though it cannot by itself name him.

He stayed on the Roslansky farm into the Second World War. On 27 April 1942, at 54, he registered for the “old man’s draft” as Anton Klenskiy of Lakefield, born at “Ribenik, Yugoslavia,” with Lawrence Roslansky as both his employer and the person who would always know his address. The registrar noted a tall man, five feet eleven, with blue eyes and a scar on the right side of his nose. He later returned to Omaha, and he died there on 6 April 1963, aged 76, living at 6820 South 30th Street, where he had been since at least 1951. His friends called him “Foots.” His survivors were a brother, Rudolph Klements of Kansas City, Kansas, and brothers Mark and Ivan Klements and a sister, Mrs. Mary Fabac, all in Yugoslavia. After a rosary and a funeral from the Larkin Funeral Home he was buried in Calvary Cemetery, Omaha.

His brother Rudolph, known as Roy (1889–1974), had come over in 1904 and settled in the Croatian community of Kansas City, Kansas. He married Barbara Srakočić, whose parents came from the same district, and raised four children there: Joseph, Frank, Dorothy and Lawrence. Anton’s parents were most likely Josip Klemenčić and Dora (Dorothea) Tomašić, who married at Lipnik on 23 November 1881; when Rudolph married in 1911 he named a Joseph and a Dorothea as his parents. Josip had tried America himself. In June 1898, at 42 and married, he crossed on the München with his brother to join kin in Pittsburgh, and he is said to have died at Ribnik in 1940. Of their children, Anton and Rudolph made their lives in America. The Lawrence from the same hamlet who was once counted as a third brother was probably a cousin. Milan sailed on the Leviathan in 1928 to join their brother Ivan on Avenue J in Chicago, and later went home; he died at Ribnik in 1981. The youngest, Mara, stayed in Yugoslavia and married Mijo Fabac, and as Mrs. Mary Fabac she outlived both Anton and Rudolph. In the 1840s and 1850s a large Klemenčić household lived in Jarnevići, very probably Josip’s parents’ generation.

stories.title: The Williams place in McNairy County
stories.hook: In 1850 Thomas Williams, an Alabama-born farmer, and his wife Dorcas were raising six children in McNairy County, Tennessee, the youngest a three-year-old boy called Thomas.
body: In 1850 the Williams family farmed in the ninth civil district of McNairy County, Tennessee: Thomas Williams, 38, a farmer born in Alabama, owning land worth $150; Dorcas, 42, born in Tennessee; and Martha, 16, Sarah, 13, Catharine, 12, John, 9, Joseph, 6, and Thomas, 3. Neither parent could read or write, but the three younger school-age children had been to school that year.

The three-year-old was very probably Thomas Henry Williams, born on 9 February 1847 in McNairy County, and so Thomas, the farmer at the head of the house, and Dorcas, his wife, were very probably his father and mother. The household, his age and his birthplace all agree.

Thomas was born about 1812, or perhaps 1808, and Dorcas about 1808, or 1807; ages were given loosely in those years. Thomas was an Alabamian, though from where in Alabama is not known. He is sometimes said to have been born at Cherokee, in Colbert County, but Colbert County was not created until 1867.

Dorcas has come down in the family as a McAfee, and two doors away lived William McAfee, a 47-year-old Tennessee-born farmer, with a son William, 12, and Sarah McAfee, 31. A McAfee household so close fits that memory, but who Dorcas’s parents were is not known. Dorcus McAfee Williams (1807–1880) is said to lie at Clear Creek Cemetery near Stantonville, and Thomas T. Williams (1808–1880) at New Hope Church Cemetery near Eastview, though just where in either ground is not known.

McNairy County, on the Mississippi line, was hill farm country, and in the Civil War it was badly divided. “A large per cent of the people of the county adhered to the Union,” as one family history puts it, and “it became impossible to live in the county without taking sides.” The family tells that young Thomas served as a drummer boy, though no one has ever found anything to bear it out. The same history gives him other parents, Thomas and Henriette Williams of Stewart County, but the McNairy household, with a boy Thomas of the right age in the county where he was born, fits much better.

By the late 1860s Thomas Henry had crossed into neighboring Hardin County and married Rebecca Jane Britton, the daughter of a Shiloh-country farmer. About 1891 the couple took their family to Texas, where both are buried at Van Alstyne. Their son Cleave was Melba Bell's father.

stories.title: The Britton farm in the Shiloh country
stories.hook: Rebecca Britton was three months old in the summer of 1850 and twelve when two armies met near her father’s farm in Hardin County, Tennessee.
body: The youngest person in William Britton’s house in the summer of 1850 was a girl of three months, Rebecca. Her father, William, was a 55-year-old farmer born in Kentucky who could not read or write. Her mother, Mary N., was 32 and born in Alabama. The rest of the Hardin County household was James, 23; Nancy, 18; John, 15; Green, 13; Charlotte, 12; America, 9; William H., 3; and Nathaniel, 2.

James and Nancy were born when Mary was only nine or fourteen years old, so they were very likely children of an earlier wife. The family’s own history says the same: William’s first wife probably died around the time Nancy was born, and he then married Mary, who was eighteen years younger. The first wife’s name is not known.

Ten years later the household was still together: William, 60, a Kentucky-born farmer with real estate worth $1,000 and a personal estate of $2,500, and Mary A., 41, now said to be Tennessee-born, with Charlotte, America, William H., Nathaniel, Rebecca J., 11, and three younger children, Emily, 8, Ann, 4, and Archiles D., three months old. William and Mary were very probably Rebecca Jane’s father and mother. She was born on 14 February 1850, just right for a girl of three months that June.

Much about her parents is uncertain. Mary was born in Alabama, or perhaps Tennessee, and may have been a Patterson. William died in 1866, perhaps on 5 June, and Mary about 1870, or perhaps after 1880; where they are buried is not known. William’s own parents are a puzzle. He is sometimes called a son of Levi Britton and Nancy Jane Daniels, and sometimes of a Frances “Frankie” Pounds Britton (1779–1850), but no one has yet found either borne out, and the titled “Sir” Brittains sometimes set above him have nothing behind them at all.

Rebecca’s own memories came down to her granddaughter Kathleen and into the Taylor family history. She remembered hearing the steamboats on the Tennessee River as a child. She said her father was a wealthy planter who held slaves and that she had her own slave to dress her. And she told how, during the Battle of Shiloh, 6–7 April 1862, a cannon shell hit a barrel of molasses in the family kitchen. They are family stories. A farm with $1,000 in land in 1860 was a working farm of middling size rather than a great plantation; how many people William held in slavery is told in the story of one girl on the Britton place.

What is certain is the setting. Pittsburg Landing, where the Union army camped in spring 1862, is in Hardin County, a few miles southwest of the county seat at Savannah. The battle fought around Shiloh Church that April was one of the bloodiest of the war up to that time. Rebecca, then twelve, married Thomas Henry Williams of McNairy County in the late 1860s. Their son Cleave was born near Shiloh in 1887, and about 1891 the family moved to Texas. Rebecca died at Sherman in 1927 and is buried at Van Alstyne.

stories.title: James Parker's war and the road to Van Alstyne
stories.hook: James Parker may have been the Jefferson County recruit who deserted the Union army in July 1864; he and Amanda Pipkin ended their days in Texas, under matching stones at Van Alstyne.
body: Two tall gray stones stand together in the Greer section of Van Alstyne Cemetery. One reads “Father / James M. Parker / Born Apr. 6, 1844 / Died Nov. 26, 1910 / Gone but not forgotten.” The other reads “Amanda / wife of J. Parker / Born Feb. 8, 1850 / Died Dec. 27, 1899.”

James was born in 1844 by his stone, or perhaps in 1843, in Jefferson County, in southern Illinois. A James M. Parker enlisted at Jefferson County on 8 March 1864 as a private in Company E, 11th Illinois Infantry, and was mustered the same day. On 16 July 1864 he deserted, and one modern remembrance of him puts it bluntly: “He was a Civil War deserter from the Union.” The county, the name and the age all fit, but whether the soldier was the Van Alstyne man is not certain.

The 11th Illinois was a hard-used regiment. It had fought at Fort Donelson and Shiloh and in the siege of Vicksburg. In the weeks before the desertion date it was based at Vicksburg, and on 1–7 July 1864 it marched on an expedition to Jackson, Mississippi, fighting three actions, before returning to Vicksburg until late July. A new recruit in that summer of heat, sickness and skirmishing was a long way from southern Illinois. Why he left is not known. He seems never to have drawn a pension, which a deserter’s record would usually have barred.

After the war James went home to southern Illinois and, in 1868 it seems, married Amanda Pipkin. Their son James Edward was born on 23 March 1870 in Franklin County, Illinois, and their daughter Agnes Catherine on 23 November 1873 in Jefferson County. By 31 October 1886, when their daughter Jennie was born, they were in Fannin County, Texas. Josephine (“Josie”) followed at Van Alstyne on 8 October 1888, and Willie, Rachel’s line, on 13 January 1891.

Amanda was born on 8 February 1850 in DeKalb County, Tennessee, very probably a daughter of Joseph and Nancy Pipkin. In 1850 an Amanda P. Pipkin, four months old and born in Tennessee, was living there in the household of Joseph Pipkin, 25, born in North Carolina, and Nancy C., 15, born in Tennessee. They were Rev. Joseph John Pipkin (1824–1895) and Nancy C. “Tennessee” Hayes Pipkin, who are said to have married in DeKalb County in 1849. Several of their other children were born in Liberty Township, St. Francois County, Missouri, between 1857 and 1872. Joseph is buried in the same Van Alstyne cemetery as Amanda, under the words “He died as he lived, a Christian.” The household, the age and the cemetery together make the parentage probable, though no one has yet found Amanda’s parents named.

Amanda died at Van Alstyne on 27 December 1899, two days after Christmas, aged 49. Willie was eight. James lived another eleven years and died on 26 November 1910 in the Monta community, the old Mantua neighborhood just over the Collin County line, the seminary town that the railroad bypassed. He was buried beside Amanda. Willie married Cleave Williams, a farmer’s son from the Shiloh country of Tennessee, and their daughter Melba was born at Van Alstyne in 1918.

Where Amanda's father came from is still an open question. A Pipkin family history follows a William Pipkin, born about 1787 in Wayne County, North Carolina, a grandson of Joseph and Susannah (Yeates) Pipkin, who moved with his wife Winnifred to DeKalb County, Tennessee, in 1841 and went on from there to Missouri. Joseph Pipkin, born in North Carolina about 1824, was in DeKalb County in 1850 with his young wife Nancy and the baby Amanda, and later had children in St. Francois County, Missouri. William and Winnifred fit as his parents in time and place, but no record yet names them as such.

stories.title: The Heffernans of Snake Creek and Winona
stories.hook: A boy who swam out after a drowning friend, a mother and son lost to consumption ten weeks apart, and a daughter who went out to teach a country school.
body: On a June evening in 1898 a fourteen-year-old named William Vondrashek went under while swimming off the Winona Lumber Company's mills. The next day's Winona Daily Herald ran the story under the headline "Search in Vain," with a second line for one of the boys who tried to save him: "Frank Heffernan Heroically Goes to the Rescue of the Drowning Boy and Narrowly Escaped Being Dragged Down Too." Frank, the paper said, "who is an apprentice boy in the Herald office, did succeed in getting hold of the drowning boy, but his struggles were so great that Hefferman could not hold him." Frank was fifteen. He was Nel Heffernan's older brother and the eldest son of John and Mary Heffernan.

Frank’s father, John H. Heffernan, was born in Limerick, Ireland, on 7 May 1862 and came to New York as a child. At seventeen he moved to Minnesota and lived on the Patrick Hickey farm at Snake Creek, near Kellogg. On 22 November 1881 he married Mary Helen Shea, daughter of the Watopa farmers Jerry and Ellen Shea. For four years the couple lived at Millville on the Zumbro, where John was a live-stock commission man. In 1885 they were nearby in Oakwood Township with Frank, two, and a baby, Ellen. That baby was Nel.

The family then moved to Winona, where they lived for sixteen years. John worked as "foreman and car inspector" on the Green Bay & Western, the railroad whose line ran from Green Bay to East Winona. Their everyday lives filled the Herald’s small print. In March 1899 "A woman to do general housework" was told to "apply to Frank Heffernan, at the Herald office." That May, Frank played second base for an East End nine. The same paper listed Nellie, Kate and Frank among the young people at a surprise party on East Wabasha Street, and in June it named Nellie in the cast of a school drama. On 6 September 1900 the personals reported that "Miss Nellie Heffernan has entered the Normal school," and that "Mrs. Jerry Shay of Wabasha" was in town visiting her daughter, Mrs. J. H. Heffernan.

Then the house was struck by consumption, the period name for tuberculosis. About 1900 Frank caught “a severe cold from which he never fully recovered,” and a year before his death “consumption began to develop and to its ravages he fell an easy prey.” He died at the family home on Saturday, 27 December 1902, aged twenty, and was buried from St. Thomas cathedral in St. Mary’s cemetery. He had “spent a good deal of his time” with his grandparents, Mr. and Mrs. Jerry Shea of Watopa. Ten weeks later, on 10 March 1903, his mother died “after an illness of several months from consumption.” Mary had been born at Watopa, and of her “large family of children,” one, “Miss Nellie, is a teacher in this county.”

Nellie was teaching at district 41, the Kinsella school in Oakwood Township, in the 1902–03 school year and again in 1903–04. By June 1905 the household in Winona had broken up. Loy, sixteen, was living at Watopa with his grandparents Jerry and Ellen Shea, his uncle P. W. Shea and his aunt Nellie, and Helen, twenty, was in the next household, that of Charles and Mary Graff.

John had come back to the Snake Creek country to rest his health, and Nel's wedding was held there. On 5 September 1906 she married James G. Canfield at St. Felix church in Wabasha, and afterwards the party went "to the home of the bride's father in Snake Creek" for the wedding dinner. Her sister Katheryn was bridesmaid, and John E. Ley of Highland stood with the groom. Katheryn later married Ley, and by 1910 she was living at Coaldale in Alberta. John spent his last four years at Kellogg, again in the live-stock business. He died there on 26 January 1910 of chronic bronchitis, with Mrs. James Canfield, Mrs. J. E. Ley, Lloyd, Maud and William "all at his bedside." His body was taken to Winona and buried in St. Mary's cemetery "beside those of his faithful wife."

stories.title: Jerry and Ellen Shea of Watopa
stories.hook: A Kerry farmer who came by way of St. Louis outlived two of his daughters on the Snake Creek farm.
body: When Jeremiah Shea was buried from St. Agnes church in Kellogg in November 1909, the Irish Standard summed up his life in a few lines: born in County Kerry in 1823, married in Ireland, emigrated "with his young wife, settling in St. Louis," and came to Minnesota about 1858 to farm in Watopa Township, "where he resided ever since." The Wabasha County Herald called him "one of the oldest settlers of Watopa." He was Nel Heffernan's grandfather, and his farm at Snake Creek was the place the Heffernan children went back to.

For forty years the Sheas stayed on the Watopa farm. In 1865 the household was Jerry, his wife, Patrick, Mary and Katy. In 1875 Jeremiah was 50 and Ellen 40, both Irish-born; Patrick, 18, had been born in Missouri, and Mary, 16, Catherine, 13, and the younger Ellen, 10, in Minnesota. Twenty years later Jerry, 69, and his wife still had Patrick, Kate and Ellie at home. In 1905 Jerry was 78, Ellen 68, Patrick 47 and Nellie 38, and their grandson Loy Heffernan was living with them.

Just when the Sheas came north is uncertain. Jeremiah was remembered as coming to Minnesota about 1858, and Mary as born at Watopa in March 1859, which fits her age in 1875. But Patrick was remembered as born at St. Louis on 2 July 1862 and a year old when the family came to Wabasha County, about 1863, and the family, it was said, lived first in Cook’s Valley before moving to the Snake Creek farm. His ages at home pointed instead to a birth about 1857, always in Missouri. The St. Louis years are certain; their dates are not.

Three daughters died before their brother. Mary, the eldest, married John Heffernan of Millville in 1881 and died of consumption in Winona in March 1903, ten weeks after her son Frank. Catherine was born in Watopa in February 1861. She married Daniel Sullivan of Highland, and the couple lived at Osage, Iowa, and then at Rochester, where he was "a locomotive fireman on the Great Western road." She died at Rochester on 2 March 1907, and her body was brought home to her parents' house in Watopa for a funeral at Kellogg and burial in St. Felix cemetery at Wabasha. A third daughter is remembered only in a count at Patrick’s death: “Three sisters are dead.”

Patrick, the only son, “remained at home to assist his aged parents, his mother being an invalid for many years.” On a January morning in 1914 he was found dead in bed. He had done business in Kellogg the day before and gone to bed “in his usual health.” He left his mother, Mrs. Ellen Shea, and “one sister, Miss Nellie Shea, who lives at home.” The Misses Mary and Sarah Holland came home for “the funeral of their cousin, the late P. W. Shea.” Holland cousins fit a mother born Ellen Holland, as she was remembered at Patrick’s death, better than the Holliham given for her when Mary died in 1903, though that is not certain. Nellie, the unmarried daughter, may be the Ellen Shea who died in Wabasha County in October 1941, but no one yet knows.

quotes.t: Mr. Shea was born in County Kerry, Ireland, in 1823. He was married in that country and emigrated to America with his young wife, settling in St. Louis. About 1858 he came to this state, and devoted himself to farming in Watopa.

stories.title: Three weddings and a stone at Sugar Creek
stories.hook: Rebecca Fails was first married at fifteen, in Mississippi in the autumn the Civil War ended. Sixty-one years later she was buried north of Soper under one stone with George Johnson, marked Father and Mother.
body: In Sugar Creek Cemetery, north of Soper in Choctaw County, one plain white stone stands for two people. JOHNSON runs across the top; below it, FATHER on one side and MOTHER on the other, the dates now weathered almost smooth. George Washington Johnson was born in Mississippi on 27 December 1851 and died at Soper on 17 February 1932, aged eighty; Marjorie Rebecca Fails Johnson was born in Jasper County, Mississippi, on 29 September 1849 and died at Soper on 1 November 1926, aged seventy-seven. They were the parents of Joel Anderson Johnson, the Boswell cattle buyer, and Rachel's great-great-great-grandparents.

George was Rebecca’s third husband. She is said to have married Peter Coleman Watters on 9 September 1865 in Smith County, Mississippi, the county just west of Jasper; William M. Farmer on 13 July 1869 in Williamson County, Texas; and George Washington Johnson about 1872, probably in Texas. If the first date is right, Rebecca was three weeks short of sixteen and the war had been over for five months. Her son by Watters, John Coleman Watters, was born in Milam County, Texas, on 10 July 1866, it seems, which would put her in Texas within a year of that wedding, though his small granite marker in Seminole County, Oklahoma, reads 1861–1926 rather than 1866–1927, and both cannot be right.

With George she had ten children, it is said: the first born in Milam County, four in Lee County, one more in Milam and the rest elsewhere in Texas. Lee County itself was new. The legislature created it in 1874 from pieces of Burleson, Washington, Bastrop and Fayette counties, and its farmers grew wheat, corn and some cotton, with cotton gaining ground after 1900. In 1880 George, twenty-nine, and Rebecca were in Lee County with five-year-old Joel. Nannie Lou was born there in 1883, or 1885 by her gravestone, and Sallie Mae on 9 May 1890, both to a mother remembered as Marjorie, or Margerie, Rebecca Fails. The youngest son, William Arthur, was born in Williamson County on 7 March 1893.

There were two George Washingtons in this family, and they are easily confused. Rebecca’s parents are said to have been Rayford Fail Sr. and Polly Anne Wallace of Milam County, and her brother George Washington Fails (1847–1923) married Margaret Ann Johnson in Milam County in 1870 and died there. So a George Washington Fails married a Johnson, and a Fails daughter married a George Washington Johnson. In 1870 George W. Johnson, with a Sarahann in his house, lived next door to George W. Failes in Milam County. They were two different men: Johnson was born about 1851 and died in Oklahoma in 1932, and Fails was born in 1847 and died in Milam County in 1923. Rebecca was very probably born a Fails, but whether she was Rayford and Polly’s daughter is not yet known.

George and Rebecca crossed the Red River too. In 1900 they were in the Choctaw Nation with Carl, Sallie and Arthur still at home, and they lived out their lives around Soper, the cotton town the Arkansas and Choctaw Railway had created in 1902. Some of the children stayed close. Elizabeth, called Penny, married a Cole, died at ninety-two in 1969, and is buried in Mount Olivet Cemetery at Hugo. Nannie Harrison died in 1964 and lies in Soper Cemetery. Joel was buried at Restland in Boswell in 1961. Others went much farther. Sallie, the wife of Sim Smith, died in 1981 and is buried at Byers in Clay County, Texas. Carl Albert died in 1976 at eighty-nine and is buried at Taft, in the oil country of Kern County, California. William Arthur died in January 1966 and lies at Palisade, in Mesa County, Colorado, under a stone that reads simply "Father." When Joel died in 1961, Penny, Nannie, Sallie, Carl and Arthur were among his survivors.

stories.title: Albert Tyson's son, and the father nobody can find
stories.hook: The seventeen-year-old in Albert Tyson's 1940 household came home from World War II as a private first class. Albert's own father is still unknown.
body: A small bronze marker in Restland Cemetery at Boswell reads: MARION O TYSON, PFC US ARMY, WORLD WAR II, MAY 27 1922, APR 20 1990. Marion Orville Tyson was the youngest person on Albert Tyson’s rented farm at Oakes in April 1940, a boy of seventeen living with his parents, two married sisters and their babies. He had been born at Boswell. On the family stone beside the bronze marker he is "Mutt" and "Daddy", next to his wife, Ruby Mae McKee (1924–2005).

His sisters' husbands served too. Joe Johnson, married first to Nettie and later to Opal, enlisted in May 1942 and spent the war in the 872nd Engineer Aviation Battalion. Marion turned twenty that May. So two of the young men in Albert Tyson's 1940 household circle came back as veterans, and both are buried at Restland under government markers.

Albert himself, perhaps Cornelius Albert Tyson, is harder to see. In 1940 he was sixty-five, born in Texas, had gone as far as the third grade, and was farming rented land; his wife Elizabeth was fifty-nine. Nettie was born in 1913, Opal at Sand Bluff in 1919 and Marion at Boswell in 1922, so the family was in Choctaw County by 1919. Albert is said to have died at Boswell in 1942, but no one has yet found his grave. Elizabeth’s maiden name is not known.

Albert’s father is sometimes named as a Cornelious Albert Ticen who died in 1883, but no one has yet found any trace of such a man, and the name looks borrowed from Albert’s own. One real Tyson did die in 1883, across the river in Texas. Henry Tyson, born in North Carolina in 1818, died on 28 April 1883 and was buried in a family graveyard on his farm near Cunningham, now the Tyson Cemetery in Red River County, beside his wife Elizabeth Freeman Tyson (1817–1877). His stone reads “Although he sleeps his memory doth live.” Cunningham, twenty miles southeast of Paris near the North Sulphur River, did not get a post office until 1912. Henry and Elizabeth were nearly sixty in 1875, and their known children, Eda Elvira (1840), A. W. (1854–1921) and Margaret L. Hardin (1859–1936), do not include an Albert. Nothing ties Albert to them, and his father is still unknown.

stories.title: Two Johns and two Maggies at Oak Ridge
stories.hook: The Frisch farm in Mount Vernon Township filled with children in the 1870s and 1880s, and Jacques and Anna gave two of their sons the name John.

quotes.t: steady, frugal Luxemburgers
quotes.c: History of Winona County, 1883, on the settlers of Mount Vernon Township

body: By 1875 the Frisches were settled in Mount Vernon Township, the township of Oak Ridge, whose people were mostly, in the words of the county history, “steady, frugal Luxemburgers.” Jacques and Anna, both born in Luxembourg and both forty, had seven children at home: Nicholas, 14; Mathias, 12; Maggie, 10; Anna, 8; John Peter, 6; Elisa, 4; and John, 2. Only Nicholas had been born in Luxembourg, which fits the family’s memory of reaching Winona in the summer of 1864 or 1865, after Jacques and Anna married at Beaufort in January 1862. The others were born in Minnesota.

Ten years later there were eleven Frisches in the house: Jacques, 47, and Annie, 48, with Nicholas, 22; Mathew, 20; Maggie, 18; Annie, 16; John S., 15; Elisa, 14; Johny, 12; Katherine, 10; and Virginia, 3. Katherine and Virginia had been born since 1875. Alois, the small son remembered in the Oak Ridge churchyard, was not among them in either year.

By 1895 Nicholas and Maggie had left home. Jacob, 56, and Anna, 57, lived with Matt, 27; Anna, 25; John P., 24; John, 21; Lizzie, 20; Katie, 18; and Virginia, 14. There had been two sons called John in the house all along: John Peter, 6, and John, 2, in 1875; John S., 15, and Johny, 12, in 1885; John P., 24, and John, 21, in 1895. They were different boys, brothers about three years apart.

That matters for the man remembered as John P. Frisch, born on 25 July 1873, the schoolteacher who married Maggie Haines in October 1901 and died in 1934. By age he was the younger John. In 1905 John, 31, was living with Maggie, 29, and Gertrude, 2, while his older brother, John P., 34, had a household of his own not far off, with Emma, 35, and three children aged 5, 3 and 1. The middle initial P. probably belonged to the elder brother, though no one yet knows for sure.

Gertrude, born about 1903, was the eldest of John and Maggie’s three children, and she was three when her mother died in 1906. When Viola died in 1975, her sister Gertrude Koetter survived her, and she was almost certainly the Gertrude Koetter, born Frisch on 7 June 1903, wife of Joseph Koetter, who died on 4 May 1984 and lies in lot 44 at Oak Ridge.

Katie, the second youngest, was 28 in 1905 and still at home with her widowed father. On 19 November 1907 Matthew Rivers, the Rollingstone postmaster’s son and his father’s assistant, married Kathryn, a daughter of Jacques Frisch. When her brother John died in 1934, “Mrs. Mathew Rivers, Rollingstone” was among his sisters. So Matthew’s wife was very probably Katie Frisch.

In 1905 Matt Frisch, 40, had a household of his own, with Annie, 36, born in Wisconsin of German parents, and children aged 7, 5 and 1, presumably his wife and children. Maggie Haines had a sister, Anna Haines Frisch (1869–1956), and a Wisconsin-born Annie of that age, with German-born parents, fits her well. If so, two Haines sisters married two Frisch brothers.

Maggie Frisch, who died in Winona County on 1 October 1906, had been born in Wisconsin about 1875 to a mother whose maiden name was Bill. That fits Margaret Bill, the wife of Christian Haines of Bill’s Valley, though it falls just short of proving that Maggie was their daughter. When Jacques died on 20 October 1906, his birthplace was given as Germany, though in life he had always been counted a Luxembourger.

The older children went their own ways. Nicholas, who died on 11 March 1926, and Mathew, who died in December 1938, have stories of their own. Virginia, the youngest, was born on 18 August 1881 and married J. B. Kronebusch, born in January 1881; she died on 4 May 1950 and he on 3 June 1959, and both are buried in lot 65 at Oak Ridge. What became of Maggie and Elisabeth is not known, and of Katherine little is known beyond her marriage to Matthew Rivers.

stories.title: Lizzie Rivers’s household at Rollingstone, 1875 to 1905
stories.hook: After Henry Rivers died in 1886, his widow Lizzie stayed on in Rollingstone with her sons, and with a Luxembourg-born George Rivers who was probably Henry’s younger brother.

quotes.t: business misunderstanding
quotes.c: Winona Daily Herald, 23 Jan. 1899, on the arrest of Henry Rivers at Avoca

body: Michel Rivers and Margaretha Adehm left Heffingen and Junglinster for Winona County in 1854. They are usually pictured with two sons, Henry and John B., the village’s two postmasters, but the family was probably larger. In 1865 Michael, Margaret, John B., Frank, George, Anne, Elizabeth and Henry Rivers were together in one household, it seems, and in 1875, in Norton Township, Michael, 70, and Margaretha, 66, had with them two more Luxembourg-born Riverses, Frank, 32, and George, 30, who were very probably their sons.

Henry had his own household at Rollingstone by 1875: Henry, 36, and Elizabeth, 24, with “J. P.,” 8, and Katharina, 4. Katharina was the Katherine born on 21 March 1871 whose own story is told separately. Who “J. P.” was is a mystery; nothing more is known of him.

Henry died in 1886, on 10 June by family reckoning, and that year J. B. Rivers succeeded “Hy.” Rivers as Rollingstone postmaster. Elizabeth, known as Lizzie, stayed on in the village, keeping a hotel and raising her sons. Edward, born in 1881, became Edward Rivers Sr., the rural mail carrier. There was another son as well, Henry, born after 1875. In 1895 Lizzie, 47, born in Luxembourg, was living in Rollingstone with Henry, 18, and Edward, 13; ten years later Elizabeth, 56, had Henry, 28, and Edward, 23, at home.

In 1905 the four were living with George Rivers, 61, born in Luxembourg, and in 1895 a Luxembourg-born George Rivers, 50, had been living right beside them. He was the right age and birthplace to be the George of the 1875 Norton household, which would make him Henry’s younger brother. How he was related to Elizabeth is not known. He may have married his brother’s widow, or he may have lived with her as brother-in-law and partner in the hotel. Where and when he died is still a mystery; it seems not to have been in Winona County, at least not before 1950.

Henry Jr. went out into the world. On 26 March 1896 the Rollingstone column of the Winona Daily Herald said Henry Rivers of Avoca was home visiting “his folks.” Three years later, on 20 and 23 January 1899, the same paper reported the arrest of Henry Rivers, agent at Avoca for the Peavey Elevator company, charged with taking more than 8,000 bushels of wheat since 27 October 1896. A Rollingstone relative, M. N. Rivers, told the paper the arrest was the result of a “business misunderstanding” and that Henry was at liberty through friends. How the matter ended is not known.

By 1900 a Henry Rivers was a machinery dealer at Rollingstone: in January he “again contracted” to handle Milwaukee binders and mowers, and by May his machinery store was nearly complete. The Avoca agent, the Rollingstone dealer and Elizabeth’s son were probably one man: the village treated him as one of its own, and he was living at home in 1905.

Elizabeth lived into her eighties. She died in Rollingstone Township on 12 January 1926, aged 81, a Luxembourger born Lehnertz and the widow of Henry Rivers. Her parents are said to have been Michael Lehnertz and Elisabeth Neuhegen. Her age was a moving target: she was 24 in 1875, was said at her death to have been born in 1845, and is remembered on her memorial as born on 23 July 1847.

stories.title: Twelve Johns children at Hart, and where Rose went
stories.hook: Jacob and Theresa Johns raised twelve children at Hart; over twenty years the house emptied, and Rose, the second youngest daughter, ended her days in Wright County.
body: Jacob and Theresa Johns had twelve children, in this order: Mary, Sophia, Lizzie, Emma, Annie, Jacob, Henry, Rose, Willie, Hannah, Eddie and George. Over twenty years their Hart Township house filled and emptied.

In 1885 Jacob was 44 and Theresa, born in Austria, 37, and at home were Mary, 14; Louisa, 12; Eliza, 10; Emma, 8; Anna, 6; Jacob, 4; Henry, 2; and Rosina, six months, the Louisa, Eliza and Rosina very likely being Sophia, Lizzie and Rose under other names. By 1895, with Jacob 59 and Theresa 46, there remained Sophia, 22; Anna, 16; Henry, 12; Rose, 10; William, 8; Johanna, 6; Edward, 4; and George, 2. By 1905 only the six youngest were at home: Henry, 22; Rosella, 20; William, 18; Johanna, 16; Edward, 13; and George, 12. A Jacob Johns, 24, and an Anna Johns, 26, both with a German-born father and an Austrian-born mother, were together elsewhere that year, very likely the brother and sister of 1885.

Rose, also Rosina or Rosella, lived a long life. When Johanna died in 1967, her sister Mrs. Rose Tiernan of Albertville survived her. Rosella E. Tiernan was born in Minnesota on 9 November 1884, just right for a baby of six months in the spring of 1885, to a mother born a Kriezer, another spelling of Kreuzer, and she died in Wright County on 28 January 1970. She was very probably the Rose of Hart.

Johanna was born on 11 November 1888, also to a Kreuzer mother. When she died in 1967 her brother George was in Canada, and five sisters and four brothers had already gone. Rose and George were the last of the twelve; little is known of most of the others.

In 1885 the old Jacob Johns, 84, lived in Hart Township with Rosina, 59, it seems a second wife, and two Missouri-born Johns men of the right age to be the younger Jacob’s brothers, August and Charles, farmed nearby with their own families. The family had lived seven years in Missouri before it reached Hart Township, but how August and Charles belonged to it is not known.

stories.title: Frances Canfield, schoolteacher of Cook’s Valley
stories.hook: One of the ten Canfield children taught school, outlived one husband and married a Pennsylvania teacher turned storekeeper, raising a new family in Cook’s Valley and Kellogg.

quotes.t: one of the early school teachers in Wabasha County
quotes.c: History of Wabasha County, 1920, on Frances Canfield

body: Frances Canfield was born in Pennsylvania, a daughter of John and Margaret (Greer) Canfield, who in 1855 settled at what became Canfield Springs, in Cook’s Valley, “being the first settlers in the upper part of the valley.” Frances was “one of ten children” and “one of the early school teachers in Wabasha County.” In 1865 she was at home in Highland with her brothers and sisters John, James, William, Elizabeth and Henry.

Frances married first George Calvin of Meadville, Pennsylvania, and they had one daughter. After Calvin died she married Martin H. Tobias in May 1876. Tobias, born on a Pennsylvania farm on 8 September 1849 to Simon and Elizabeth (Handshue) Tobias, had taught school in Pennsylvania and Ohio, drifted through St. Louis, Minneapolis, Chicago and southern Illinois, and then located at Plainview for a year or two of farm work and teaching. In spring 1874 he began sixteen months as a clerk in Robert Cochren’s hardware store at Kellogg, then farmed in Cook’s Valley until 1881 and lived retired in Kellogg afterward. He served as village recorder and for thirty years as justice of the peace of Greenfield. Frances died in 1895. She and Martin had six children, five of them living in 1920: Elizabeth, wife of John Bricher of Kellogg; Alta, wife of Curtis Siebe of California; Wilma, wife of Clifford Cloe of Montana; Harry M., who served in France with the 318th Engineers; and Ida E., wife of Forrest Cleveland of California.

Frances’s daughter by Calvin was Sarah Margaret, known by either name. She married first Bert Odell, and had two daughters, Vera and Bessie, and after his death she married, on 11 October 1904, the Kellogg furniture dealer Joseph C. Schierts. He had been born at Glasgow Township on 7 June 1876, the son of Joseph and Elizabeth (Rohler) Schierts. Sarah Margaret Schierts died in Wabasha County on 9 January 1928, and Joseph on 27 February 1965.
Martin Tobias, for thirty years Greenfield’s justice of the peace, lived out his retirement in Kellogg and very probably died in Wabasha County on 20 January 1922.

Of Frances’s brothers and sisters, little is known. A William Canfield, 33, born in Pennsylvania of Pennsylvania-born parents, was living at Greenfield in 1875 with a wife born in Ohio and three young sons; he may have been her brother William. Two Canfields who served in the Third Minnesota Infantry may have been brothers too.

stories.title: Sarah Hall and her sons: Greenfield to Prairie View
stories.hook: George W. Hall’s widow kept two Wabasha houses and raised three sons, one who settled at Greenfield, Minnesota, and two who went to Prairie View, Kansas.
body: George and Sarah Hall had four children. Anna was “the third child and only daughter,” and she married John A. Canfield of Kellogg and was dead by 1884. Her brothers were, in order of birth, Henry W., who settled at Greenfield, and William Parker and George W., who went to Prairie View, Kansas. Sarah was still living in 1884, and she kept the two adjoining Allegheny Street houses that George left in 1870.

In 1875 Sarah, 50, born in Pennsylvania of Pennsylvania-born parents, was living in Greenfield Township, Wabasha County, with her son Parker, 18, born in Iowa about 1857 during the family’s Muscatine years, before they came to Wabasha. Henry also settled at Greenfield, so the widow probably lived near him in the 1870s, though where Henry himself was then is not known.

Early in January 1866 the Wabashaw County Herald reported the annual festival of a parish school, held at Wright’s Hall before 165 children, where the rector received $25 and other gifts. On its roll of honor were Annie Hall and Parker Hall, and a third Hall whose first name is lost. George favored the Episcopal church, and these were probably his children, Anna, about ten, and her brother Parker, though just where the school was is not known.
Sarah may have followed her sons west in the end: she is said to have died at Almena, Kansas, in 1907. What became of Henry, Parker and George is not known.

stories.title: Arthur Beeman’s Winona parents
stories.hook: Arthur Oscar Beeman married Winnie Nelton in Winona; his own parents were very probably James and Luzinda Beeman, in whose house he was growing up by the age of four.
body: Arthur Oscar Beeman was the husband of Winnie Nelton and the father of Arthur Chester, Harold and Berniece, and he died in Winona on 19 January 1932. As a boy of four, in 1885, he was very probably the Arthur in the Winona household of James H. Beeman, 45, born in New York; Luzinda, 38, born in New York; James G., 14, born in Wisconsin; Charles H., 11, born in Minnesota; and Arthur, 4, born in Minnesota.

In 1895 James H., 57, and Lucinda E., 48, had Arthur, 14, at home, with James G., 24, close by. In 1905 Arthur, 24, the son of two New Yorkers, had a wife, Winnie, 22, and a little Arthur, 3, and with them, or right beside them, were James, 66, born in New York to an Irish-born father, and Lucinda, 58, whose parents were New Yorkers. James H. and Lucinda were very probably Arthur Oscar’s parents.

James George Beeman, very probably Arthur’s eldest brother, was born outside Minnesota on 19 February 1870 and died in Winona County on 20 April 1955, and his mother was a Thurber. So Lucinda was very probably born a Thurber.

Winnie A. Beeman herself was born in Minnesota on 4 March 1882, as her family remembered it, the daughter of a Zenk. Where and when James and Lucinda died is not known; it seems not to have been in Winona County. The middle brother may have been the Charles H. Beeman born in Minnesota on 22 December 1872 who died in Olmsted County on 24 August 1959, though no one knows for sure.

stories.title: Cleave Williams's four sisters
stories.hook: When Arch Williams died near Tom Bean in 1938, four of his sisters were still living, scattered from Van Alstyne to the new towns of West Texas.
body: Arch Williams, sixty-seven, died in a Sherman hospital on a Thursday evening in 1938, and after services at the Van Alstyne Baptist church he was buried in the town cemetery. He had been born in Tennessee on 27 November 1871, had come to Texas forty-seven years before and lived west of Tom Bean. He left three brothers, Bud and Cleve of Van Alstyne and John of Dallas, and four sisters: Mrs. J. M. Hulsey of Van Alstyne, Mrs. Lillie Fields of Hamlin, Mrs. Mollie Crocker of Brownfield and Mrs. Emma Rockford of Sherman. Cleve was Cleave Williams, Rachel’s great-great-grandfather. These were the sisters of the five brothers in the family photograph, and the four towns were where they lived.

Thomas Henry Williams and Rebecca Britton married, it is said, on 29 May 1869 in McNairy County, Tennessee, and the family remembers their children in this order: William H., called Bud, born in March 1870, within a year of the wedding; Arch, 28 November 1871, or the 27th; Callie, 4 September 1874; Mary Lee, called Molly, 20 May 1878 or 1880; Emma, May 1882; Lillie, 6 June 1886; Cleave, 1887; John, 1888; and George, 1 February 1891.

Callie, the eldest sister, married James M. Hulsey, born on 11 December 1868, who died on 1 January 1960. She outlived him by nearly twelve years and died on 19 November 1971, aged ninety-seven. Molly married Ell Crocker, a name that may be short for a longer one, on 10 July 1898 and had children from 1899 to 1919; the first, James Otis, was a ginner at Brownfield, where Molly was living in 1938. Lillie married Henry I. Fields, born on 13 February 1876, who died on 13 July 1945, and the Fieldses lived in Jones County, Texas, where Hamlin lies, in its northwest corner on the line with Fisher County. She died on 6 May 1961. Emma is the hardest of the four to see. She was Mrs. Emma Rockford of Sherman in 1938 and had been born in May 1882, and nothing more is known of her husband, her children or her death.

Both western towns were young. Hamlin was laid out in anticipation of the Kansas City, Mexico and Orient Railway, which reached it in 1906, and it had 2,406 people in 1940. Brownfield, the seat of Terry County forty miles southwest of Lubbock, was platted in 1903, got its railroad in 1917 and was incorporated in October 1920 with about 1,200 people. Two of Cleave's sisters were living in West Texas towns that were not yet forty years old when Arch died, a long way from the Tennessee farms where the older children were born and from the Grayson County cotton country where their brothers stayed.

Not everything the family remembers fits. Cleave’s wife, Willie Parker Williams, died a widow on 18 November 1974, and Tommy Williams, 1928–1964, very probably their son, is buried at Van Alstyne too. A family photograph, which the family dates to 1909, shows Mary Lee Williams Crocker holding a baby called Otis; but James Otis was born on 6 April 1899, and Molly’s youngest child before 1909 was Lillie Ruth, born on 1 August 1908, so either the photograph is older than its date or the baby was not Otis. A Thomas F. Williams, 1874–1923, lies with Thomas Henry and Rebecca at Van Alstyne; he is not remembered among their children, and 1874 is Callie’s birth year, so who he was is not known. Thomas Henry himself was born on 9 February 1847 by his stone, or in 1848 as the family has it.

The sisters’ dates come down through the family and may not all be exact, but the four women themselves, and the names they married into, are certain: all four were living when their brother Arch died in 1938.

stories.title: Moses McAfee and a marriage in Davidson County
stories.hook: By one family account, Dorcus McAfee Williams was the daughter of Moses McAfee, a Tennessee carpenter who married in Davidson County in 1798; that marriage is real, and the rest is still unconfirmed.
body: Dorcus Williams came down in the family as a McAfee, and the name is on her memorial, but who her parents were is not known for certain. By one family account she was the daughter of a Moses McAfee: born in Tennessee in 1807, married about 1833 to Thomas T. Williams, born in Alabama about 1810, and living in McNairy County in 1840 and still in 1870, dates said to come in part from a McAfee family Bible.

Moses, by that account, was born in 1776, died in 1846 and was a carpenter by trade, and he lies at Clear Creek near Stantonville, where Dorcus herself is said to be buried. He had two wives, said to have been sisters: Sarah Chamberlain, married on 23 November 1798, and Sally Chamberlain, married on 31 December 1800, both in Davidson County, Tennessee, where Nashville stands. One or both of their families came, it is said, from Chamberlain Creek in Georgia. His children are given as William (born 1803), Dorcus (1807), Catherine (1812), Jacob (22 February 1814 to 24 January 1881), Nancy J. (25 February 1818 to 25 December 1904), Sarah (1820), Susan (30 September 1825 to 3 February 1897) and Sally (1827). Several of them lived in McNairy and Hardin counties, and two of the daughters are said to lie in the cemeteries at Pisgah in Hardin County and Mount Olive in McNairy County.

One part of the story is certainly true: a Moses McAfee did marry a Sarah Chamberlin in Davidson County on 23 November 1798. That does not make him Dorcus’s father, and no one has yet found the second marriage, of December 1800.

Some of it fits. Moses’s son William, born in Tennessee in 1803, could well be the William McAfee, forty-seven, a Tennessee-born farmer who lived two doors from Thomas and Dorcas Williams in 1850; a brother living two doors from his sister is common enough, though a neighbor is not proof. The same family account ties the McAfees, Williamses and Brittons together. Nancy J. McAfee married Bartlett Greer on 1 July 1841; their daughter Nancy J. Greer married W. H. “Deck” Britton on 28 March 1870; and John Williams, Thomas Henry’s older brother, is said to have married, about 31 December 1900, Mary Kay Britton, a half-sister of a Britton called Doc. Rebecca Britton’s brother William H. was three in 1850, so a William H. Britton marrying in 1870 would be the right age, but whether he was the same man is not known.

How far to trust it is a fair question. The McAfee story seems to come from a single branch of the family, told more than once, so it is one family’s tradition rather than two independent memories. It also gives Thomas Henry Williams dates, 9 February 1848 and 23 December 1933, that differ from the 9 February 1847 and 25 December 1933 on his gravestone, and a wedding date for him and Rebecca, 29 May 1869 in McNairy County, that no one has yet confirmed. So Moses McAfee may have been Dorcus’s father, but for now that is only a possibility.

The same family history holds one more clue to where Moses came from. A parcel of land was sold as his share of the estate of a Thomas McAfee, in what its compiler called the only record of him found in Lincoln County, Tennessee. A share in an estate usually means a son or a grandson, so Thomas may well have been his father, but no will or settlement naming the heirs has been seen, and the date of the sale was illegible even to the compiler.

stories.title: Raford Fails's land in Jasper County
stories.hook: In 1857 a Raford Fails was granted land in Jasper County, Mississippi, and in 1859 a Raford Fail, in the county where the Fail children are said to have been born.
body: In 1857 a Raford Fails was granted land in Jasper County, Mississippi, in Township 2, Range 11, Section 7, and in 1859 a Raford Fail was granted land in the same section, one of eight people who took land there between 1857 and 1891. How much land each grant held, and what kind of grant it was, is not known.

The name was spelled every way. In Milam County, Texas, in 1870, the old North Carolinian of sixty was Raford Failes, and his descendants wrote Fail and Fails. Raford is an uncommon name, and a man of that name holding land in Jasper County in the 1850s fits the story of Rayford Fail, whose children are said to have been born in Jasper County between 1847 and 1863. It may have been one man or two, and a grant of land tells nothing of his family.

Other Fails lie in the county’s graves. L. Fail, 14 February 1818 to 10 October 1900, and S. M. Fail, 3 August 1833 to 26 June 1900, are buried at Bay Springs Cemetery; M. J. Fail, wife of L., 20 October 1823 to 20 April 1887, and J. H. Fail, 2 October 1859 to 4 January 1888, at Holder Cemetery on the highway east of Bay Springs; and E. M. Fail, 5 October 1875 to 17 July 1907, at Enon Cemetery nearby. L. Fail was twelve years younger than Rayford, and whether they were kin is not known, but not every Jasper County Fail need have belonged to the family that went to Texas.

So a man of the right name held land in Jasper County in the very years his children are said to have been born there, though nothing about the land tells of a wife or children. Rebecca Fails, said to have been born in Jasper County in 1849, married first in neighboring Smith County in 1865. Whether she was Rayford’s daughter is still not known.

stories.title: Two Georges, four doors apart
stories.hook: In June 1880 George W. Johnson and George Fails were farming four doors apart in Lee County, Texas, and in Johnson’s house were a thirteen-year-old stepson and two little daughters otherwise unknown.
body: On 23 June 1880 George W. Johnson, 29, a farmer born in Mississippi, was living in Precinct 4 of Lee County, Texas, with his wife, M. Rebecca, 29, also born in Mississippi, and five children, all born in Texas: John Waters, 13, counted as a son; Mary A., 6; Joel A., 5; Elizabeth, 3; and Margarett P., 1. A farm laborer, W. H. Bounds, 18, lived with them.

The thirteen-year-old was not a Johnson. He was, it seems, John Coleman Watters, Rebecca’s son by her first husband, Peter Coleman Watters, whom she is said to have married in Smith County, Mississippi, in 1865. Born in Milam County, Texas, on 10 July 1866, he was a few weeks short of fourteen that June, and he was living with his mother and stepfather. His small granite marker in Seminole County, Oklahoma, gives his birth as 1861, but the boy of 1880 was too young for that.

There were two little daughters who are otherwise unknown. Mary A., six, was born about 1874, and Margarett P., one, about 1879. Neither was at home with George and Rebecca in 1900, when Carl, Sallie and Arthur were, and neither was among Joel’s surviving brothers and sisters in 1961. They may have died young or married and gone; no one knows which. With the six who are known, they make eight of the ten children Rebecca is said to have borne George.

Four doors along lived George Fails, thirty-two, a farmer born in Mississippi, with his wife, M. A., thirty-three, born in Mississippi to Georgia-born parents, and their six-year-old son, Joel, born in Texas. George’s father had been born in North Carolina and his mother in Alabama, just as Rayford Fail and Polly Anne Wallace are said to have been. He was very probably George Washington Fail, Rayford’s eldest son, born in Mississippi in August 1847, who had married Margaret Ann Johnson in Milam County in 1870, and so Rebecca’s brother; M. A. would be Margaret Ann.

In 1870 George W. Johnson and George W. Failes had been next-door neighbors in Milam County, and ten years and one county later they were still within a few doors of each other. Neighbors who moved together like that were often kin or in-laws. A Fails who married a Johnson in 1870, and a Johnson who married a Fails about 1872, raise the question whether Margaret Ann Johnson was George W. Johnson’s sister. If she was, it would be a first clue to his own parents, but no one knows.

One thing does not fit. George Fails’s parents came from North Carolina and Alabama, as Rayford’s and Polly’s did, but Rebecca’s were both said to be Alabamians. If she was Rayford’s daughter, her father should have been a North Carolinian, like George’s. Perhaps she named the state where her father had lived longest, for Rayford’s own father is said to have died in Alabama in 1840, but the difference is real, and it leaves Rebecca’s descent from Rayford Fail and Polly Wallace uncertain, close as the two households stayed. Where George Johnson’s own parents were born is not known.

stories.title: Annie Haines, the second Haines bride on Oak Ridge
stories.hook: Two Frisch brothers from Oak Ridge married two young women from Wisconsin, and both women, it seems, were daughters of a mother born a Bill.
body: Maggie Haines Frisch had a sister, Anna Haines Frisch, and in 1905 Matt Frisch, 40, was living in Mount Vernon Township with an Annie, 36, born in Wisconsin to German-born parents, and three children: Gilbert, 7, Lorana, 5, and a one-year-old, Cleo. Annie was very probably that sister.

Annie Haines Frisch was born outside Minnesota on 25 October 1870, or perhaps on 25 November 1869, to a mother whose maiden name was Bill, the same as Maggie’s mother’s. She died in Olmsted County on 27 October 1956, at eighty-five or eighty-six, and lies at Oak Ridge in lot 24 beside Mathias Frisch, born 11 April 1865, who died of a heart attack in December 1938, on the 15th or the 18th.

Their children were born to a Haines mother. Gilbert Nicholas Frisch was born on 9 December 1898; Cleo, or Cleon Edward, was born in Winona County on 28 March 1904 and died in Wabasha County in February 1963; and Clarence John was born on 2 October 1912 and was buried in his parents’ lot when he died in 2000. A baby boy “of Mathias & Annie” died soon after birth, in 1904 or 1910. What became of Lorana, five in 1905, is not known.

Matt was certainly Jacques Frisch’s son. When his elder brother Nick married in September 1894, “Mr. Matt Frisch, brother of the bridegroom,” stood up with him, and in 1895 Matt, 27, was still at home with Jacob and Anna. He married Annie between 1895 and December 1898, perhaps across the river in Wisconsin, for the wedding seems not to have taken place in Winona County.

Annie and Maggie were each born in Wisconsin to German parents, each had a mother born a Bill, each was a Haines buried at Oak Ridge, and each married a son of Jacques Frisch. They were very probably sisters, and very probably two of the fourteen children of Christian and Margaret Bill Haines of Bill’s Valley, nine of whom were still living in 1917, though no one has yet found the girls named as their daughters. Annie outlived her sister by fifty years.

stories.title: Nick and John Peter: the older Frisch sons
stories.hook: Two of Jacques Frisch’s sons left the Oak Ridge farm in the 1890s: Nick, with a wedding dance that lasted into the small hours, and John Peter, the elder of the two brothers named John.
body: Nicholas, the only Frisch child born in Luxembourg, left his parents’ house in 1894 to marry. “Nick Frisch and Mary Burbach were married in the Catholic church of Oak Ridge by Rev. Schmitz, of Rollingstone,” the Winona Daily Herald’s Bethany column reported on 10 September; the wedding, it seems, was on the 4th. The attendants were “Mr. Matt Frisch, brother of the bridegroom, and Miss Katie Burbach, sister of the bride.” Afterward the families went to the home of Jos. Burbach, the bride’s father, for dinner, and the dancing and card playing went on “until the small hours of the morning.” The couple were to live on a farm.

Nick and Mary lie together at Oak Ridge, in lot 36: Nickolas Frisch, 1863 to 1926, and Mary Burback, 1864 to 1927. He very probably died in Winona County on 11 March 1926. They may also have been the Nicholas Frisch, 40, born in Germany, and Mary, 40, born in Wisconsin, who were living in Whitewater Township in 1905, though Nick was Luxembourg-born.

Of the two brothers named John, the elder was John Peter. He married Emma Kramer on 19 October 1897, and by 1905, at 34, he had Emma, 35, and three children, Lucille, 5, Waldemar, 3, and Alfred, 1. John Peter Frisch was born on 28 December 1870 and died in Wabasha County on 18 December 1949, at seventy-nine; Emma, born on 1 August 1869, died in Winona County in March 1938, on the 10th or the 11th. Their son Edward Waldemar, born on 3 February 1902, became the Reverend Waldemar Frisch, and he died in Nobles County on 10 November 1946, at forty-four.

Waldemar studied the classics and philosophy at St. Mary's College in Winona, took his bachelor's degree in 1932 and finished theology at the St. Paul Seminary, and Bishop Francis Kelly ordained him in the chapel of the College of Saint Teresa on 6 June 1936. He was assistant at St. Peter's in Caledonia until 1941 and at St. Felix in Wabasha until 28 April 1943, when he became pastor of St. Patrick's at West Albany with the mission of St. Clement at Hammond. A heart attack on 1 October 1945 and another on 16 March 1946 made him give up West Albany that April, and he spent the summer at St. Elizabeth's Hospital in Wabasha. After six months' rest he took the lighter parish of St. Mary's at Dundee, in Nobles County. On Sunday, 10 November 1946, when he did not come out for the morning Mass, his parishioners found him dead in bed. He was forty-four. His body lay in state at Holy Trinity in Rollingstone, and his brother, Father Alfred Frisch of Immaculate Conception at Conception, offered the requiem.

The younger brother, Rachel’s ancestor, born on 25 July 1873, is remembered at Oak Ridge simply as John, with his wife, Margarite Haines. So the “P.” of “John P. Frisch” very probably belonged to his elder brother. A John Frisch of Oak Ridge was engaged to teach the winter term of 1891; which of the two it was is not known.

The elder John was very probably also the J. P. Frisch who helped found the Altura State Bank. It was incorporated on 1 December 1910 by sixty men and opened on 23 December, and its first five directors were L. E. Kramer, M. Timm, Frank J. Kramer, Ferdinand Nelson and J. P. Frisch, “a well-to-do farmer.” J. P. Frisch, Wm. Reiland, Henry Kohner and Mike Jung were also among the incorporators. The Kramers ran the bank, with L. E. as president and Albert as cashier, and John Peter’s wife was a Kramer, though how Emma was related to them is not known.

Emma’s own parents are not known. Jacques’s daughter Maggie may also have married a Kramer. An Edward Kramer married a Maggie Frisch on 16 October 1894, and in 1905 Edward, 37, and Margaret, 36, were farming in Elba Township with Alsadie, 8, and Gregor, 4. Jacques’s Maggie, born about 1867, had left home before 1895 and is the right age, but Winona County had other Frisch families, and whether she was the bride is not known.

stories.title: Anna Nelton and the Knopp household
stories.hook: At fifteen Anna Nelton was living at home and, it seems, working in the Knopp house as well; four years later she married Joseph Knopp.
body: Anna Bertha Nelton, the eldest of the Minnesota-born Nelton children, was born on 7 June 1879 to George and Eda (Zenk) Nelton. In 1895 she was sixteen and living at home in Winona’s First Ward, but she seems also to have been working in another Winona house, that of Charles Knopp, 44, a Wisconsin-born man with a German-born wife, Amelia, and five children from Sam, 11, to Elsie, 2. Charles’s brother Joseph Knopp, 39, also Wisconsin-born, lived there too, and so, listed there at fifteen, did Anna Nelton, very probably as a hired girl in the house.

Charles and Joseph were brothers, sons of Michael Knopp. By his own account Michael was born in Westphalia on 13 March 1819, a stonecutter who sailed for America at twenty-three, cut wood and worked the Mississippi steamers, and then went overland to California. On reaching the Sacramento River in 1846 he enlisted in the United States Army and served seven months in the war with Mexico, for which he drew a Mexican War pension; he stayed on the Pacific coast about two years, mined a little, and, by his own account, built the first schoolhouse in Monterey. After a trip to the Sandwich Islands and a visit home to Germany he came back to farm in Sheboygan County, Wisconsin, ran a mill at Kewaunee, and moved to a farm in Winona Township in 1864. In 1895 Joseph “carries on agricultural pursuits in Winona County in partnership with his brother Charles.”

Michael’s marriage was a long one. He took Gertrude Doetsch, a German-born woman, as his wife on 6 May 1849, and they raised ten children, Charles first, born in Wisconsin on 8 April 1850. By 1895 nine were living: John, a contractor and builder in Winona; Mary, still at home; Gertrude, who had married Henry Felenger; Joseph; George, who worked the old homestead; Martha, the wife of Charles Richardson; William, in St. Paul; and Lena, a teacher. Jacob had drowned at the age of three. Michael, a Republican and a member of the Evangelical Church, was by then a retired farmer living in Winona, with the Winona Township farm he had bought in 1864 still his. Where in Germany the couple came from is told two ways: Westphalia, by Michael’s own account, which calls Gertrude only a native of Germany, or Nassau for both of them, by their son Charles’s.

Charles was fourteen when the family moved from Wisconsin to Minnesota. He worked beside his father until he was about thirty-three and then joined Joseph on the three hundred acres of section 30 in Winona Township, where he also grew fruit. On 2 February 1882 he married Amelia Roehning, born in Germany, and by 1895 they had five children, Samuel, Paul, Walter, Martha Mary and Elsie Elizabeth. A Democrat, he was for two terms chairman of the town board, then town clerk and constable, and he belonged to Friendship Lodge No. 98 of the Ancient Order of United Workmen and to Oak Grove Lodge No. 15 of the Order of Druids.

Joseph Knopp and Anna B. Nelton were married at Winona on 7 January 1899, or 1898 as the family remembered it at her death. By 1905 Joseph, now given as 44, headed his own household with Anna B., 26, Helen L., 4, and Joseph H., 1. Close by were three more Knopp children, Suella, Leon and Edward, with a German-born mother. They almost certainly belonged to Charles and Amelia, whose household was close by, and Leon and Edward’s mother was a Roening.

One of those boys, Edward C. Knopp, born in Winona on 30 June 1900, was very probably Edward Carl Knopp, the son of a Roening mother. He became a game warden, and in the autumn of 1928 he put himself forward as a nonpartisan candidate in the special primary of 30 October for state senator in the district, winning 774 votes, 12.48 percent, and losing. He died on 9 October 1974.

Anna and Joseph’s daughter Helen Laura Knopp was born in Winona County on 30 November 1900. Joseph Harold Knopp was born on 13 December 1903 and died in Winona County in December 1998, and Clarence A. Knopp, born on 28 February 1913, died in Hennepin County in 1992.
Joseph is harder to follow. His ages in 1895 and 1905, 39 and 44, are five years apart over a ten-year span, and he died on 1 December 1936.

Anna Bertha Knopp died at Community Memorial Hospital in Winona on the evening of Saturday, 2 March 1974, at ninety-four, after several years of illness. She still lived out on Winona Route 1, a widow for thirty-seven years. When her sister Winnie died in 1966, Anna Knopp was among the sisters who survived her, and Anna outlived every brother and sister remembered then.

Another sister, Lizzie, is a puzzle. When Winnie died, a sister Lizzie Plank was remembered among those who had gone before, and it is not known whether she was the Lizzie, 11, at home in 1895. An Alfred W. Plank was born in Minnesota on 30 August 1900 to a mother whose maiden name was Nelton, and died in Winona County in 1981. A Nelton mother named Plank, in Winona, at that date, fits Lizzie, then about sixteen, better than anyone else in the family. Still, no one knows for sure that she was his mother.

stories.title: George and Wilson, James Canfield’s brothers
stories.hook: James Garfield Canfield had two full brothers who outlived him. One stayed around Kellogg with his fast team; the other went north to run grain elevators and was once fired on as a burglar.
body: John A. Canfield had three sons by his first wife, Anna Hall: George, Wilson and James. James, Rachel’s ancestor, died at thirty in 1912. In 1895 all three were at home at Greenfield, George, 18, John W., or Wilson, 16, and James, 13, with their stepmother Anna and six younger half-brothers and half-sisters. Their own mother had died when James was five months old.

Wilson made the Wabasha County Herald in June 1899 under the headline “War at Kellogg.” A man in the hotel across from John Costello’s store saw a red light at the vault door near midnight, heard what sounded like burglars’ tools, and roused the village. Within fifteen minutes about thirty armed men had surrounded the building. A warning shot brought a man to the door, who fired a revolver at the crowd, and the crowd fired back. The “burglars” were the clerk, C. Cook, and Wils Canfield, developing Kodak plates by red light in the darkest corner of the store; the rattling tools were the bath pans. Cook took a charge of duck shot in the calves of his legs, and the paper added that “it was all his companion could do” to keep him from reloading. The Herald called it “a comedy of errors that might have had a tragic ending.”

Wilson followed his father into the grain trade, but farther away. A John W. Canfield, 26, born in Minnesota, was living in Hillsdale Township, Winona County, in 1905 with a Pearl L., 19; he was probably Wilson, though his parents were said to have been born in Pennsylvania. In August 1911 “Mrs. Wilson Canfield and children” left for Brandon, expecting to meet him at Minneapolis on the way to their new home. In September 1912 Harry Tobias of Kellogg went “to Brandon, Manitoba, Canada, to work in the elevator conducted by Wilson Canfield, formerly of Kellogg.” In 1913, when his stepmother died, he was at Brandon, and in 1915 J. W. Canfield, visiting relatives, was said to have “a lucrative position with an elevator company at Brandon” and reported crops “immense.” By October 1925 a Greenfield man travelling in North Dakota had met him at Carrington, where “Mr. and Mrs. Canfield and their seven children” were prospering. When his father died that November, Wilson was still at Carrington.

George stayed nearer home. In February 1900 he was back from Hayfield, Minnesota, where he, Joseph Eischen and William Keating had baled more than a hundred tons of hay. In June 1901 he “was up from Kellogg Tuesday with his fast team.” He served on committees for Modern Woodmen dances at Kellogg in 1901 and 1903, and the town of Greenfield elected him constable in 1903 and again in 1912. When his stepmother died in August 1913 he was “George, at home.” His father moved to Spooner, Wisconsin, in 1914, and by 1925 George was “of Spooner” too. A George Canfield of Plainview announced himself for sheriff in the 1906 Republican primary; whether that was this George is not known.
What became of the two brothers after 1925, in Wisconsin, North Dakota or Manitoba, is not known, nor much about Wilson’s wife and seven children.

stories.title: Michael and Katherine Reiland’s Rollingstone years
stories.hook: Schoolteacher, sewing-machine agent, juror, merchant, telephone man and, at sixty-four, a candidate for county office: Michael Reiland’s Rollingstone life was a busy one.
body: Katherine Rivers, born on 21 March 1871, was a daughter of Henry Rivers and Elizabeth Lehnertz. On 20 August 1891 she married Michael N. Reiland. His parents, Peter Reiland and Christine Krier, had come from Luxembourg and brought Michael from Wisconsin to Winona County in 1862, the year he was born, and developed a farm in Norton Township. Michael studied in Winona and at St. Francis College in Milwaukee, then taught for twelve years in Winona’s public schools before he moved into the dry-goods business at Rollingstone in 1892. He also served as village clerk and school treasurer. By 1913 he and Katherine had four children: Arthur taught school, Leonard worked in the Rollingstone grocery trade, Adelaide attended a domestic-science school in Sparta, Wisconsin, and Lorenda was still at home. Their lives place another Rivers household within the village’s schools and businesses, alongside the mail carrying, hotel keeping and retail work of their relatives.

In November 1891, eleven weeks after he married Katherine Rivers, M. N. Reiland of Rollingstone was engaged to teach the winter term in one of Winona County’s district schools. In February 1895 he was advertising as an agent for the “New Davis” sewing machine: “Drop a postal card and I will call. M. N. Reiland, Rollingstone, Minn.” In August 1899 his name was drawn for the petit jury.

In 1895 Michael, 30, born in Wisconsin, and Katie, 27, were at Rollingstone with Arthur, 3, and Leonard, 2. By 1905 the household was Michael, 43; Kate, 33; Arthur, 12; Leonard; Adelaide, 8; Lorenda, 3; and Peter Reiland, 82, born in Luxembourg, Michael’s widowed father, who had come to live with his son. Ten years before, a Peter Reiland, 74, had been living in Norton Township with a Mary, 25, and a Bertha, 23, who may have been his daughters.

The youngest, Lorenda, was born in Winona County on 11 or 12 November 1901, and her birth was registered under the name Laurentia. Leonard J. Reiland, born on 25 December 1893, died in Winona County on 14 November 1972, and Adelaide, born on 8 June 1897, died in Wabasha County on 22 April 1966.

Michael was a founder as well as a merchant. In January 1905 he put his name among the incorporators of the First State Bank of Rollingstone, and the bank’s cashier from 1907 was Andrew Rinn Jr. Three years later the two were partners again. On 26 September 1908 Michael, Rinn and Henry Speltz filed articles for the Rollingstone Telephone Company, with $10,000 in capital; Speltz was president, Michael vice-president and Rinn secretary-treasurer. In 1915 Michael was elected a director of the Southeastern Telephone Association at its annual meeting at the Zumbro Hotel in Rochester. By 1920 he was the company’s secretary. On 8 June of that year the state Railroad and Warehouse Commission let the company raise its business rates at Rollingstone by 50 cents and its rural multi-party rate by 25 cents a month, and refused any increase for residence lines. The company was incorporated again in February 1921 with $15,000, Speltz as president and Michael as secretary. It lasted until 1928, when the commission allowed the Winona County Telephone Company to buy it, together with the Mount Vernon Farmers Telephone Company and the Lewiston exchange. By then it was serving about 110 town and 236 rural telephones at Altura and Rollingstone.

Michael stayed in business at Rollingstone. In the spring of 1926, by then described as a Rollingstone merchant and “a public spirited citizen,” he ran for Winona County register of deeds, paying for notices in the Inter-County Press of St. Charles ahead of the 21 June primary: “Have tried to see as many of the voters as I could, but find that time does not permit me to see all personally.” How he fared at the polls is not known.

Michael and Katherine kept their golden wedding at Rollingstone on Saturday, 23 August 1941, beginning with the 7:30 Mass and holy communion, then a noon dinner for relatives and an open house all afternoon and evening. All four children came, with twelve grandchildren. Katherine had been born in the village and had lived there all her life; her one living brother was Edward Rivers Sr. Michael's three sisters came too: Maggie Kalmes of Winona, Anna Zeches of St. Charles and Mary Miller of Mazeppa.

He was then in his fiftieth year in the dry-goods trade. He had been one of the founders of the St. Nicholas Society and its secretary for fifty-four years, and when he died at home early on 4 December 1947, at eighty-six, after six months' illness, he was its last charter member. Katherine survived him; his son Arthur had died six weeks before. At his death Michael's birth was given as 6 April 1861 at Granville, Wisconsin.

Michael’s father very probably died in Winona County on 8 August 1914, at about ninety-one. In the autumn of 1947 the family lost two men within six weeks: Arthur P. Reiland died in Hennepin County on 24 October and Michael N. Reiland in Winona County on 4 December. Katherine may have followed them soon after; a Catherine Reiland died in Wabasha County, where Adelaide later died, on 22 January 1948, but whether she was Michael’s widow is not known.
