stories.title: Ralph Fails and a baby named Rebecca, 1850
stories.hook: In September 1850 a Fails family in Jasper County, Mississippi, had a baby daughter named Rebecca, not quite a year old.
body: In September 1850 Ralph Fails, thirty, a farmer born in North Carolina, was living in Jasper County, Mississippi, with Polly Anne Fails, twenty-five, also born in North Carolina. Neither could read or write, and they seem to have owned no land. Six children lived with them. Anderson, eight, John, six, and Margaret, five, had been born in North Carolina, and the two boys had been to school that year. James and George, both two, and Rebecca, one, were born in Mississippi.

This may well have been Raford Fail, who held land in Jasper County in 1857 and 1859. His wife’s name, Polly Anne, is the name the family gives Rayford Fail’s wife. A George born in Mississippi about 1848 fits George Washington Fail, said to have been born in Jasper County in August 1847, who in 1880 was living four doors from the Johnsons in Lee County, Texas. And the baby Rebecca fits Marjorie Rebecca Fails, born in Jasper County on 29 September 1849, who would have been a few weeks short of her first birthday that September.

Other things do not fit, and they matter. Rayford Fail was born on 16 March 1806, so in 1850 he should have been about forty-four, not thirty. His wife Polly Anne Wallace is said to have been born on 7 June 1814 in Dallas County, Alabama, but this Polly Anne was twenty-five and a North Carolinian, and in 1880 George Fails’s mother, and both of Rebecca’s parents, were said to be Alabamians. The name is a puzzle too: Ralph is not Raford, though a stranger meeting an unusual name could easily write down a familiar one.

There were also four children who are otherwise unknown. Rayford and Polly’s known children were George Washington, Young Rayford, Jeremiah Marsh, Thomas and Temperence, most of them born after 1850; Anderson, John, Margaret and James are strangers. They may have been Ralph’s children or a relative’s, or both, and the two boys of the same age, James and George, may have been twins or cousins. Their birthplaces show the family’s road: North Carolina until about 1845, Mississippi by about 1848. No Fail headed a household in Jasper County in 1840.

Ralph’s was not the only Fails household in the county. Not far away Priscilla Fails, forty-three and born in Georgia, headed a house of five children aged five to seventeen, all born in Alabama; whether she was kin to Ralph is not known. With the other Fails in the Jasper County graves, she is a reason not to assume that every Fails in the county belonged to the family that went to Texas.

What is certain is narrow but real. In 1850 a Fails man and his wife Polly Anne were raising a baby Rebecca in Jasper County, where Rebecca Fails Johnson is said to have been born the year before. They are the nearest anyone has yet come to her parents. But their ages and birthplaces are a poor match for Rayford and Polly, and whether Rebecca was their daughter is still not known, though it now seems more likely.

stories.title: Another Polly Ann Wallace
stories.hook: Polly Anne Wallace Fail is sometimes made a daughter of John Campbell Wallace of Fountain County, Indiana, but in 1860 that man had a Polly Ann Wallace of his own, living in his house.
body: Rayford Fail’s wife, Polly Anne Wallace, is said to have been born on 7 June 1814 in Dallas County, Alabama, and to have died in Texas in 1893. She is sometimes given a long ancestry: a father, John Campbell Wallace, born in Burke County, North Carolina, on 14 December 1782 and dead in Fountain County, Indiana, on 3 April 1869; a grandfather, Benjamin Wallace, who died at Casstown in Miami County, Ohio, in 1833; and a great-grandfather, Joseph Wallis Wallace. None of it rests on anything firm.

The Indiana man was real. In June 1860 John Wallace, seventy-seven, a gardener with $400 in personal property, born in North Carolina, lived in Van Buren Township, Fountain County, with Catharine, sixty-six, born in Pennsylvania, and Polly Ann Wallace, forty-seven, a weaver, born in Ohio. The next three households were Wallaces too: Harvey, thirty-four, a cooper and farmer born in Indiana, with a son John C., two; Joseph L., thirty-six, born in Ohio; and a farmer called Camel, or perhaps Campbell, forty-two, born in Ohio, with a son John C., seventeen. In 1830 a John Wallace in his forties headed a household of seven in the county, and in 1840 a John Wallace lived in its Jackson Township.

This John Wallace fits John Campbell Wallace well. He was born about 1783 in North Carolina, he lived in the county where John Campbell Wallace died, and his grandsons named John C. and a son who may have been Campbell point the same way. His Ohio-born sons fit a family that had lived in Ohio, where Benjamin Wallace is said to have died.

The trouble is the woman in his house. The Polly Ann Wallace of 1860 was forty-seven, born about 1813, almost exactly the age of Polly Anne Fail. She still went by Wallace, worked as a weaver and lived in Indiana; whether she was John’s daughter, a widowed daughter-in-law or another relative is not known. But Rayford Fail’s wife was not in Indiana. A Polly Anne Fails was in Jasper County, Mississippi, in 1850, and the family was in Texas from the late 1860s.

Who the Texas Polly’s parents were is not known. Even her birthplace shifts: North Carolina in 1850, if Ralph Fails’s wife was she, and Alabama in 1880, when her son George answered for her. Neither is the Ohio of the Indiana woman. Most likely two women named Polly Ann Wallace, born about the same year, have been run together, and the Texas Polly given the Indiana Polly’s family. That is only a guess, but it means the Wallace line above Polly Anne Fail cannot be trusted, and John Campbell Wallace, Benjamin Wallace and Joseph Wallis Wallace may be no kin of hers at all.

stories.title: Tenant farmers at Stantonville, 1860
stories.hook: Ten years on, Thomas and Dorcas Williams were renting land near Stantonville with the same six children, the youngest of them Cleave Williams’s father.
body: In September 1860 the Williams family was in McNairy County’s tenth civil district, whose families took their mail at Stantonville: Thomas Williams, fifty-one, a tenant farmer with $527 in personal property; Dorcas, fifty-six; and six children, Martha, twenty-six; Sarah, twenty-two; Catherine, nineteen; John, seventeen, a farm laborer who had been to school that year; Joseph, thirteen; and Thomas, eleven. Thomas, Dorcas, Martha and Sarah could not read or write. All of them, that year, were said to be Tennessee-born.

Ten years before, the same parents had had the same six children, in the same order: Martha, sixteen; Sarah, thirteen; Catharine, twelve; John, nine; Joseph, six; and Thomas, three. A family that holds together like that across ten years is one family, and Martha, Sarah, Catherine, John and Joseph were very probably the brothers and sisters of Thomas Henry Williams, the youngest, who took his family to Texas about 1891 and was Cleave Williams’s father.

The ages slip, as ages often did. Thomas the son should have been about thirteen, not eleven, and Joseph about sixteen. Dorcas aged fourteen years in ten, and her husband thirteen. The father’s birthplace moved too, from Alabama in 1850 to Tennessee in 1860. And his circumstances had changed. In 1850 he had owned land worth $150; in 1860 he was a tenant farmer, renting the ground he worked. Dorcas is said to be buried near Stantonville, at Clear Creek Cemetery.

A few miles away, in the ninth district at Monterey post office, lived a Jacob McAfee, forty-seven, a farmer born in Georgia, with Elizabeth, thirty-eight, and seven children from twenty-one down to three. Moses McAfee is said to have had a son Jacob, born on 22 February 1814, and a man of forty-seven in August 1860 would have been born about 1813. Georgia is harder to explain, since Moses married in Davidson County, Tennessee, in 1798 and Dorcas was born in Tennessee in 1807, though the family of Moses’s wives is said to have come from Georgia. Jacob may have been Dorcas’s brother, but no one knows.

What became of the five brothers and sisters after 1860 is not known. John is said to have married a Britton, which would make him one more link between the Williams and Britton families of the Shiloh country.

stories.title: One girl on the Britton place
stories.hook: Rebecca Britton remembered a slave of her own on her father’s Tennessee farm. In 1850 and 1860 a William Britton of Hardin County held one enslaved girl.
body: Rebecca Britton Williams remembered, as her granddaughter wrote it down, that her father was a wealthy planter who held slaves and that she had her own slave to dress her.

When the government counted enslaved people, it counted them under the names of the people who held them, by age, sex and color, and without names of their own. In 1850 a William Britton of Hardin County’s tenth civil district held one person: a Black girl of eight. In 1860 William Britton of the tenth district again held one person, a Black girl of sixteen, and there was one slave house on the place. An eight-year-old in 1850 would have been about eighteen in 1860, close enough that she may have been the same girl, but her name is not known.

In 1860 the slaveholder was very probably Rebecca’s father. That September he was sixty, taking his mail at the Hamburg post office in the tenth district, with Mary A., Rebecca J. and seven more children at home, and he was then the only William Britton heading a household in Hardin County. In 1850 it is less certain, for the tenth district then had two William Brittons: Rebecca’s father, fifty-five, born in Kentucky, and another William, forty-five, born in North Carolina, a few households away. Either could have been the man who held the girl of eight.

So Rebecca’s memory was true at its core, and also larger than life. Her father did, very probably, hold an enslaved person, a girl not far from Rebecca’s own age; Rebecca was ten in 1860. But one enslaved person, $1,000 in land and $2,500 in personal property do not make a great planter. William Britton was a farmer of middling means who held one young girl in slavery. Her name, and what became of her after the war, are not known.

Hamburg, where the family took its mail, is on the west bank of the Tennessee River, south of the county seat at Savannah. Rebecca remembered hearing the steamboats on the river as a child, and the family’s post office was a river town. Nineteen months after that September of 1860, the armies met at Shiloh Church.

stories.title: Dixon Fail, a Johnston County private at Fort Moultrie
stories.hook: At seventy-six Dixon Fail swore in a North Carolina courthouse that he had been on Sullivan’s Island when the British fleet attacked in 1776, and a kinsman remembered him coming home “naked, and covered with lice.”

subject.name: Dixon (Dickson) Fail
subject.rel: Possible ancestor on the Fails line

body: Dixon Fail was born about 1756. In 1776 he enlisted on Big Lynches Creek in South Carolina and served in Colonel William Thomson’s regiment of South Carolina Rangers, under a captain whose name comes down as Dollison, for eighteen months in all. He served at Camden, at Charleston and on Sullivan’s Island.

Sullivan’s Island was the scene of the battle of 28 June 1776, when a British fleet attacked the palmetto-log fort at the mouth of Charleston harbor, later named Fort Moultrie, and was driven off. Thomson’s Rangers held the island’s northern end against the British troops trying to cross from Long Island, and the defense of the fort became one of the first American victories of the war. Fail was there, he said, for the attack.

More than half a century later, on 28 August 1832, Dixon Faile, aged seventy-six and living in Johnston County, North Carolina, came before the county’s Court of Pleas and Quarter Sessions to claim a pension under the act of Congress passed that June. His claim needed witnesses. In an amended declaration of May 1833, John and Hardy Avera, said to be his nephews, vouched for his service, and one of them remembered seeing him come home from the army “naked, and covered with lice.” The government allowed him $60 a year as a private of the South Carolina line, from 4 March 1831. He signed with his mark.

He was still living when that amended declaration was made in 1833. The date sometimes given for his death, 28 August 1832, was really the day of his first declaration, when he was alive and seventy-six; and that age puts his birth about 1756, not on the 5 September 1760 sometimes given.

His place in Rachel’s line is less certain than his service. He is said to have been the father of William Dixon Fail (1778–1840), who married Elizabeth Bryan in Johnston County in 1804, and the grandfather of Rayford Fail (1806–1885), Rebecca Fails Johnson’s probable father. But whether William Dixon was Rayford’s father is not known, so the old soldier may or may not be Rachel’s ancestor.

stories.title: Levi Brittain, of McMinn County, in a Knox County deed
stories.hook: A deed recorded at Barbourville, Kentucky, on 29 November 1836 is the one sure trace of Levi Brittain, and it raises the old question of whether the William Britton of the Shiloh country was his son.
body: On 29 November 1836 a deed bearing the name of Levi Brittain was entered in the courthouse at Barbourville, Knox County, Kentucky. It called him “of McMinn County, Tennessee.” So the man who put his name to a Knox County deed was living, that year, in the East Tennessee valley, several days’ ride to the south.

He had been a grown man for forty years by then. In 1796 a Levi Brittain paid taxes in Lee County, Virginia, the far southwestern corner of the state beside Cumberland Gap, and the mountains between that tax roll and Knox County are the same mountains. Nancy Daniels, his wife, was born in South Carolina or Virginia about 1780 and was said to be eighty when she died in Knox County in August 1860. A copied family tree disagrees: it has her born about 1774, dead on 12 May 1853 and buried in the Brittain cemetery in Knox County, and it gives Levi a death in Claiborne County, Tennessee, before December 1851. No marriage record has turned up. The first child came in 1800, and a marriage about 1799 is simply the sum.

McMinn County held a handful of Brittains in the early 1830s, but Levi was not among them. Nathaniel was taxed on 160 acres in each of the years 1829 to 1832 and again in 1836. William held 224 acres, a John owned no land at all, and a William C. had a poll, then eighty acres, then seventy. No Brittain is buried in the county, and none left a will. The only Brittain marriage there before 1850 was William C.’s, to Jane Robison, in 1847. Whatever Levi was doing in McMinn, he left no tracks.

The children are easier to find than their father. Parks Daniels Brittain was born in 1800, and Nathaniel in 1804. George W. was born on 18 January 1810 in Knox County and married Kitty Moody on 11 July 1834; he died at Neosho, Missouri, in 1882. Archibald, born about 1812, married Martha Woods in Campbell County, Tennessee, in 1841 and died in Knox County on 23 July 1883 after two more marriages. America, born 1 August 1819, married Alexander Sevier at Barbourville in January 1836, the year of the deed, and lies in the Brittain family cemetery twenty-four miles from town.

A William is on the family list too, but his place in it does not settle. The William Britton who farmed in the Shiloh country of Hardin County, Tennessee, was fifty-five in 1850 and born in Kentucky, which puts his birth about 1795, four or five years before the supposed marriage. Either Nancy was older than her age at death suggests, or William was a half-brother or a cousin, or the list has borrowed a William from a neighbour. The deed does not say.

stories.note: Evidence: probable for the facts about Levi (deed, 1796 tax, McMinn tax lists) as reported by the lineage paper, whose author did not find a marriage record, a will or his death; lead for Levi as father of the William Britton (b. 1795) of Hardin Co. The paper names Nathaniel Brittain and Elizabeth Parks as his parents on circumstantial evidence only. CONFLICTS with the tree: tree has Levi b. 1768 Virginia, d. before 15 Dec 1851 Claiborne, Tennessee, and Nancy b. abt 1774 Louisiana(Louisa), Va., d. 12 May 1853 in the Brittain Cemetery, Knox Co., Ky.; the paper has Nancy age 80 in 1860, d. Aug 1860, b. 1780 South Carolina, and no Claiborne link. The paper also lists William second among the children (so b. about 1801-03), which contradicts the 1850 census age of the Hardin Co. William (b. about 1795). The paper's ages for Levi (b. by about 1775) and the 1796 tax date are inferences. I did not open the Knox Co. deed book or the 1860 census. (Find a Grave / KYGenWeb). The final paragraph about naming is interpretive and could be cut.

stories.title: Catherine Orris and the Orris farm at Ickesburg
stories.hook: Catherine Orris, who married Moses Hall and lived in Saville Township, Perry County, shares a name with the Ickesburg family that gave Princeton its Greek professor; nothing yet proves she belonged to it.
body: Catherine Orris was born on 12 December 1803 in Pennsylvania and died on 20 February 1860 in Perry County. She married Moses Hall, a Berks County man born in Albany Township in 1801, and their son George Washington Hall was born in Perry County on 6 December 1824, the boy who grew up to keep a furniture store in Wabasha, Minnesota. Moses died at Eshcol, in Saville Township, in June 1849. Where Catherine came from is not known.

In Saville Township, north of Ickesburg, there was an Orris farm, and its story begins before the Orrises. It had been the Nicholson place, and in 1763, in the Indian uprising that followed the French war, a party of settlers hurrying to help their neighbours was ambushed at the gap above the farm; five of them were killed. The Orris family took the land later, and the Orrises of the farm were two Adams, father and son, and three grandsons.

One of those sons was born at the farm near Ickesburg and left it for a classroom. S. Stanhope Orris was graduated at Princeton in 1862 and from its seminary in 1865, and he was ordained and preached at Spruce Creek before he spent a year in Germany. He taught Greek at Marietta College in Ohio from 1873 and at Princeton from 1877, where he held the new Ewing chair until 1902. He directed the American School of Classical Studies at Athens in the academic year 1889–90 by one account and 1888–89 by another, and he was a lifelong student of Plato. A stroke struck him in Hong Kong in 1903, a second at Harrisburg in 1904, and he died there on 17 December 1905. He had never married.

The family went to war too. His brother David C., called Captain, served in Company F of the 104th Pennsylvania, which fought at Fair Oaks and Malvern Hill, and was later a first lieutenant in a hundred-day company. Another Orris of the township, Nicholas I., of the Perry County company of the 47th Pennsylvania, was killed at Pleasant Hill, Louisiana, in the Red River campaign, far from Ickesburg. Whether these Orrises were Catherine’s nephews and cousins or only neighbours of the same name is the whole question; Saville was not a large township, and Catherine’s marriage to a Saville man makes it likely, but no one has put a will or a baptism on the table.
src: H. H. Hain, History of Perry County, Pennsylvania (1922): Saville Township, the Nicholson place and the Orris family (pp. 1048–1049); biography of S. Stanhope Orris (pp. 765–766); 104th Regiment Company F, 47th Regiment Company H and 100-day rolls (pp. 561–564 and neighbouring pages); Moses Hall as a signer of the 1833 Ickesburg tavern remonstrance (already cited on the Rachel site). stories.note: Evidence: lead. Proven: that an Orris family of Saville Township, Perry Co., produced S. Stanhope Orris, D. C. Orris and a Nicholas I. Orris; that Catherine Orris married Moses Hall of Saville. Nothing seen names Catherine's parents or links her to Adam Orris's family. DATE CONFLICT: Hain says S. Stanhope Orris was born 19 Feb 1832; Wikipedia mirrors say 1838 (Princeton class of 1862 fits 1838 better; the Wikipedia date is Princeton Alumni Weekly-derived, not opened). The story uses neither; add the year only after checking Princeton Alumni Weekly, 6 Jan 1906. The Athens directorship year also differs (Hain 1889-90; Wikipedia mirror 1888-89), both given. 'Brothers' is Hain's wording for the sons of Adam Orris Jr. (three sons: Capt. D. C., Dr. H. O. of Newport, Solomon Stanhope); the story calls them his brothers only in that sense, and Nicholas I. Orris's parents are unknown, so his link is not claimed. D. C. Orris appears in Hain both on the 104th Regiment Company F roll (Saville) and as 1st Lieut. of Company D, First Battalion 100-day men (Saville); the same man is assumed from the name and township. Nicholas I. Orris is on the roll of the 47th Regiment Company H list and in the 'killed at Pleasant Hill' sentence for that company (Hain p. 563-564); his regiment is read from the surrounding headings, so confirm in Bates. Next steps: Perry Co. will and deed indexes for Orris; Lutheran/Reformed church registers at Ickesburg/Eshcol; the 1850 census for Saville Township (Catherine Hall, a widow, and her neighbours); PAW 6 Jan 1906 obituary of Orris. Side N (Hall line) for consistency with the Hall stories.

stories.title: The White Church at Loysville
stories.hook: Moses Hall and the Orris young people were confirmed together at the log church in Sherman's Valley about 1821, three years before Moses and Catherine Orris had their first son.
body: The Halls and the Orrises went to the same white church. Lebanon Church stood at Loysville, in Tyrone Township, on two acres that Martin Bernheisel and Michael Loy had given for a church and a school. Some thirty Lutheran families and two or three German Reformed ones raised it in 1794 from big pine logs, each man with a team hauling his share on an appointed day. Zachariah Rice set out before dawn to bring the first log and arrived to find that Abraham Bower had beaten him by leaving his log partway there the evening before, which the neighbors thought hardly fair. In 1808 the logs were weatherboarded and painted white, and from then on the valley called it the White Church.

From June 1815 its pastor was the Rev. John William Heim, who rode a circuit of a dozen or more congregations across Perry, Juniata and Mifflin counties and preached at each, in German, about once in four weeks. Every three or four years he gathered the young people for catechism, and they came from miles around in large classes. In the spring of 1821, as near as anyone could later remember, he confirmed seventy-one of them at Loysville. Among the names that were recalled were Moses Hall, George Orris and two Orris girls whose first names had been forgotten. Moses was nineteen. Catherine Orris was seventeen; whether she was one of those two girls is not known. Three years later she and Moses had their first son, George Washington Hall, born on 6 December 1824.

Heim's own book of baptisms and confirmations did not survive him: after his death his papers were scattered and torn up, some of them used as wrapping paper, so the lists that come down were gathered from the memories of the old members when the congregation's history was written in 1862. That is why the class is dated with a question mark, and why fewer than a third of its names are known. An earlier class, confirmed at Lebanon Church on 9 December 1815, included a Daniel Hall and a Mrs. Hall; Daniel, who married Nancy Hartman and died in 1850, may have been kin to Moses, but nothing yet ties them together. Moses's father, John Hall, born in Albany Township, Berks County, in 1764, died at Loysville in April 1836. The old log church was sold in 1850 for eighty-three dollars, and on 20 September 1857 a brick church was dedicated in its place.

John Peter Frisch, the elder of the two Johns, marries Emma Kramer on 19 October, according to the county marriage index.
Gilbert Nicholas Frisch, eldest son of Matt Frisch and Annie Haines, is born on 9 December.
Anna Nelton marries Joseph Knopp in Winona on 7 January, according to the county marriage index.
Wils Canfield and a store clerk, developing photographs by red light in a Kellogg store, are taken for safe-blowers and fired on.
Wilson Canfield, formerly of Kellogg, is running a grain elevator at Brandon, Manitoba.
Michael N. Reiland, Rollingstone merchant, runs for Winona County register of deeds.
Annie Haines Frisch dies on 27 October; her death record, like her sister Maggie’s in 1906, names her mother as a Bill.
The census in Jasper County, Mississippi, lists Ralph and Polly Anne Fails with six children, the youngest a one-year-old Rebecca (14 Sept).
A John Wallace, 77, born in North Carolina, is enumerated in Fountain County, Indiana, with a Polly Ann Wallace, 47, born in Ohio, in his household (6 June).
Thomas and Dorcas Williams are tenant farmers near Stantonville, McNairy County, Tennessee, with six children, among them eleven-year-old Thomas (6 Sept).
The Hardin County slave schedule lists one enslaved girl of sixteen in the household of Wm Britton, Rebecca Britton's father, in the tenth district.
Michael Knopp marries Gertrude Doetsch on 6 May; their ten children include Charles, born in Wisconsin in 1850, and Joseph, who later farms with him near Winona.
The Altura State Bank is incorporated on 1 December by sixty men, with J. P. Frisch among its first five directors.
The First State Bank of Rollingstone is incorporated on 2 January; the incorporators include M. N. Reiland, Mathew and John Speltz, Frank Jung and Jacques Frisch.
Henry Speltz, M. N. Reiland and Andrew Rinn Jr. incorporate the Rollingstone Telephone Company on 26 September.
Anton Hoeneß of Trochtelfingen marries Genofeva Würz at Hörschwag in Hohenzollern.
Christian Hoeneß, later Christian Haines, is born on 11 October and baptized at Stetten unter Holstein in Hohenzollern, the son of Anton Hoeneß and Genofeva Würz.
Anton and Genofeva Hoeneß (Haines) bring their family from Hohenzollern to Herkimer, New York; Anton dies there about two years later.
A deed bearing the name of Levi Brittain, “of McMinn County, Tennessee,” is entered at Barbourville, Knox County, Kentucky, on 29 November.
Josip Klemenčić, 42, crosses to Baltimore on the München with his brother, bound for kin in Pittsburgh.
Tom Klensky (Anton Klemenčić) marries Hazel Stevens in Jackson County, Minnesota, on 3 August.
Evelyn Anna Kocak is born in Jackson County, Minnesota, on 15 February.
Evelyn Kocak and Henry Garms marry on 20 February at St. Joseph’s parsonage in Lakefield.
Dixon Faile, 76, of Johnston County, North Carolina, comes before the county court on 28 August to claim a Revolutionary War pension.
Settlers hurrying to help their neighbours are ambushed at the gap above the future Orris farm near Ickesburg; five are killed.
S. Stanhope Orris, born on the Orris farm at Ickesburg, dies at Harrisburg on 17 December, a Princeton professor of Greek.

17 July 1937 at Buckhorn, Oklahoma, not "about 1938".
24 July 1908 at Soper (draft card, obituary, headstone application), not "about 1909".

Her birth father was probably Anton "Tom" Klemenčić (Klensky), a Croatian-born farmhand in Minneota Township (probable; see his story). She was also known as Diane Antony.

fixes.who: Earls of Annandale, Lady Sophia Fairholm, "Sir" Brittains
fixes.fix: A former tree identified the Virginia William Johnston who reportedly died in 1778 as a son of the Marquess of Annandale and Sophia Fairholm. Westminster Abbey records their son Lord William died in 1721 at age 26. The parental links have been removed; the Virginia man’s birth and parents, and any connection to Rachel, remain unproved. https://www.westminster-abbey.org/abbey-commemorations/commemorations/sophia-fairholm-marchioness-of-annandale-sons
Born 20 Oct 1910 at Rollingstone, died 14 Jan 1980; son of Edward Rivers Sr. and Johanna Johns (draft card, obituary).

A 1949 death certificate is for Lee Hercules Bell, who died in 1949, and names his parents as Charles H. Bell and Clara Shelton. Whether that Charles is the father of Wayne Bell needs independent confirmation.
Mantua was a separate seminary town about five miles northwest of Anna, abandoned after the railroad bypassed it in 1872–73; it is not the same place as Anna.

fixes.who: Photos attached to David John Nelton
fixes.fix: Two different David Neltons appear in yearbooks. A younger David Nelton was a student at Winona High School in 1968–70 and appears in the 1974 Aldine of the College of St. Teresa; those photos are not Rachel's grandfather. The Holmen High School faculty portraits of 1969–73 are a different man: in 1969 he already held a B.S. in physics and a B.A. in English from Winona State College, while the younger David was still in high school. Rachel's grandfather, then 31 and living near Holmen by 1971, fits, and the family recalls him as an English teacher, so the Holmen portraits are attached to his story (probable). His obituary describes only his later YMCA job.

No record seen yet ties him to Joel Anderson Johnson or to Kentucky. A George Washington Fail, son of Rayford Fail, married a Margaret Ann Johnson in Milam County in 1870, so the two men may have been blended. Treat the parentage of Joel Anderson Johnson as a lead.
Find a Grave lists Margaret C. Osborne (1910 to 2002) as a child of Ernest and Augusta Brose, but Augusta was 53 in 1910 and Anna's 1928 obituary names no such sister. Treat as a misattached link.
Find a Grave gives Winifred's birth as 4 March 1882 and George John's as 17 January 1882, only seven weeks apart; one date is wrong.
Transcription says Monday 9 November 1928; death is 8 April 1928 (a Sunday), so the paper is dated 9 April.

Decatur (Tex.) High School, class of 1957, and Decatur Baptist College, per Army hometown releases in the Hugo Daily News (1958) and Durant Daily Democrat (1961). His 2024 obituary says Savoy, where his mother Nettie later lived and is buried.
Johnson (by 1937), McCarter (1958, Route 2, Sherman) and Tillery (1961 and at her death in 1980). Buried Sunnyside Cemetery, Savoy, Texas.

Birth: 28 Oct 1837, Beaufort (Beaufort parish baptism no. 56 of 1837, parents Nicolas Frisch and Maria Simon). This agrees with his 1906 memorial; the cemetery index’s 18 Oct 1836 is wrong. The frisch-1906 story’s "birth date remains uncertain" can be dropped.

The rivers-heffingen story says "an earlier Luxembourg form of the name has not been established." The 1832 Heffingen marriage register already writes "Rivers" (Michael Rivers, son of Johann Nicolas Rivers), so that sentence can go.

oak-ridge-frisch-church says the book "does not establish how the Speltz men were related to Annette." Peter and John Speltz were probably her brothers: Nicholas Speltz’s 1914 obituary names brothers Peter and John of Winona, and their mother is buried in the Frisch lot.
The Oak Ridge cemetery index gives "Wagoner" and 2 Dec 1799; her gravestone gives 2 Feb 1799, and Anna’s baptism and marriage name her as Catharina Michels.
Born 16 Oct 1807 at Junglinster (baptism), not just "1807, Luxembourg"; died 9 Oct 1884 at Rollingstone (gravestone). Her parents were Johann Adam, blacksmith, and Margaretha Michels.

No record supports a mother of George Nelton named Elsie, born about 1837. She is absent from all Minnesota state censuses 1865–1905, and the only Elsie in the records is George's daughter, born 1894–96. Mark as unverified, or remove her.

The birthplace 'Pommern, Cochem-Zell, Rheinland-Pfalz' has no record behind it. Records say Germany, so use 'Germany' until her death certificate or obituary gives more. Pomerania is the likelier meaning of 'Pommern'.
The headstone and Find a Grave give 1856; state censuses give ages 25 (1885), 40 (1895) and 48 (1905); the tree gives 30 Dec 1855. Leave the date but note the conflict.

Rename to Sarah Florence (Wilkinson) Bozarth Menton; she was born 8 Aug 1861 in Texas and died 28 Feb 1929 at Taylor, Williamson Co., Texas (Texas death certificate 13314; informant her son M. T. Bozarth). "Minton" in the 1920 census is a variant of Menton.

His sons' death certificates name their mother differently: Clara Snow (Lewis, 1955) and Clara Shelton (Lee, 1949). Her memorial gives Clara Jane Snow (1875-1902). Troy (12 Aug 1897) and Lee (4 Sep 1897) cannot both have those birth dates if both were Clara's.
No record supports this person, the name or the 1883 death date; it appears to be a copy of his son's name. Keep as tree only (lead) until a record names Albert Tyson's father.

fixes.who: Thomas T. Williams and Dorcas (McAfee) Williams
fixes.fix: The 1850 McNairy County census lists Thomas Williams, 38, born in Alabama, as farmer and head of household, with Dorcas, 42, born in Tennessee, and a son Thomas, 3. Thomas is Thomas Henry Williams's father and Dorcas his mother. The census age puts Thomas's birth about 1812, not 1808. Her McAfee maiden name is unproven, though a William McAfee lived two doors away.

fixes.who: William Britton and Mary A. Britton
fixes.fix: The 1850 and 1860 Hardin County censuses list William Britton (born in Kentucky about 1795–1800) and Mary (born about 1818) with Rebecca, aged 3/12 in 1850 and 11 in 1860. James (23) and Nancy (18) in 1850 were very likely from an earlier marriage. The middle initial 'H.', the 1866 death date, Mary's Patterson surname and her 'after 1880' death are not found in any record. The Levi Britton and Nancy Jane Daniels parentage and the 'Sir' Brittain line are unsupported.
His Van Alstyne gravestone gives his birth as 6 April 1844, not 1843.

The 'John Hefferman d. 1910 Wabasha Co.' lead is confirmed: his obituaries (Wabasha County Herald 27 Jan. 1910; Irish Standard 5 Feb. 1910) name Mrs. James Canfield and his other children. Update the sentence in nel-heffernan-canfield-miller that calls him untraced after 1903.
Frank was not a survivor after 1903: he died 27 Dec. 1902 in Winona, which explains why his mother's March 1903 notice names only five children.
John A. Canfield had three children with Anne Hall (George, Wilson, James), not only James; add George W. and John Wilson Canfield as James's full brothers.
Benjamin B. Wallace and John Campbell Wallace sit above Polly Anne Wallace Fail on Rachel's father's (J) side, not on the Canfield/Hall line; they were not researched in this N-side pass.

fixes.who: George Washington Johnson (I392657396086) and Marjorie Rebecca Fail (I392657396947)
fixes.fix: These tree records describe the same couple as Joel's parents X_joel_george_w_johnson and X_joel_m_rebecca_johnson (same dates on Find a Grave 57684474/57685052). This site now keeps one record for each of them, built on the census-backed records, with their parents left unlinked: the Kentucky (Jonathan T./Joel Johnson) chain is unproved and Rayford Fail/Polly Wallace as Rebecca's parents is a lead.

fixes.who: George Washington Fails (1847–1923) vs George Washington Johnson (1851–1932)
fixes.fix: Two different men: Fails, Rebecca's brother, married Margaret Ann Johnson in Milam Co. in 1870 and died in Milam Co.; Johnson married Rebecca about 1872 and died at Soper, Okla. Do not merge their dates or spouses.
Find a Grave memorial 58023629 gives 10 Jul 1866–6 Jun 1927, but the marker photographed there reads 1861–1926; an 1861 birth would predate Rebecca's 1865 Watters marriage. Not added to the tree.
Extracted birth index gives 9 May 1883; her gravestone memorial gives 1885.
No record found. Henry Tyson (1818 NC–28 Apr 1883), Tyson Cemetery, Red River Co., Tex., matches the 1883 death year only; his linked children do not include Albert. Keep as lead or remove.

Parents still unidentified. First child Willie Ben Bell born Red River Co., Tex., 1 Jun 1903 (Find a Grave 6689204), so the 1902 marriage may not be in Collin Co. Wayne Co., Ky., Baker marriages 1868–1873 (Andrew H. Baker–Martha Eads 1868; Isaac W. Baker–Burnetta J. Lair 1869; James H. Baker–Rebecca Jane Loveall 1869; C. W. Baker–Amanda J. Pate 1872; Thomas S. Baker–Eliza Corder 1873) are unlinked candidates only; her 1945 Texas death certificate is the record to get.

The Ancestry tree holds two copies each of Joseph Wallis Wallace (1720–1751), William Daniel Brittain (1649–1687) and Sir Thomas Brittain (1558–1636), with identical dates and places. This site keeps one record for each. The copies' extra parent links (to John Brittain and Hewgh Brittyen) are unverified and are noted on the kept records rather than shown in the tree.

The tree gives her birth in 1814 in Dallas County, Alabama, but Dallas County was not created until 1818, so the place can only mean the area later in that county. The birthplace has not been checked against a record.

Maggie Haines's marriage record names Christian Haines and Margareta Bill as her parents, so the link is no longer a lead. The record is dated 6 October 1901, while earlier stories give 1 October 1901 from the 1906 obituary's “fifth wedding anniversary”; both dates are kept until a county register is seen.
